title: Clinical Trials in Practice
text:
Preface
A compound that looked decisive on the bench can still turn out inert, unsafe, or no better than placebo in real people. Laboratory results do not settle what helps patients. The clinical studies that do are large, slow, expensive, and tightly regulated. There is no substitute for them.
A well-run trial can show that a treatment extends life or eases suffering. A poorly designed one can hide a real benefit, miss a serious harm, or burn years and produce nothing usable. When you account for failed programs and the decade of capital tied up along the way, bringing a drug to market costs billions of dollars (DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016).
The work is also getting harder. Trials enroll fewer patients, with tighter entry criteria, because the diseases are rarer or the treatments more selective, while the protocols grow denser: biomarkers, multiple arms, sites across many countries. Adaptive designs, Bayesian methods, and master protocols exist to meet that pressure. They work only when the planning and oversight are as serious as the mathematics.
This book treats clinical trials as science and as regulated operations, and it gives Phase III the most room, because that is where approval is won or lost. Methodology, operations, and technology are treated together, not as separate subjects. Where it turns to automation and AI, one test applies: the tool must stand up in an inspection. Without validation, governance, and a named person accountable for the decision, it does not belong.

title: Clinical Trials in Practice
text:
Who This Book Is For
Medical directors, study managers, and others in clinical development who need design, execution, and technology in one place. Investigators and site staff who want to understand what sponsors mean by quality. Students and managers deciding whether AI has a place in regulated research.

title: Clinical Trials in Practice
text:
Organization
Part I: Foundations covers how clinical research took its present shape, where a trial sits in drug development, the regulatory frame, and the ethics of research with human subjects.
Part II: Clinical Trial Phases takes up development economics and the aims, designs, and decision points from Phase I through Phase IV.
Part III: Phase III Deep Dive is the core of the book: confirmatory methods and the daily work of a study, from design and endpoints through sites, data, monitoring, safety, and documents, then the systems and automation underneath that work.
Part IV: Trial Completion and Beyond ends with closeout, the clinical study report, and submission: the last steps that decide whether years of clinical work become an approved medicine.

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.1 The Elixir Sulfanilamide Disaster (1937)
The rules that govern clinical trials were not written in the abstract. They were written after people were harmed. A liquid antibacterial mixed with a toxic solvent killed more than a hundred patients in 1937, many of them children. Nazi physicians ran experiments on concentration camp prisoners without consent. In Tuskegee, researchers watched syphilis progress in Black men for forty years and, once penicillin was the cure, kept it from them. Thalidomide left thousands of infants with ruined limbs after their mothers took it for morning sickness. Each failure forced a new protection into law or ethics: safety testing before marketing, voluntary consent, independent review, proof of efficacy. The protocols, monitors, and oversight committees of the modern trial are scar tissue from wounds inflicted on subjects who had no voice.
Sulfanilamide worked. To reach patients who had difficulty swallowing tablets, the S.E. Massengill Company dissolved the antibacterial in diethylene glycol, a sweet-tasting but toxic industrial solvent related to the ethylene glycol used in antifreeze. What followed was the first disaster to show that commercial drug manufacturing without safety testing could kill on a large scale (U.S. Department of Agriculture 1937).
The Secretary of Agriculture’s report to Congress traced the deaths to a gap in the law (U.S. Department of Agriculture 1937):
The chief chemist testified that no tests were made to determine the toxicity of either the separate ingredients or of the finished product (U.S. Department of Agriculture 1937). The “control laboratory” checked the elixir for appearance, flavor, and fragrance, not for safety. The formula used (see Table 1.1) was:
The product was labeled simply as “Elixir Sulfanilamide,” with no disclosure of diethylene glycol and no warning of danger, and most of it was administered on physicians’ prescriptions (U.S. Department of Agriculture 1937). Of the 240 gallons manufactured and distributed, all but about 6 gallons were recovered before they could be consumed; that small quantity was enough to kill, and the report to Congress counted 93 deaths in fifteen states as it was written in late 1937 (U.S. Department of Agriculture 1937). The final toll is generally put at more than 100 people, many of them children (Ballentine 1981).
Seizure had to rest on a technicality: the word “elixir” implies an alcoholic solution, but this product was a diethylene glycol solution. Had it been called a “solution,” no charge could have been brought.
Congress responded with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938, which for the first time required manufacturers to demonstrate the safety of new drugs before marketing them. The 1938 Act left the boundary between physician-prescribed and self-medication drugs unsettled; the Durham-Humphrey Amendment of 1951 fixed that line in statute, defining which drugs require a practitioner’s supervision and may be dispensed only on prescription (United States Congress 1951).

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.2 The Nuremberg Code (1947)
After the war, a U.S. military tribunal put 23 German physicians and administrators in the dock for war crimes and crimes against humanity, among them experiments on concentration camp prisoners, without consent, that caused suffering and death under the banner of medical science. Before naming who was guilty, the judges set down what lawful human research requires. That statement became the Nuremberg Code: ten principles forged in a criminal judgment (Nuremberg Military Tribunal 1949; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill 2024). The first principle is still the one that matters most: no one may be enrolled without free, informed consent. The rest follow from it. The study must be worth doing, the risks must not outrun the possible gain, the investigators must be competent, and the subject must be free to walk away. If the experiment turns harmful, the physician in charge must stop it.

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.3 The Thalidomide Tragedy (1961-1962)
FDA medical officer Dr. Frances Kelsey refused to approve thalidomide for marketing, citing insufficient safety data. The drug was already selling in Europe as a sedative for sleep and nausea, including morning sickness, and it caused severe birth defects, primarily phocomelia (limb malformations), in an estimated 10,000 infants worldwide. Kelsey’s refusal kept it off the U.S. market; about 17 birth-defect cases were still reported from investigational use.
The episode showed that proof of safety alone was not enough: drugs needed demonstrated efficacy, and there were still no systematic rules for studying drugs in pregnancy or for reporting adverse events. The Kefauver-Harris Drug Amendments of 1962 followed directly (see Figure 1.1). Manufacturers now had to prove efficacy as well as safety before marketing, and proof of efficacy had to rest on substantial evidence from adequate and well-controlled investigations: the statutory phrase that still anchors modern Phase III practice (Chapter 9). Clinical pharmacologist Louis Lasagna was among those who pressed Congress for that standard, testifying that adequately controlled drug comparisons were almost impossible to find under the old regime (Junod 2008). The Amendments also established the formal Investigational New Drug (IND) application. Clinical work had to be grounded in prior animal studies, adverse reactions had to be reported, and research subjects had to give informed consent.

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.4 The Declaration of Helsinki (1964)
The Nuremberg Code came out of a criminal judgment. The Declaration of Helsinki came from the medical profession itself: the World Medical Association (WMA) adopted it in 1964 as detailed ethical guidance for physicians conducting medical research (World Medical Association 2013). The 1964 text distinguished therapeutic from non-therapeutic research, required that studies rest on adequately performed laboratory and animal work and be conducted by scientifically qualified persons, and sharpened Nuremberg’s vague proportionality principle into a more operationalized standard: research risk must be outweighed by the scientific importance of the objective.
Several protections now regarded as central to the Declaration came later. Independent committee review of protocols before enrollment entered with the 1975 Tokyo revision, the conceptual ancestor of today’s ethics committees and IRBs; explicit obligations around trial registration and the publication of results, including negative findings, were strengthened in the revisions of the 2000s. Revision has continued, most recently in 2024 (World Medical Association 2025).

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.5 The Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932-1972)
Between 1932 and 1972, the U.S. Public Health Service conducted the Tuskegee Syphilis Study on approximately 600 low-income African-American men in rural Alabama (399 with syphilis and 201 controls without) to observe the natural progression of untreated syphilis. Participants were misled into believing they were being treated for “bad blood,” a local catch-all that obscured syphilis. After penicillin became standard therapy in the mid-1940s, researchers both withheld it and blocked men from getting treatment elsewhere. The study ran until it was exposed in 1972.

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.6 The Belmont Report (1979)
In response to Tuskegee and other ethical violations, the National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research produced the Belmont Report in 1979 (National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research 1979). Its three principles (Table 1.2) still guide clinical research:



Table 1.2: The Three Principles of the Belmont Report










Principle
Core Requirement
Application to Research




Respect for Persons
Individuals should be treated as autonomous agents; persons with diminished autonomy are entitled to protection
Informed consent: Subjects must voluntarily agree to participate with full understanding of risks, benefits, and alternatives. Vulnerable populations require additional protections.


Beneficence
Do not harm; maximize possible benefits and minimize possible harms
Risk-benefit assessment: Research risks must be reasonable in relation to anticipated benefits. Study design must maximize benefits and minimize risks.


Justice
Fair distribution of research burdens and benefits
Equitable subject selection: The selection of research subjects must be fair. Those who bear the burdens should potentially benefit. Vulnerable groups should not be exploited.






In the United States they became binding federal rules through the Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects, the Common Rule, adopted in 1991 and codified for HHS (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2024). It requires prior IRB review and approval, documented informed consent, and additional protections for pregnant women, prisoners, and children; at adoption it aligned those requirements across fifteen federal departments and agencies. For clinical investigations of drugs and devices, FDA imposes parallel obligations for informed consent and IRB review (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a, 2023b). The 2018 revision, among other changes, generally requires a single IRB for U.S. multi-site research funded by Common Rule agencies and a concise “key information” section at the start of consent forms. How IRBs exercise that authority is taken up in Chapter 4. Internationally, the Declaration of Helsinki and the CIOMS guidelines fill the corresponding ethical role.

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.7 ICH and Global Harmonization (1990s-Present)
Pharmaceutical development had gone global; its standards had not. The International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) was established in 1990 to bring together regulatory authorities and pharmaceutical industries from Europe, Japan, and the United States.

ICH E6 GCP
The ICH Guideline for Good Clinical Practice (E6) was first adopted in 1996 as an international ethical and scientific quality standard for designing, conducting, recording, and reporting clinical trials (International Council for Harmonisation 1996). It rests on the Declaration of Helsinki, and it starts where this chapter started: subject welfare takes priority over scientific objectives. Risks must be justified by expected benefits; trials need clear protocols, qualified investigators, and documented consent. E6(R2) in 2016 added risk-based monitoring and quality management (International Council for Harmonisation 2016). E6(R3) restructured GCP into Principles plus Annexes (Quality by Design, risk-proportionate oversight, decentralized trials, technology-neutral data standards); Principles and Annex 1 became effective in the EU on July 23, 2025, while Annex 2 (decentralized, pragmatic, and other non-traditional interventional trials) reached Step 4 in June 2026 and takes effect in the EU on January 15, 2027 (International Council for Harmonisation 2025b; European Medicines Agency 2024).

title: 1  Historical Context and Evolution
text:
1.8 Recent Developments (2020s)
COVID-19 forced sponsors and sites to improvise continuity (remote visits, local labs and care, shipment logistics, documented deviations), and FDA captured much of that practice in its public-health-emergency trial-conduct guidance (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021). What began as contingency stuck. FDA finalized digital health technology guidance for remote data acquisition in 2023 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023d), then in 2024 a framework for decentralized elements (telehealth, in-home visits, local healthcare providers, direct-to-participant investigational product, electronic consent) that treats decentralization as design choices, not a separate trial species (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024c).
Method and evidence rules moved with the operations. Adaptive designs, already framed by FDA’s 2019 guidance on pre-specified adaptations, integrity protections, and simulation of operating characteristics (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019), gained a draft international counterpart in ICH E20 (Step 2b, June 2025) (International Council for Harmonisation 2025a). Building on its 2010 device guidance (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2010), FDA’s January 2026 draft for drugs and biologics treats Bayesian primary inference, including borrowing from external information, as acceptable when sponsors pre-specify success criteria, justify priors, evaluate operating characteristics by simulation, plan sensitivity analyses for prior-data conflict, and document the work for review (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b).
Real-world data followed the same arc from permission to proof: 2023 guidance on using RWD/RWE for regulatory decisions (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023c), then 2024 expectations for EHR and claims sources that demand provenance, completeness, linkage quality, and outcome ascertainment (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b). Master protocols and platforms, accelerated in the pandemic, drew their own FDA guidance on governance and multiplicity, issued as a draft in December 2023 and revised in June 2026 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a).
Who gets into trials became a statutory fight. FDORA (2022) required Diversity Action Plans for trials that start enrolling more than 180 days after FDA finalizes its guidance on them; FDA’s 2024 draft said when and how (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a). After the January 2025 executive order on diversity programs, FDA pulled that draft from its website, restored it weeks later under court order, and then missed the statutory deadline to finalize it, so the requirement has yet to take effect (Grossi 2025). A December 2025 final guidance on trial participation, revising older eligibility-criteria advice under a different mandate, kept the demand for representative enrollment while dropping the “diversity” label (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025).
Oversight got more analytical. Risk-based quality management and centralized monitoring now lean on statistical signals and machine learning to prioritize sites and source review (Association of Clinical Research Organizations 2025). The same stack is used for protocol drafting, feasibility, safety triage, and TMF work, and whatever it produces still has to be validated, attributable, and inspectable (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023).
In Europe, the 2020s turned the Clinical Trials Regulation (2014) into working infrastructure. The Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS) became the single submission and coordinated-assessment channel for multinational trials; it went live on January 31, 2022, became mandatory for new applications on January 31, 2023, and finished transitioning legacy trials by January 31, 2025 (European Medicines Agency 2022).
Remote visits, CTIS portals, and model-assisted monitoring change how trials run. They do not change what the history in this chapter was for: keeping subjects from being harmed so that someone else can finish a study.

title: 2  Lifecycle of a Clinical Trial
text:
2.1 The Big Picture
The molecule that enters a Phase I trial has already survived years of discovery research and preclinical testing, and the Clinical Study Report that trial produces is just one element of a regulatory submission that synthesizes evidence across multiple studies. In between sits a sequence of interconnected stages, each with its own deliverables and regulatory checkpoints. This chapter maps that sequence from initial concept through regulatory approval, with pointers to the chapters that take each stage in depth.
Clinical development, the stretch of the arc in Figure 2.1 where human trials occur, typically spans many years and represents the largest single investment in bringing a drug to market (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018; DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016).

title: 2  Lifecycle of a Clinical Trial
text:
The Pipeline Misnomer
The linear “chevron” model (Figure 2.3) is a useful high-level roadmap and a “deeply engrained misnomer” that connotes a consistent, unidirectional flow (Wagner et al. 2018a). In reality, therapeutic development is a “diverse web of failure-prone iterative learning loops” traversed by scientists, physicians, regulators, payers, and patients.
The Forum on Drug Discovery, Development, and Translation of the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine proposed the Drug Discovery, Development and Deployment Map (4DM) to capture that complexity (see Figure 2.2). The 4DM replaces the pipeline with a set of interacting “neighborhoods” (the full map has eight; the simplified view here highlights five: basic science, biomarker development, clinical research, regulatory review, and the medical landscape) in which discoveries in one area can render earlier results irrelevant or open new shortcuts to later stages. The map captures this reality with “reiterative loops,” indicating that many “shots on goal” are often required before success is achieved at any step (Wagner et al. 2018a, 2018b).

Failure rates are not uniform across therapeutic areas. In the Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO)’s analysis of 2011-2020 development programs, the overall likelihood of approval (LOA) from Phase I was 5.3% for oncology versus 9.3% for non-oncology programs, with the largest attrition occurring at the Phase II transition (oncology Phase II-to-III success 24.6%) (Biotechnology Innovation Organization, QLS Advisors, and Informa Pharma Intelligence 2021). Oncology carries high scientific uncertainty, heterogeneous patient populations, and intense competition all at once. Academic analyses of trial outcomes reach a similar qualitative conclusion: oncology has among the lowest probabilities of advancing from early clinical testing to approval, even as biomarker-enriched programs can outperform historical averages (Wong, Siah, and Lo 2019).

2.3 Anatomy of a Phase III Trial
Phase III trials represent the largest investment and the highest operational complexity, and the lifecycle of a single one (Figure 2.4) is a template that applies, with variations, to earlier phases.






flowchart LR
    subgraph Planning["Planning & Design"]
        A1["Protocol Development"] --> A2["Statistical Design"]
        A2 --> A3["Site Selection"]
        A3 --> A4["Protocol Authorization<br/>(IND amendment / CTA)"]
    end
    
    subgraph Startup["Startup"]
        B1["Ethics/IRB Approval"] --> B2["Site Contracts"]
        B2 --> B3["Site Training"]
        B3 --> B4["Site Initiation"]
    end
    
    subgraph Execution["Execution"]
        C1["Recruitment"] --> C2["Treatment"] --> C3["Data Collection"]
        C4["Monitoring"]
        C1 -.-> C4
        C2 -.-> C4
        C3 -.-> C4
    end
    
    subgraph Closeout["Closeout & Reporting"]
        D1["Last Patient Visit"] --> D2["Database Lock"]
        D2 --> D3["Statistical Analysis"]
        D3 --> D4["CSR & Submission"]
    end
    
    Planning --> Startup --> Execution --> Closeout




Figure 2.4: Lifecycle of a Phase III clinical trial






Planning and Design
A poorly designed protocol creates problems that cannot be fixed during execution, which is why months of work precede the first enrollment. The protocol (the scientific and operational blueprint for the trial) specifies the objectives, design, patient population, treatments, assessments, endpoints, and analysis plan, and drafting it takes clinical, statistical, regulatory, and operational input.
Statistical design (Chapter 11) determines sample size, randomization scheme, and analysis approach, while adaptive and Bayesian methods (Chapter 12) extend it to platform trials and designs that update as data accumulate. Study design (Chapter 13) addresses the broader scientific architecture: parallel vs. crossover, superiority vs. non-inferiority, adaptive vs. fixed. When a concurrent randomized control is impractical, real-world evidence and external control arms (Chapter 14) offer an alternative source of comparison. Protocol benchmarks (Chapter 15) examines what makes a protocol operationally feasible.
Site selection (Chapter 18) identifies the investigators and institutions that will conduct the trial. Regulatory authorization for a Phase III protocol usually rides on an existing IND (as a protocol amendment) in the US, plus Clinical Trial Applications (CTAs) in countries that require them; a new IND is the exception, not the rule, by this stage.


Startup
Startup runs from regulatory approval to first patient enrollment, and it is one of the more variable and time-consuming phases to plan. The work includes obtaining ethics committee/IRB approval (Chapter 4), negotiating site contracts and budgets, training site staff on the protocol and systems, and conducting site initiation visits to verify readiness; the logistics and project management chapter (Chapter 20) covers the operational mechanics of site activation and vendor coordination. Recent Tufts CSDD benchmarking of site activation and patient enrollment gives sponsors reference metrics for setting realistic startup timelines (Lamberti et al. 2024).


Execution
Recruitment (Chapter 19) is frequently the most challenging operational element. Enrollment performance varies widely across studies and sites, and recruitment delays remain a leading cause of timeline slippage (Lamberti et al. 2024). Once patients are enrolled, randomization and blinding (Chapter 16) assign them to treatment arms while protecting the integrity of the comparison, and endpoints (Chapter 17) define what is measured and how success is determined.
Data management (Chapter 21) ensures that the information collected is accurate, complete, and ready for analysis, while monitoring (Chapter 22) provides oversight: verifying that sites are following the protocol, that data matches source documents, and that patient safety is protected. Safety (Chapter 23) is a continuous concern throughout execution, since adverse events must be identified, documented, and reported according to regulatory requirements.
The Clinical Trial IT Infrastructure chapter (Chapter 25) examines the technology systems that carry all of this: Electronic Data Capture (EDC), Clinical Trial Management Systems (CTMS), electronic Trial Master File (eTMF), and Randomization and Trial Supply Management (RTSM). The AI Agents in Clinical Development chapter (Chapter 26) explores how AI is beginning to change operational workflows.


Closeout and Reporting
After the last patient completes the last visit, closeout begins. Database lock freezes the data for analysis. Biostatisticians execute the pre-specified analysis plan. Medical writers prepare the Clinical Study Report (Chapter 28), the document that presents the trial’s findings.
The CSR becomes part of the regulatory submission (Chapter 29): the New Drug Application (NDA), Biologics License Application (BLA), or Marketing Authorization Application (MAA) that requests marketing authorization. The essential documents chapter (Chapter 24) covers the documentation requirements that must be maintained throughout and archived after the trial, and the closeout chapter (Chapter 27) addresses the operational side: site closeout visits, document archiving, and the administrative closure of the trial.

Regulatory compliance shapes everything from initial protocol design to long-term data retention. Ethics and patient protection requires informed consent and IRB oversight maintained from first participant to last. Quality and data integrity rests on adherence to the Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, and Accurate (ALCOA) principles. Economic constraints are the multi-billion-dollar investments that define the feasibility of modern clinical development.

title: 3  Regulatory Framework
text:
3.1 The Code of Federal Regulations
An investigational drug does not reach its first human subject in the United States until a sponsor has filed an Investigational New Drug (IND) application and either 30 days have passed since FDA received it without a clinical hold or FDA has told the sponsor the study may begin sooner. For most INDs, silence is permission. Much of the framework works that way: obligations fixed in advance, verified afterwards by inspection, with consequences that reach as far as debarment. The focus here is the United States, with the international requirements a multinational program must also satisfy.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates drugs, biologics, and medical devices (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b). It sits in the Department of Health and Human Services as part of the Public Health Service, alongside the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with a mission to protect public health by ensuring that regulated products are safe, effective, and not adulterated or misbranded.
Which scientific center holds jurisdiction over a product is a developer’s first question, because the center sets the requirements (Table 3.1):
The agency also works with numerous interagency partners, including the Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP) on clinical trial matters, NIH on scientific investigation, CDC on epidemiological matters, and the Department of Homeland Security on bioterrorism and food safety.
Clinical research rules are codified in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (21 CFR). It runs to thousands of pages; a few parts carry nearly all the weight for a trial.
Part 50 establishes what informed consent must include and how it must be documented (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023b). Potential participants must be told the purpose of the research, the procedures involved, the foreseeable risks and potential benefits, the available alternatives, and how their privacy will be protected. They must also be told that participation is entirely voluntary and that they can withdraw at any time without penalty.
That list is easy to satisfy on paper. Explaining a novel gene therapy to a patient with limited scientific background is not, and neither is obtaining meaningful consent from someone who is seriously ill and may see the trial as their best hope. The framework is in the regulation; the judgment is not.
No FDA-regulated clinical investigation begins until an Institutional Review Board (IRB) has reviewed and approved it, apart from narrow exceptions such as the emergency use of a test article, which need only be reported to the IRB within five working days (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023c). The IRB is an independent ethics committee of at least five members with diverse backgrounds, including scientific expertise and community representation. Its fundamental question is whether the research balances potential benefits against risks to participants appropriately; it also examines the equity of subject selection, the adequacy of the consent process, and the safeguards in place. Its authority is broad: it can require design modifications or additional protections, and it can refuse approval entirely.

The Clinical Trial Stakeholder Framework
Figure 3.1 shows how responsibility runs among the parties to a trial.

        Sponsor["Sponsor"]

        Subject["Research Subject"]
        IRB["IRB / Ethics Committee"]
    end

    Sponsor -->|Submits / holds IND| RA
    RA -->|Oversees; may inspect| Sponsor
    RA -->|May inspect| CRO
    RA -->|May inspect| PI
    RA -->|May inspect| IRB

    Sponsor -->|Selects, monitors| PI
    CRO -.->|Acts for sponsor| PI

Figure 3.1: Clinical Trial Stakeholder Relationships





The sponsor bears ultimate responsibility for the trial’s conduct and for regulatory compliance. Tasks can move to a CRO by written transfer; accountability for oversight does not move with them. The principal investigator runs the research at the site, obtaining informed consent and protecting participant safety, under the IRB’s independent ethical oversight. Over all of them, the regulatory authority may inspect sponsors, CROs, investigators, and IRBs, and can halt research that fails to protect participants adequately.


The IND Application (21 CFR Part 312)
Part 312 governs the IND, and arguably no part of the title matters more to a development program (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a). Without an IND in effect, there is no first dose.
Three sections carry the application. Chemistry, manufacturing, and controls describes what the drug is and how it is made, information critical to ensuring that every batch is consistent and safe. Pharmacology and toxicology summarizes the nonclinical studies (typically in animals) that support the safety of proceeding to human trials. The clinical protocol details exactly how the proposed study will be conducted.
Thirty days is the review window; absent a clinical hold, the sponsor proceeds. The arrangement trades a measure of regulatory control for the urgency of bringing new therapies to patients. Planned emergency research conducted without prospective informed consent under 21 CFR 50.24 is an exception: it needs a separate IND and may not start without FDA’s prior written authorization (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a, 2023b).
Part 11 sets the requirements for electronic records and signatures, with one goal: an electronic record should be as trustworthy as a paper one (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a). That means validated computer systems, secure audit trails that track every change to the data, controlled access, and electronic signatures that reliably identify the signer.






NotePart 11 in practice



Part 11 dates from 1997, but the FDA’s current approach focuses on the controls most directly related to data integrity. Not every electronic system requires the same level of validation; a risk-based approach guides compliance decisions.

title: 3  Regulatory Framework
section: 3.2 AI and Automation in a Regulated Trial
text:
3.2 AI and Automation in a Regulated Trial
The logic behind Part 11 (data integrity, traceability, accountability) now shapes how sponsors deploy AI and automation in clinical development. Most of that activity does not involve a model making an approval decision; it automates processes while keeping the evidence chain auditable.
Many high-volume regulatory deliverables are already partly automated through workflow systems: eTMF filing against the TMF Reference Model, query management, and risk-based quality management (RBQM) signals that support targeted monitoring. These can be rules engines plus machine-learning classifiers (e.g., document type classification, completeness checks) that cut manual effort while producing an inspectable audit trail (TMF Reference Model Initiative 2024; Association of Clinical Research Organizations 2025). This matters because inspection findings are frequently about process, not statistical methods: missing essential documents, inconsistent data corrections, inadequate oversight. Automation can reduce variance in execution, but only when it is controlled, validated, and monitored like any other regulated computerized system (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a).
Generative AI increasingly drafts narratives, summarizes deviations, and prepares sections of reports and submission documents. The regulatory risk is fluency itself: text that reads well can obscure uncertainty or introduce untraceable statements that do not faithfully reflect the source record (Messeri and Crockett 2024). Empirical work in clinical research document generation has highlighted compliance and factuality issues requiring governance, source linking, and review workflows (Wang et al. 2025).
Governance for AI-enabled workflows mirrors general risk management frameworks: define intended use, identify hazards (hallucinated facts, biased triage, missed signals), implement controls (retrieval with provenance, checklists, dual-review, monitoring), and document residual risk and responsibilities (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023). For AI/ML built into products such as medical devices, regulators and partner agencies have articulated Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) principles emphasizing lifecycle management and transparency, which translate well to internal clinical operations tooling (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Health Canada, and UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency 2021).
Regulators do not require sponsors to avoid AI; they require sponsors to manage risk. The posture is less “ban or bless” than “show your work”: keep the decision trace, keep the data lineage, and make it clear where humans remain accountable.

The filing is often not the first contact: a Pre-IND meeting commonly precedes it, where sponsors align development plans with FDA expectations (Figure 3.2).

Figure 3.2: The IND Application Process





Not every IND has the same purpose. A Commercial IND supports research aimed at marketing approval; a Research IND typically comes from an academic institution for non-commercial study. An Emergency IND permits use of an investigational drug when time is of the essence, and a Treatment IND gives broad pre-approval access to promising therapies for patients with serious conditions and no alternative options.
The Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act (FDORA), enacted in 2022, directs the FDA to require Diversity Action Plans for pivotal and Phase III studies that begin enrolling more than 180 days after its final implementing guidance is published (U.S. Congress 2022); the FDA’s draft implementing guidance called on sponsors to set enrollment goals for underrepresented populations (defined by race, ethnicity, sex, and age) and to describe how those goals would be met. That implementing guidance remains unsettled: the June 2024 Diversity Action Plans draft was withdrawn after a January 2025 executive order, restored by court order weeks later, and had not been finalized by its statutory deadline (Grossi 2025). A separate FDA guidance, the December 2025 final Enhancing Participation in Clinical Trials (a revision of the agency’s earlier eligibility-criteria guidance, issued under a different statutory mandate), retains recommendations for representative enrollment while dropping the earlier “diversity” framing (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025). The statutory mandate for Diversity Action Plans stands, though it takes effect only once that guidance is final, and the specifics of compliance, particularly sex- and gender-based enrollment goals, became genuinely contested in 2025, leaving diverse recruitment somewhere between an ethical best practice and a firm regulatory requirement.
The 21st Century Cures Act (2016) directed the FDA to establish a framework for using real-world evidence (RWE) (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018); subsequent guidance has expanded the role of data from electronic health records, registries, and wearables in supporting new indications and post-marketing safety studies, and, in some rare-disease programs, external or synthetic control arms.

title: 3  Regulatory Framework
text:
3.4 International Considerations
The International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) brings together regulatory authorities and pharmaceutical industries from the United States, European Union, Japan, and beyond to develop harmonized guidelines. Those guidelines are not law and bind nobody by themselves. Member countries adopt them, and that adoption has made them the de facto international standards for an enterprise that now runs trials across many countries and files submissions with agencies around the world.
Key guidelines (Table 3.2) include E6 on Good Clinical Practice, E8 on general considerations for clinical studies, E9 on statistical principles, and M4 on the Common Technical Document format for regulatory submissions.



Table 3.2: Key ICH Guidelines for Clinical Trials









Guideline
Topic




E6
Good Clinical Practice (R3 updates focus on Quality by Design & Data Governance)


E8
General Considerations for Clinical Studies (R1 introduces Quality by Design & Critical to Quality factors)


E9
Statistical Principles (R1 adds “Estimands” framework)


E2A
Clinical Safety Data Management


E3
Structure and Content of Clinical Study Reports


M4
Common Technical Document (CTD) Format for Regulatory Submissions







Regional Regulatory Frameworks
In the European Union, clinical trials are governed by the EU Clinical Trials Regulation 536/2014, applicable since January 2022. It introduced a single submission portal (the Clinical Trials Information System, or CTIS), harmonized assessment timelines across member states, and opened trial information to public access. For multinational sponsors, that replaced a fragmented process requiring a separate submission to each country.
Beyond the EU, major authorities include Japan’s Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA), China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), Health Canada, and Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA). Requirements differ, reflecting different healthcare systems, patient populations, and regulatory traditions, but the ICH guidelines give global programs a common foundation and let one body of clinical data support submissions in several jurisdictions.

title: 3  Regulatory Framework
text:
3.5 Good Clinical Practice
ICH E6 GCP is the international ethical and scientific quality standard for clinical trials (International Council for Harmonisation 2025b). The 2025 revision (R3) builds on the risk-based quality management that E6(R2) introduced in 2016 (International Council for Harmonisation 2016) with an explicit Quality by Design (QbD) approach, in which quality is built into the trial design from the outset through systematic identification of critical factors, risk assessment, and implementation of appropriate controls.
E6(R3) also adds requirements for data governance, since a modern trial draws data from electronic health records, wearables, patient-reported outcomes, and central laboratories, all needing appropriate controls throughout the data lifecycle. It presses for risk-proportionate oversight, letting sponsors match oversight intensity to each trial’s complexity and risk, and it addresses technology-enabled designs explicitly: decentralized trials, electronic consent, digital health technologies.
E6 assigns duties to three parties. The IRB or Independent Ethics Committee reviews and approves trial documents before research begins, then conducts continuing review and receives reports of safety events and protocol deviations. The investigator, typically a physician, conducts the trial according to GCP and the approved protocol, obtains informed consent from each participant, reports adverse events, and maintains accurate records. The sponsor, whether a pharmaceutical company, academic institution, or government agency, is responsible for the overall design and conduct of the trial: selecting qualified investigators, providing the investigational product, ensuring proper monitoring, and reporting safety information to regulatory authorities.
Investigators and sponsors must maintain essential documents throughout: the records that demonstrate GCP compliance and let an outsider verify the data independently. They accumulate chronologically: the protocol and investigator’s brochure at startup, consent forms and monitoring reports during conduct, final study reports and treatment allocation records at completion.






TipThe Trial Master File



All essential documents should be organized in a Trial Master File (TMF). The sponsor maintains a central file, while each investigator site maintains a site file. These records must be retained for years after the trial concludes. While historically ICH E6(R2) specified a minimum of two years following marketing approval or program discontinuation, the updated ICH E6(R3) (2025) framework defers to applicable regional regulatory requirements for the sponsor’s records and asks investigators to keep theirs for the regional period or until the sponsor says they are no longer needed, whichever is longer; in the United States, FDA 21 CFR 312.57(c) requires sponsors to retain records for a minimum of two years. That two-year minimum does not begin at study close: the clock runs from a trigger event (two years after the marketing application is approved, or after investigational shipments cease and FDA is notified), and other regions impose far longer periods: the EU Clinical Trials Regulation requires the trial master file to be archived for at least 25 years after the trial ends (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2014), so a trial with EU sites keeps its records for decades (see Chapter 24).

title: 3  Regulatory Framework
section: 3.6 Adaptive and Bayesian Trial Design: Regulatory Guidance
text:
3.6 Adaptive and Bayesian Trial Design: Regulatory Guidance
Adaptive and Bayesian designs were once negotiated one product at a time. Over the past decade that case-by-case practice hardened into published guidance defining what a sponsor must provide to use these approaches.

FDA Adaptive Design Guidance (2019)
FDA’s 2019 guidance on adaptive designs for drugs and biologics sorts adaptive modifications by how much they threaten the Type I error rate (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019). Non-comparative adaptations use pooled data without reference to treatment assignment, as in blinded sample-size re-estimation based on nuisance parameters like the overall variance or event rate; they carry little risk of inflating the false-positive rate and are generally acceptable when pre-specified. Comparative adaptations use interim results broken down by treatment group (even if the groups are labeled only A and B), including dropping doses or treatment arms and response-adaptive randomization, and they directly risk inflating Type I error and biasing the estimated treatment effect, so they demand rigorous, typically simulation-based justification and regulatory agreement in advance. (The “well-understood versus less well-understood” labels sometimes attached to adaptive designs come from the FDA’s superseded 2010 draft, not the 2019 guidance.)
Four principles run through the guidance:

Pre-specification. Adaptation rules must be written into the protocol and statistical analysis plan before enrollment begins. Unplanned changes prompted by comparative interim results make Type I error hard to control and the trial hard to interpret, however beneficial they look, so FDA strongly discourages making them without first meeting with the agency, unless patient safety requires immediate action.
Type I error control. The overall probability of a false-positive result across all adaptation points must be maintained at the pre-specified level, typically 5% (two-sided) or 2.5% (one-sided). Sponsors must demonstrate that control analytically or through simulation.
Operational integrity. Comparative interim results must be kept from the people managing and conducting the trial, through firewalled statistical teams and procedures that keep adaptive information away from anyone who can influence trial conduct. FDA generally recommends that no sponsor representative see them, although limited access for a few sponsor staff who take no other part in conducting or managing the trial can be justified, as for a dose-selection decision.
Reliable effect estimation. Controlling false positives is not enough; the design must also yield treatment-effect estimates and confidence intervals that the adaptation has not systematically biased. Adaptive selection and early stopping distort naive estimates, so the guidance expects sponsors to anticipate that and apply bias-adjusted estimation where needed.



FDA Bayesian Guidance
A Bayesian design raises a question of its own: how much of the evidence may come from outside the current trial. For medical devices, a 2010 guidance applies (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2010). For drugs and biologics, FDA issued a draft guidance in January 2026 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026); before it, the adaptive design guidance and Complex Innovative Design meeting interactions had established the operating norms (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019). The draft distinguishes Bayesian approaches used with Type I error control (calibrating the trial to a pre-specified frequentist error rate, with Bayesian machinery used for computational convenience) from those used without it (where an informative prior from prior studies or related evidence reduces the required evidence from the current trial, and the combined posterior probability is the decision criterion).
For the “without control” category, the draft frames the central question as whether the borrowed prior information is valid, reliable, and interpretable (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026). Several factors bear on that judgment: the quality and reliability of the contributing data, whether the prior is pre-specified, the relevance of the prior evidence to the current population and question, the rigor of the design of the studies that produced it, and the availability of patient-level data. An informative prior can reduce the evidence the current trial must supply on its own, but the draft is explicit that a design may skip calibration to a fixed Type I error rate only where the sponsor and FDA have agreed to that approach in advance. Even then, it cautions, the Type I error rate alone will not provide a complete assessment of the prior’s influence, which makes sensitivity analyses showing that the trial’s conclusions are not driven entirely by the prior essential.
The draft also addresses discounting: information borrowed from historical or prior studies should be discounted for the possibility that the historical and current populations differ (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026). Dynamic discounting, which automatically reduces borrowing when the current trial data diverge from the prior, is often chosen over static discounting (a fixed fraction) because it has better operating characteristics, such as less bias, when the populations do differ; the price is more parameters to specify, and the draft leaves the choice of method to case-by-case discussion with FDA.


ICH E20: International Harmonization
ICH E20, the first international harmonized guideline specifically addressing adaptive clinical trials, was released as a Step 2 draft in June 2025, and EMA’s public consultation on it closed in November 2025 (International Council for Harmonisation 2025a). It proposes common principles for judging adaptive designs across FDA, EMA, and the other ICH regions: pre-specified decision rules, simulation to characterize operating characteristics, appropriate error control. For a global program, E20 alignment should reduce the risk of region-specific redesign, but until the guideline is final the draft does not confirm regulatory acceptance of its contents, current regional guidance remains valid, and its section on Bayesian methods is not fully harmonized.






ImportantRegulatory engagement for adaptive designs



Engage regulators before the protocol for any novel adaptive design is final. For FDA that typically means a Type C meeting or similar interaction, at which the agency reviews the proposed adaptation rules, the simulation package, and the decision thresholds. Where the design uses Bayesian methods with informative priors or borrowing, agreement on the prior and discounting scheme should be reached before enrollment. Negotiating adaptive design choices after enrollment has begun is far harder.




Simulation as Regulatory Evidence
Both the FDA adaptive design guidance and ICH E20 treat simulation as the primary tool for demonstrating that a proposed adaptive design has acceptable operating characteristics, and FDA reviewers read a simulation package as they would statistical analysis code: for correctness, completeness, reproducibility. It should characterize four things:

Type I error rate: the probability of a false positive across a range of null scenarios, including those where the adaptation rule might inflate error
Power: the probability of correctly concluding efficacy across a range of true effect sizes and interim trajectories
Sample size distribution: expected and worst-case sample sizes under null and alternative scenarios, including those where adaptation causes substantial expansion
Bias: whether adaptive allocation or early stopping produces estimated effect sizes that systematically differ from the true treatment effect

Sponsors should plan to submit simulation code and seed values that allow FDA to reproduce results independently.

title: 3  Regulatory Framework
text:
3.7 Inspections and Enforcement
The regulatory framework has teeth. FDA inspections of clinical trial sites verify compliance and data integrity: routine inspections as part of a marketing application review and for-cause (also called directed) inspections triggered by specific concerns, such as a complaint or a problem identified during application review.
Following an inspection, the FDA classifies findings as NAI (no action indicated) when no objectionable conditions or practices are found, VAI (voluntary action indicated) when objectionable conditions are found but FDA leaves their correction to the site and recommends no action, or OAI (official action indicated) when FDA recommends regulatory or administrative action.
Serious violations can mean rejection of trial data from regulatory submissions, clinical holds on ongoing trials, and disqualification of investigators, which bars them from receiving investigational products and from conducting clinical investigations that support applications to FDA. In extreme cases involving fraud or egregious misconduct, criminal penalties are possible, and a conviction can lead to debarment, which bars the individual from providing services in any capacity to anyone with an approved or pending drug application.

title: 4  Ethical Principles
text:
4.1 Seven Requirements for Ethical Research
Clinical research asks people to accept risks and inconveniences not primarily for their own benefit, but so that future patients might have better treatments. The rules governing that arrangement emerged largely in response to abuse: the Nuremberg Code and the Belmont Report arose from the failures described in Chapter 1, while the Declaration of Helsinki built on the Nuremberg Code as the medical profession’s own statement of principles. But the absence of abuse is not the same thing as ethical research.
For many people, “ethical research” is synonymous with “informed consent.” Consent is essential. It is not sufficient: a scientifically worthless study remains unethical even if every participant provides exquisitely informed consent, because it exposes people to risks without any possibility of generating knowledge that could benefit others (Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady 2000).
Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady proposed seven requirements (Table 4.1) that clinical research must satisfy to be considered ethical (Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady 2000). Satisfying six is not enough.

4  Ethical Principles

title: 4  Ethical Principles
text:
Table 4.1: Emanuel’s Seven Requirements for Ethical Research











Requirement
Ethical Principle
Key Question
Example Application




1. Value
Research must have social or scientific value
Will this research improve health or increase understanding?
A study duplicating existing knowledge is unethical regardless of consent, as it exposes participants to risk without potential benefit.


2. Scientific Validity
Research must be methodologically rigorous
Is the study designed to answer its research question?
Underpowered studies that cannot detect meaningful effects cannot justify participant risks.


3. Fair Subject Selection
Burdens and benefits should be distributed fairly
Are subjects chosen for scientific reasons, not convenience or vulnerability?
Testing drugs only in young men while marketing to all populations violates this principle.


4. Favorable Risk-Benefit Ratio
Risks must be justified by potential benefits
Do potential benefits outweigh risks to participants and society?
High-risk procedures require proportionately important research questions.


5. Independent Review
Conflicts of interest must be managed through oversight
Has the research been reviewed by unaffiliated experts?
IRB approval is mandatory; investigators cannot approve their own studies.


6. Informed Consent
Participants must voluntarily agree with understanding
Do participants understand and freely agree?
Consent forms must be readable; participants can withdraw at any time.


7. Respect for Participants
Researchers have ongoing responsibilities
Are participants’ interests protected throughout and after the study?
Privacy must be maintained; participants should be informed of new findings.

title: 4  Ethical Principles
text:
4.2 Applying Ethical Principles
The seven requirements are easier to state than to apply. In practice they collide, and honoring one can mean compromising another.

Placebo Controls
Placebo controls are contentious wherever an effective treatment already exists, and most contentious where that treatment works, but imperfectly. A placebo-controlled trial often provides the clearest evidence of efficacy. It can also mean withholding a known-effective treatment from patients who need it.
The Declaration of Helsinki takes a strong position: new interventions should generally be tested against the best current proven intervention, not against placebo. However, placebo controls may be acceptable when no proven intervention exists, or when compelling methodological reasons require a placebo comparison and participants will not be subject to serious or irreversible harm (World Medical Association 2025).
Beneath the debate sits clinical equipoise, introduced by Benjamin Freedman in 1987 (Freedman 1987): randomizing patients between two arms is ethical only when the expert medical community is genuinely uncertain which arm is better. That uncertainty is the standard justification for assigning anyone to a control arm, placebo included. It is also perishable. As outcome data accumulate during a trial, equipoise can erode, which is precisely the situation that response-adaptive randomization exploits by shifting allocation toward the better-performing arm (Section 12.8). Judging when the accumulating evidence has disturbed equipoise enough to justify reallocating patients, or stopping the trial, is one of the central ethical decisions in adaptive design.


Vulnerable Populations
Vulnerable populations are not protected by being excluded from research: they too deserve therapies developed and tested in relevant populations (Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady 2000). What their vulnerability requires is safeguards matched to it, and Table 4.2 pairs each recognized vulnerability with the protections it triggers (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2024):



Table 4.2: Vulnerable Populations in Clinical Research











Population
Specific Vulnerability
Additional Protections Required
Ethical Consideration




Children
Cannot provide legal consent; may not understand research
Parental/guardian permission plus child assent when capable
Risks must be justified by direct benefit or minimal risk with generalizable knowledge


Pregnant Women
Risks extend to fetus
Preclinical and clinical data on pregnancy risks required
Research must minimize risk to fetus; consent must address fetal risks


Prisoners
Institutional coercion may compromise voluntariness
Research limited to the categories at 45 CFR 46.306(a)(2): incarceration and criminal behavior, prisons and prisoners as subjects of study, conditions particularly affecting prisoners, and practices likely to improve the subject’s own health
Payment and conditions must not be coercive


Cognitively Impaired
Reduced capacity for informed consent
Legally authorized representative consent; subject assent when possible
Ongoing assessment of capacity; respect for objection even if representative consented


Economically Disadvantaged
Payment may be unduly influential
Compensation must not be coercive
Payment for time/inconvenience appropriate; credit should accrue as the study progresses, with at most a small, non-coercive completion incentive








Research in Resource-Limited Settings
A trial run in a resource-limited setting by a sponsor based in a wealthier country raises two questions with no universal answer. The first is what the control group gets: the best treatment available globally, or the local standard of care. The second is what happens when the trial ends, and researchers must establish clear plans for post-study access to beneficial interventions (World Medical Association 2025). Both demand thoughtful engagement, and both come back to the same requirement: that the study leave the host population with tangible health benefits and long-term improvements, not merely exploit the community for data (Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) 2016).

title: 4  Ethical Principles
text:
4.3 Modern Ethical Challenges
Decentralized trials (DCTs) can collect patient data continuously, via wearables and smartphone apps. GPS location and sleep patterns carry re-identification risk, and they invite “function creep,” where data collected for one purpose becomes useful for another. Researchers must weigh the scientific value of that high-frequency record against the participant’s right to digital privacy (World Health Organization 2021).

Electronic informed consent (eConsent)
Electronic informed consent is now widely used in clinical investigations, and its multimedia tools (videos, quizzes) can improve a participant’s understanding. Digitizing the signature is not what makes it ethical. The ethical standard remains comprehension and voluntariness, while the operational standard extends to reliable documentation, auditability, and appropriate protections for privacy and participant autonomy (Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady 2000; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016, 2024a).
Remote consent in a decentralized or hybrid trial reduces travel burden and broadens access. It also increases the risk that participants with lower digital literacy, limited broadband access, or limited accessibility accommodations are systematically excluded. That is a fair subject selection concern: an operational convenience can become a structural enrollment bias unless alternative pathways are offered (Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady 2000; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b).






TipChecklist: eConsent Implementation (Ethics-Facing)




Use plain-language explanations and layered disclosure (short summary plus details), and verify comprehension (e.g., teach-back or comprehension checks); a completed “click-through” is not by itself evidence of understanding (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016).
Provide equivalent non-digital pathways (paper or staff-assisted workflows) to avoid excluding participants who cannot or prefer not to use digital tools (Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady 2000).
Specify identity verification, version control of consent content, and procedures for re-consent when new information emerges (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016).
Ensure documentation and auditability are suitable for regulated electronic records and signatures (e.g., validated systems, audit trails, access control, retention) (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a, 2024a).
Define privacy-by-design boundaries for any data collected during consent (device identifiers, contact methods, metadata) and ensure participants understand what is collected and why (World Health Organization 2021).





AI and automation in clinical research ethics
The ethical question about AI in a trial is rarely whether it is allowed. It is whether a particular use satisfies the same seven requirements that make any study ethical (Emanuel, Wendler, and Grady 2000). The same system that detects a safety signal earlier, assesses protocol feasibility better, or lowers site burden can also amplify bias, reduce participant understanding, and shift accountability in ways that are hard to justify.
Fair subject selection and justice. Recruitment algorithms trained on historical site performance, claims, or EHR data can reproduce inequities by systematically under-identifying eligible participants in under-resourced health systems or under-represented groups. Bias auditing should therefore be treated as an ethical safeguard, not an optional “model improvement” step (World Health Organization 2021; Saleiro et al. 2018). Dataset “datasheets” and model “cards” help make these limitations explicit to reviewers and users (Gebru et al. 2021; Mitchell et al. 2019).
Informed consent and understanding. If AI influences eligibility triage, monitoring intensity, or what a coordinator asks a participant to do (e.g., app-based prompts), then “what participants are consenting to” includes the role of automated systems. There is a risk that fluent, confident outputs create an illusion of understanding (among staff and participants) without reliable grounding in the source record or the evidence base (Messeri and Crockett 2024; Bender et al. 2021). Transparency therefore belongs in the consent conversation: what is automated, what is reviewed by humans, and how an error gets corrected.
Respect for participants (privacy, dignity, and autonomy). Continuous sensing and “always-on” monitoring can feel intrusive even when clinically informative. Ethical review should explicitly consider minimization (collect only what is necessary), proportionality (match intrusiveness to expected value), and participant control (pause/opt-out mechanisms) (World Health Organization 2021).
Accountability and governance. Who is answerable when an algorithm misclassifies, misses a safety signal, or increases burden for a subgroup? Regulators and professional bodies emphasize that AI should augment (not replace) clinician and researcher judgment (European Medicines Agency 2024) and that accountability for medical decisions remains human (World Medical Association 2025). Governance can be structured with risk management concepts (intended use, hazards, controls, monitoring) rather than marketing claims (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023; U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Health Canada, and UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency 2021).

title: 4  Ethical Principles
text:
4.4 The IRB in Practice
Independent review is the fifth of Emanuel’s seven requirements, and the IRB is where it happens. It does not happen once. A study comes back to the committee at least once a year while it runs, and again whenever a serious or unexpected event raises the question of whether it can continue safely (Table 4.3) (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023b):



Table 4.3: Types of IRB Review











Review Type
Timing
Purpose
IRB Action




Initial Review
Before research begins
Evaluate protocol for ethical compliance
Approve, require modifications, or disapprove research


Continuing Review
At least annually during study
Verify ongoing compliance and assess new information
Reapprove, require changes, suspend, or terminate


Modification Review
When protocol/consent changes proposed
Evaluate impact of changes on risk-benefit
Approve or disapprove modifications


Adverse Event Review
When serious/unexpected events occur
Assess whether study can continue safely
May require protocol changes, additional monitoring, or suspension


Final Review
At study completion
Close out study oversight
Document study completion and any findings












ImportantIRB Authority



The IRB’s authority is not advisory: it is decisive. Research cannot proceed without IRB approval. Except for changes necessary to eliminate immediate hazards, all modifications must be approved before implementation.

title: 5  Overview of Drug Development
text:
5.1 Development Path from Molecule to Medicine
Most compounds that reach human testing never make it to a pharmacy shelf. The ones that do have typically taken 10 to 15 years from laboratory discovery and billions of dollars to get there, and they can transform (and in many cases save) millions of lives.
The constraints accumulate. Biology is uncertain: a mechanism that looks compelling in cell culture may fail in animals, and a signal seen in Phase I or II may disappear in larger, more heterogeneous Phase III populations. Safety is non-negotiable, and rare adverse events can emerge only after thousands of exposures, forcing sponsors to design studies large enough to detect clinically meaningful risks. Manufacturing and quality systems must scale from milligrams in a lab to reproducible commercial production, with tight control of impurities, stability, and batch-to-batch consistency. And every step must be documented in a form that regulators can inspect and independently verify.
So the process is best thought of as a sequence of risk-reduction decisions. Early work asks “does it plausibly work and is it safe enough to test?” Later stages ask “does it work better than existing options, in the patients who will actually use it, with an acceptable benefit-risk profile?”
Development proceeds in stages (see Figure 5.1), each designed to answer a specific question and retire some of the uncertainty of working with a novel therapy.

Discovery comes first: researchers identify a biological target (a protein, receptor, or pathway involved in disease) and search for molecules that can interact with it. The search may mean screening thousands of compounds, designing molecules from structural knowledge, or modifying natural products with known activity.
Preclinical research then evaluates a promising compound in laboratory and animal studies. Three questions have to be answered before anyone is dosed: does the compound hit its target and produce the desired biological effect, what are its toxic effects in animals, and how is it absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and eliminated?
In the United States, the gate between preclinical and clinical development is the Investigational New Drug (IND) application to the FDA (see Chapter 3 for the full regulatory framework). The IND contains chemistry, manufacturing, and controls data; preclinical pharmacology and toxicology results; and the clinical protocol. FDA has 30 days to review the IND; if no clinical hold is placed, the sponsor may begin clinical trials (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024).

title: 5  Overview of Drug Development
text:
5.2 Understanding the Clinical Phases
Clinical development is traditionally divided into four phases, numbered I through IV. The designations are useful and a little misleading: the boundaries between phases are not sharp, and different types of studies may occur at various points in development.
The ICH E8(R1) guideline offers a complementary classification based on study objectives rather than timing, and the 2021 revision renamed three of the four categories that the original 1997 guideline had called “therapeutic exploratory,” “therapeutic confirmatory,” and “therapeutic use” (see Figure 5.2 and Table 5.1) (International Council for Harmonisation 2021). Human pharmacology studies assess tolerance, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics, and increasingly cover immunogenicity, tolerance in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, and cardiac toxicity. Exploratory studies explore efficacy, estimate doses, and evaluate biomarkers, patient-reported outcome measures, and adaptive designs. Confirmatory studies provide the definitive evidence of efficacy and safety for regulatory approval, and post-approval studies refine our understanding of the drug in clinical practice after marketing.

Human pharmacology does not stop at the end of Phase I: it continues throughout development as new formulations are tested, drug interactions are characterized, and effects in special populations are evaluated.
ICH E8(R1) also brings Quality by Design into clinical studies through Critical to Quality (CtQ) factors: those attributes of a study whose integrity is fundamental to protecting participants, to the reliability and interpretability of the results, and to the decisions made on the basis of those results (International Council for Harmonisation 2021). Which attributes those are depends on the study objective. For a Phase I first-in-human study, CtQ factors might include dose escalation safety rules and pharmacokinetic sampling accuracy; for a Phase III confirmatory trial, they typically include endpoint ascertainment, treatment adherence, and minimization of missing data. The guideline also encourages sponsors to build patient input into development planning, endpoint selection, and trial design, so that studies address outcomes meaningful to patients and the burden of participating is justified by the scientific objectives.

title: 5  Overview of Drug Development
text:
5.3 Regulatory Pathways
The standard path runs Phase I, II, and III trials, then a New Drug Application (NDA) or Biologics License Application (BLA) for FDA review. The agency targets 10 months for a standard review. Not every drug takes that path.
For drugs addressing serious conditions, the FDA offers expedited programs that can significantly reduce development time and regulatory burden. Fast Track designation provides more frequent FDA interaction and supports the rolling review of application sections for drugs aimed at an unmet medical need. Breakthrough Therapy status offers more intensive guidance for drugs showing substantial improvement over existing treatments, while Accelerated Approval allows marketing based on surrogate endpoints reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. Priority Review compresses the final agency review timeline from ten months to six for drugs representing significant advances in care.
These programs can be combined. Breakthrough Therapy designation already carries all of the Fast Track features, and most drugs holding either designation also receive priority review, significantly accelerating the path to patients.

title: 5  Overview of Drug Development
text:
5.4 The Target Product Profile
The Target Product Profile (TPP) is the label a sponsor intends to earn, written down before the data exist: the indication it will treat, the patient population that will use it, the dosing regimen, the claims that can be made about efficacy and safety, and how it will be positioned against competitors. It is not fixed in stone; it evolves as data accumulates and the commercial environment changes. What it buys is alignment. A development team that has agreed on the intended label can check every planned study against the data that label will require.

title: 5  Overview of Drug Development
text:
5.5 The Economics of Attrition
Drug development is an exercise in managing failure. Historic data indicated that only about 10% of drugs entering Phase I reached the market. More recent analysis from 2023-2024 shows overall success rates remaining at 6-7% as a composite probability across all phases, held up by higher stability in Phase I and Phase III and dragged down by Phase II, a formidable “valley of death” where nearly three-quarters of all programs fail (Table 5.2).



Table 5.2: Clinical Development Success Rates, 2020-2024 Averages (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025)










Stage
Success Rate (2020-2024)
Key Attrition Drivers




Phase I -> Phase II
~48%
Safety signals, toxicity, strategic portfolio pruning


Phase II -> Phase III
~28%
Primary bottleneck: Lack of efficacy, dose-response uncertainty


Phase III -> Submission
~54%
Failure to hit endpoints, safety signals in large populations


Submission -> Approval
~94%
Regulatory questions, manufacturing (CMC) issues


Overall: Clinic -> Market
~7%
Cumulative probability from Phase I start (composite success rate)






A Phase III failure is the expensive kind. By the time the program fails, the sponsor has typically invested several hundred million dollars and 5 to 7 years of clinical development (DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016), and those losses are ultimately borne by successful products and by investors. Chapter 6 takes up R&D costs and the economics of attrition in detail.
Attrition also falls unevenly across the industry. Emerging Biopharma (EBP) companies originate over half of all new drugs, and they face a significantly more difficult path to approval than their larger counterparts: they receive Complete Response Letters (CRLs) from the FDA more frequently (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025). In 2024, 70% of CRLs were issued for non-clinical reasons such as manufacturing quality, product quality, or chemistry data, but the EBP pattern is distinctive: since 2020, 41% of CRLs for EBP sponsors included clinical reasons, while the share of clinical CRLs for non-EBP companies has declined by 81% (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025). This suggests that EBPs, strong as they are at scientific innovation, often face challenges with both clinical evidence packages and the industrial-scale regulatory and quality infrastructure required to cross the final approval threshold.
Programs most often fail because the drug does not meet its primary outcomes, or because an unacceptable safety signal emerges during larger-scale testing. Failure can also be commercial, when market shifts leave a scientifically successful drug unable to compete with existing or emerging standards of care.

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.1 The Cost Structure
Clinical trials are expensive. The pivotal trials behind FDA’s 2015-2016 approvals had a median estimated cost of $19 million, and the costliest, a noninferiority trial with clinical-benefit endpoints, about $350 million (Moore et al. 2018). Bringing a new drug to market, counting the trials that fail along the way, requires an estimated $2.6-2.7 billion per approved drug over 10-15 years (Deloitte’s 2025 cohort average is $2.7B; the Tufts CSDD study’s capitalized estimate is $2.6B) (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2026; DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016). Historical success rates ran near 10%. The composite rate was 6% in 2023 and 7% in 2024, the improvement driven by Phase III (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025).
These economics shape every decision in drug development: which diseases a company pursues, where the trials are run, whether a sponsor builds internal capability or buys it from a CRO, and whether a small biotech partners with a large one or goes it alone. The science does not happen in isolation from the money.
Money enters the system from pharmaceutical and biotechnology sponsors, who fund the vast majority of research and treat each trial as an investment that must yield an approved product and eventually drive revenue. Much of this work is outsourced to Contract Research Organizations (CROs), which provide specialized services ranging from study design to data management in a market Grand View Research put at $59.6 billion in 2025 for healthcare CRO services (Grand View Research 2026), and which are also the largest end users of clinical trial software (Grand View Research 2025). The trials themselves are conducted at clinical sites, hospitals and private practices compensated for their resources and staff time, supported by specialized vendors providing everything from laboratory processing to data capture software. Patients remain the primary participants: often altruistic or hoping for therapeutic benefit, and bearing personal costs (travel expenses, time away from work) that are frequently invisible in formal trial budgets.
In the early 2000s, estimates pegged the total cost of bringing a drug to market at $800 million. Modern analysis paints a starker picture.
