title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
Stratospheric R&D Costs
The top 20 biopharma companies spent $7.7 billion on terminated trials for assets that failed during the 2024 analysis cycle alone (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2025). In Deloitte’s 2025 analysis of its cohort, the average cost to develop a drug from discovery to launch rose to $2.67 billion ($2,671 million, up from $2,229 million in 2024), and even that widely cited benchmark often underestimates the full economic burden of modern development (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2026). The Deloitte 2026 report finds a continued rebound in headline productivity, with a forecast internal rate of return (IRR) of 7.0% in 2025 (up from 5.9% in 2024 and 4.3% in 2023), driven largely by a few high-value GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP assets in late-stage pipelines. Without those assets the forecast IRR would be just 2.9% (down from 3.8% in 2024), so the rest of the pipeline weakened even as the headline improved. Average forecast peak sales per asset have also increased, to $598 million (from $510 million in 2024), though excluding GLP-1-based assets (mainly obesity and diabetes drugs) would drop this benchmark to $353 million (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2026).
Adding post-approval R&D (new indications, formulations, and post-marketing studies) raises the Tufts CSDD estimate to a lifecycle cost of $2.87 billion per approved drug in 2013 dollars (DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016). That figure bundles the actual cash spent on successful and failed projects alike, the heavy investment in the approximately 93-94% of compounds that never reach the market (the corollary of composite success rates of 6-7% (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025)), and the opportunity cost of tying up billions over a 10-15 year development horizon. For the scientific drivers of phase-by-phase attrition, see Chapter 5.
These widely cited cost estimates have been challenged in the academic literature. Avorn (2015) argued that the Tufts CSDD methodology overstates true development costs by including a large opportunity-cost-of-capital adjustment and by relying on confidential, self-reported industry data that cannot be independently verified. An alternative analysis by Prasad and Mailankody (2017), using publicly available data from oncology companies that brought a single drug to market, estimated the median out-of-pocket R&D cost at $648 million ($757 million once capitalized at a 7% cost of capital), less than a third of the Tufts mean, which is capitalized at a higher 10.5% rate. The debate remains unresolved because true R&D expenditures are proprietary, and methodological choices (which costs to include, how to allocate shared overhead, what discount rate to apply) drive large differences in headline figures. Any single cost-to-market number should be interpreted with attention to the assumptions behind it.
A sponsor must fund the successful drug and also provide enough “economic cover” for the nine others that failed. That is where the extreme pressure on clinical trial timelines and success rates comes from.
Cost rises with protocol complexity and enrollment size. In U.S. data from 2004 to 2012, not adjusted for inflation, the average study cost $1.4-6.6 million in Phase I (safety in small cohorts of 20-80 participants, with high per-patient costs from intensive PK/PD sampling), $7.0-19.6 million in Phase II (100-300 participants), and $11.5-52.9 million in Phase III, depending on the therapeutic area (Sertkaya et al. 2016). Among the pivotal trials behind FDA’s 2015-2016 approvals, the median estimated cost was $19 million; the costliest were noninferiority trials with clinical-benefit endpoints and trials that needed large populations to detect small effects or accrue rare events, at up to about $350 million (Moore et al. 2018).
The direct cost of operating a standard Phase II/III trial is approximately $40,000 per day (Z. P. Smith, DiMasi, and Getz 2024). The opportunity cost of a delay is larger still: for a newly launched drug, a lost day of sales now averages roughly $800,000 (about a fifth of the $4-5 million per day long assumed from 1990s blockbusters), rising by therapeutic area to a median of $1.3-1.4 million per day for cardiovascular and hematology products (Z. Smith, DiMasi, and Getz 2024).

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
section: 6.2 How AI and Automation Can Change Trial Economics
text:
6.2 How AI and Automation Can Change Trial Economics
The most expensive failure is the late failure. When Phase III fails, years of work and hundreds of millions of dollars are already sunk, and the “cost of failure” must be recovered by the few programs that succeed (DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016). If the economics of development are dominated by timelines and failure, then the economic value of AI is primarily indirect: it comes from shifting when and how confidently sponsors make decisions, and from reducing high-friction operational work that does not add scientific value. AI cannot eliminate biological uncertainty, but it can support earlier termination of low-probability programs by improving evidence synthesis across preclinical, translational, and early clinical signals, especially when combined with more structured protocols and better data integration. Even modest improvements in decision timing can have large economic consequences because capital is tied up for a decade or more, and because time-to-market directly affects expected returns (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2025).
The second lever is timeline compression. Enrollment delay is the canonical case, because feasibility errors, inefficient patient identification, and retention failures can drive substantial schedule slippage and therefore opportunity cost (Lamberti et al. 2024). Protocol amendments are another: they trigger IRB/ethics resubmissions, re-consent, electronic data capture rebuilds, and supply-chain re-forecasting, and substantial changes can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars once downstream disruption is accounted for (Getz et al. 2016; Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development 2021). Monitoring and data cleaning can then become a “long tail” of repetitive query generation, verification, and follow-up, which is the argument for risk-based quality management (RBQM) approaches that concentrate effort where it changes outcomes (Association of Clinical Research Organizations 2025).
AI-enabled tools create economic value mainly by automating classification, triage, and routine drafting (document indexing, query suggestion and clustering, standardized narrative scaffolds) so that expert time is shifted from low-information coordination to higher-judgment work. The intended outcome is not the removal of expertise, but a reduction in coordination overhead and in the reconciliation debt that delays interim decisions and final reporting.

Internal Discovery vs. External Acquisition
Sixty-one percent of the assets in the late-stage pipelines of the top 20 biopharma companies are now externally sourced through mergers, acquisitions, and licensing agreements, unchanged from 2024 and up from 59% in 2023 (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2025, 2026). The R&D model at large pharmaceutical companies has shifted decisively toward buying innovation: “bolt-on” acquisitions offset looming patent expiries, and early-stage risk is offshored to smaller, more agile biotech firms. Bought assets carry their own risk. Externally sourced assets are consistently more likely to be terminated in late-stage development than those developed in-house (14% vs 12% termination rate in 2024); Deloitte’s prescription is an M&A strategy built around long-term strategic fit rather than short-term pipeline gap-filling (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2025).


The Shift Toward Rare Diseases and High-Value Targets
In 2025, 36% of the late-stage assets in Deloitte’s top-20 biopharma cohort were focused on rare diseases (orphan indications), holding steady after a significant increase from 31.1% in 2023 to 37.4% in 2024 (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2025, 2026). The pivot is toward precision medicine and high-unmet-need populations, where regulatory pathways may be faster and pricing power is greater. The consequence is extreme concentration: oncology alone accounted for 37% of the cohort’s late-stage assets in 2024, which leaves sponsors in intense competition for trial sites and eligible participants (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2025). These categories are not mutually exclusive, since many oncology assets also carry orphan designations.


Shifting the cost structure: labor vs. software and governance
Automation does not “remove” cost; it changes its composition. Some labor costs can decline (less manual reconciliation and administrative follow-up), while software, integration, validation, and oversight costs increase. In regulated settings, sponsors must budget for governance: validation of computerized systems, audit trails, monitoring of model performance, and clear accountability for errors (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a; National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023).
If routine work becomes more software-mediated, CRO margins based on manual throughput are pressured, while differentiated value moves toward execution excellence, specialized expertise, and quality systems that can demonstrate control and traceability. The clinical trial software market, projected to grow more than 10% a year to nearly $29 billion by 2033, reflects this shift toward technology-mediated operations (Grand View Research 2025).
Global R&D spending has risen for two decades, and both time and attrition dominate what that money buys. Table 6.1 traces the shift.



Table 6.1: Evolution of Drug Development Economics. The cost row sets the 2003 Tufts CSDD estimate beside Deloitte’s 2025 cohort average, which use different methods; the success rows use IQVIA’s five-year windows, as labeled in the cells. Therapeutic area dramatically influences cost. Oncology trials are among the most expensive, driven by complex protocols, specialized imaging and biomarker testing, and extended survival follow-up; neurology and cardiovascular trials are similarly costly, while dermatology and infectious disease trials tend toward the lower end of cost ranges. Table 6.2 projects global pharmaceutical spending by therapeutic area through 2028, and Figure 6.1 ranks the top therapy areas by projected 2028 spending.

The Globalization of Clinical Trials
Geography is a primary driver of cost. Because clinical research costs are driven largely by labor, trials cost far less where physicians, nurses, and study coordinators earn lower salaries, which is why sponsors have moved Phase II and Phase III trials to countries such as India (Glickman et al. 2009).
These cost variations reflect fundamental differences in healthcare systems and medicine utilization patterns. Per capita medicine use varies dramatically by region: Western Europe and Japan average 1,150-1,200 defined daily doses per capita, compared to North America’s 800 doses per capita, despite North America having the highest GDP per capita. Eastern Europe demonstrates over three times higher medicine use per capita than China, despite GDP per capita being only 50% higher. These disparities stem from differences in healthcare system structure, reimbursement policies, patient cost-sharing requirements, and disease burden, all of which directly influence both trial site selection and per-patient costs (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2024).
That differential, combined with the need for large patient pools, drove a massive shift toward global participation. Glickman and colleagues documented the transition in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2009, noting that industry-sponsored Phase III trials were increasingly being conducted at sites outside the United States: more than half of all Phase III study sites (13,521 of 24,206) were already located ex-U.S., with approximately one-third of trials conducted solely outside the United States (Glickman et al. 2009). The economic driver was stark: a first-rate academic medical center in India charged approximately $1,500-$2,000 per case report, less than one-tenth the cost at a second-tier U.S. center (Glickman et al. 2009).
Glickman and colleagues also pressed the point on generalizability: more than two-thirds of 42 genetic variants associated with pharmacologic response show significant frequency differences between persons of African ancestry and those of European ancestry, and geographically distinct populations can have different genetic profiles that affect drug safety and effectiveness. Differences in medical infrastructure and physician training are often not transparently reported, making it difficult to assess whether standards of care are consistent across regions. Ethically, the “translation” of results is complicated by the fact that many drugs tested in developing countries never become readily available or affordable there after approval, potentially violating the principle that research should be responsive to the health needs of the host community (Glickman et al. 2009).
China’s share of global trial country-uses grew from 9% in 2019 to 15% in 2024, a 66% increase that moved it from fifth to fourth place globally, just behind Asia-Pacific as a whole (Figure 6.2).








Figure 6.2: Country Utilization as Percent of Trial Country-Uses, 2019 vs 2024. Data from IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science (2025).







The Regional Pivot: The Rise of China
China now accounts for 30% of all global trial starts by headquarters location, up from just 1% in 2009 (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025). Independent data corroborates this trajectory: China-sponsored trial registrations grew from 1,333 cumulative studies in 2009 to over 32,500 by 2018, a 24-fold increase (Xu, Dong, and Liu 2020). China has now approached the United States (35% in 2024) and surpassed Europe (21%) in terms of trial initiation volume, making the innovation ecosystem genuinely multi-polar.
This growth in trial activity reflects substantial capital investment. The market value of publicly listed Chinese biopharma innovation players (innovative biotechs plus CRO/CDMO companies) grew from about $3 billion in 2016 to more than $380 billion by July 2021, more than a hundredfold increase in five years (Figure 6.3). China’s share of the global innovation pipeline grew from 4.1% in 2015 to 13.9% in 2020, and the number of innovative molecules entering clinical trial applications in China grew by an average of 32% a year, from 114 in 2016 to 344 in 2020, with Chinese biotechs the largest group of submitters by 2020 (Han et al. 2021).








Figure 6.3: Total Market Value of Listed Innovative China Biotechs and CRO/CDMO Players on Major Stock Exchanges (2021 data as of mid-year). Data from Han et al. (2021).





The composition of that growth matters: CRO/CDMO companies (contract research and manufacturing organizations) grew from a negligible base to represent over half of the total market value by 2021, reflecting both the outsourcing trend and China’s emergence as a global services hub for clinical development. Growth in innovative drug development and in clinical services infrastructure together position China as both a source and destination for clinical trial activity.
Where a company is headquartered is not necessarily where its trials are physically conducted. Chinese emerging biopharma companies (EBPs) are prolific, but Chinese companies ran 83% of their trials domestically between 2020 and 2024 (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025), while Western sponsors remain heavily tethered to U.S. and European site networks for global regulatory submissions.
Capacity is shifting underneath all of this. As discussed in Chapter 18, WCG’s preliminary, partial-year 2024 count of unique U.S. investigators on industry-sponsored interventional trials was 78% below its pandemic-inflated 2020 peak (closer to 73% against the pre-pandemic base), and new trial starts fell sharply from their post-pandemic peak (WCG Clinical 2024). Trial activity is geographically broader, but this suggests that the absolute density of the global investigative environment is under significant strain.


Budgeting Checklist
Budgeting is granular work. Table 6.3 and Table 6.4, adapted from Beal et al. (2004) on industry-sponsored trials, outline the key direct and indirect costs that sites must anticipate.

Decentralized elements and digital endpoints change the cost structure as much as they change operations. Sponsors and sites increasingly incur costs for computerized systems, integration work, validation and oversight, and vendor-managed data flows, costs that are distinct from traditional per-visit procedure budgets (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b, 2023c, 2023a). Quality management also remains a material cost driver: Meinert (2013) noted that there is “reason for concern” when quality assurance and control are allocated less than 10% of total direct costs. Quality is purchased through discipline and oversight.
The incremental line items follow the technology. eConsent and participant communication tooling brings platform licensing, configuration, accessibility review, and staff training costs (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016, 2024a). DHT and device operations add procurement, provisioning, support, replacement rates, data transmission, and monitoring of the device data itself (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023c). Every vendor data pipeline needs interface build, testing, reconciliation, and sustained change control (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023b, 2024a). Remote monitoring needs secure remote source access solutions, redaction workflows where applicable, and expanded centralized monitoring analytics (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b; International Council for Harmonisation 2025). All of it needs governance: computerized system validation and qualification, audit trail review capacity, and inspection readiness drills (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a, 2024a).

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.3 How Money Flows
The sponsor sits at the center of the financial web, paying out to everyone else.
When a sponsor hires a CRO, the fee covers project management, site monitoring, data management, biostatistics, regulatory affairs, medical monitoring, and quality assurance, and it includes a margin over the CRO’s direct costs. In fiscal 2025, four large publicly listed CROs reported gross margins (revenue less direct costs, before depreciation) of about 18% to 33%, and operating margins that ranged from a loss at Fortrea to 21% at Medpace, with IQVIA at 13% company-wide and ICON at 5% after impairment charges (IQVIA Holdings Inc. 2026; ICON plc 2026; Medpace Holdings, Inc. 2026; Fortrea Holdings Inc. 2026). Because pass-through costs such as investigator payments are booked as both revenue and direct cost (IQVIA Holdings Inc. 2026; ICON plc 2026), margins on service revenue alone are higher: Medpace, which reports reimbursed out-of-pocket expenses separately, earned a gross margin of about 51% on revenue net of those expenses (Medpace Holdings, Inc. 2026). Across the itemized costs of U.S. pharmaceutical trials from 2004 to 2012, clinical procedures accounted for 15-22%, administrative staff for 11-29%, and site monitoring for 9-14%, excluding site overhead and sponsors’ own costs of monitoring the study (Sertkaya et al. 2016).
The CRO in turn pays its vendors: central laboratories per specimen processed, electronic data capture companies by licensing fee plus per-patient or per-site charges, interactive response technology vendors for randomization and drug supply management. Each service generates revenue for the vendor and represents a pass-through cost to the sponsor.
Sites are paid by sponsors or CROs against negotiated budgets covering investigator time, coordinator time, overhead, and study-specific procedures. One CRO’s published cost guide puts the cost of starting a new clinical trial site at $20,000 to $75,000 or more, covering site selection, regulatory submissions, staff training, and infrastructure setup (Andhalkar 2025).
Site payments are typically structured around per-patient or per-visit fees. A site might receive $3,000 for screening a patient, $500 for each study visit, and defined amounts for specific procedures, plus payments for protocol amendments, additional monitoring burden, and other non-standard activities.
Trial budgets calculate per-subject payments by mapping protocol procedures to specific visits. One-time activities, such as obtaining informed consent or reviewing medical history, are typically billed at the screening visit. Recurring activities (physical exams, vital sign collections, and laboratory tests) are usually billed at every study visit, while specialized assessments like ECGs or pharmacokinetic (PK) sampling occur only at designated intervals. The sponsor also pays professional fees to the investigator (PI) and a coordinator fee to the site for each visit conducted. The per-subject budget is the sum of these procedural and professional components across the screening period, treatment visits, and the final end-of-study assessment.
On top of per-subject costs, sites negotiate start-up fees to cover the administrative burden of opening the trial: regulatory document preparation, contract negotiation, pharmacy setup, source document creation, and archiving fees for long-term record storage.
The money that reaches sites must cover personnel time (investigators, coordinators, nurses, regulatory staff), the largest expense, along with administrative and regulatory costs such as IRB submissions, informed consent development, and training. Medical procedures, laboratory costs, and participant reimbursements (meal stipends, travel allowances) are often paid from site budgets as well.

6  Economics of a Trial

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.4 The CRO-Site Relationship
CROs control payment flow to sites but are paid based on sponsor satisfaction. That asymmetry is where the friction starts. A CRO’s business depends on meeting sponsor timelines, controlling costs, and delivering quality data, while sites are focused on patient care and, increasingly, on the operational challenges of running a clinical research enterprise.
Communication breakdowns are common. A 2024 industry column, citing a 2022 ZS Associates report on the voice of sites and patients, reported that 52% of sites were dissatisfied with how communication is handled and that 59% found contracting delayed and inefficient, largely because too many third parties, including CROs, are involved (Bronner 2024). Sites report repeating the same information to multiple contacts from the same sponsor or vendor, dealing with fragmented decision-making, and feeling disconnected from the decisions that shape the trial. The contracting layers (sponsor, CRO, legal departments, institutional offices) slow trial startup, and sites may wait months for executed contracts and first patient payments.
High staff turnover at CROs compounds these problems. When CRO personnel rotate frequently, sites must continuously re-educate their contacts about the trial and their capabilities, and inexperienced CRO staff may not understand protocol requirements, leading to errors that sites must correct.
Sites feel squeezed between CRO cost pressures and the realities of delivering quality research, and that structural tension underlies many operational conflicts.
crumbs: Part II: Clinical Trial Phases
6  Economics of a Trial

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.5 Where the Money Actually Goes
In 2023, the biopharmaceutical industry spent over $30 billion directly at clinical trial sites across the United States, generating more than $62 billion in total economic activity (Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America 2024). These expenditures support jobs (investigators, coordinators, nurses, regulatory staff, administrators) and purchase goods and services from local economies.
CROs employ hundreds of thousands of people globally, and the industry supports specialized vendors, technology companies, and service providers. Academic medical centers derive substantial revenue from clinical research, which supports teaching and infrastructure beyond the trials themselves.
A development program that costs $1 billion may never yield an approved product, and the majority do not. The oft-cited figure of $2.6 billion to bring a new drug to market (from a Tufts University study) is an average that already includes capitalized R&D expenditures and the cost of failure, so the out-of-pocket cost of a typical successful program, taken on its own, is lower. This high cost of failure increasingly drives larger pharmaceutical companies to license assets later in the development cycle, shifting much of the early-phase risk, and the majority of trial activity, onto Emerging Biopharma (EBP) companies (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025).
crumbs: Part II: Clinical Trial Phases
6  Economics of a Trial

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.6 Patient Economics
In early-phase oncology trials, nearly half of patients (48%) report monthly out-of-pocket costs of at least $1,000 (Huey et al. 2021). Investigational drugs and many study procedures are covered, but patients face out-of-pocket expenses for travel, parking, meals, and accommodations, and those costs fall disproportionately on patients with lower incomes and those who live far from trial sites.
Time is the other cost. Participation requires clinic visits, sometimes frequent ones: time away from a job for working patients, arranged coverage for patients with caregiving responsibilities. These costs are real even if they do not appear in any budget.
Decentralized trial elements (home visits, remote monitoring, direct-to-patient drug shipment) address some of these burdens but introduce new logistical challenges and costs.

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.7 Funding Interims and Portfolio Management
Interim analyses are usually framed as scientific tools, but they also serve a financial one: deciding whether to commit capital to the next stage of a program.

Administrative Interim Analyses
A funding interim (also called an administrative or financial interim analysis) is a pre-specified analysis of accumulating trial data conducted specifically to trigger an investment decision, not to change trial design or stop enrollment. A scientific interim (for futility, efficacy, or dose selection) changes something about the trial. A funding interim changes nothing about the trial at all. It simply answers a binary question for an external funder: “Has the pre-specified threshold been met?”
The trial protocol specifies that an independent statistical group will perform a blinded or unblinded analysis when a defined number of patients have completed follow-up. That group delivers a checkbox (yes/no) to the sponsor and to the funder under a non-disclosure agreement, and the criterion is typically based on predictive probability of trial success, described below. The funder uses the checkbox to decide whether to commit capital to complete the trial; if the threshold is not met, the funder may decline to invest but the trial continues unchanged under its original protocol.
The naming convention is not a semantic nicety. Calling this analysis a “futility” interim creates a regulatory problem, because futility implies that failing the analysis triggers a protocol change. An administrative analysis that changes nothing does not require the same pre-specification, alpha-allocation, and regulatory disclosure as a scientific futility analysis. Sponsors should use “administrative analysis” or “financial analysis” in the protocol and charter, clearly distinguished from any scientific interim planned.
This design solves a structural problem in smaller biotech development. A company that can fund the Phase II portion of a seamless Phase II/III program may need external capital to fund the Phase III expansion, and a standalone Phase II trial requires a gap between studies (unblinding, data readout, fundraising, regulatory interaction) that adds roughly a year or more to the development timeline and costs additional months of patent life. A seamless design with a built-in funding checkpoint can eliminate that gap, with the funder committing based on the interim checkpoint result.


Predictive Probability of Success as a Funder’s Tool
The funding criterion is almost always some form of predictive probability of success (PPoS), the probability that the trial will achieve statistical significance at the planned final analysis, given the data accumulated so far (Marion et al. 2025). This is distinct from power, which is fixed at design time based on an assumed effect size and does not change as data accumulate. PPoS does change with interim data: it rises as the treatment effect looks larger than assumed, falls as it looks smaller, and can swing dramatically depending on what the data show. The full statistical treatment is at Section 12.7.1.
For funders, PPoS is intuitive in a way that p-values and confidence intervals are not. A funder is, in effect, buying a lottery ticket with a stated probability of a payoff. A 70% PPoS at the time of the funding checkpoint means that, given the available data and the model’s assumptions, there is a 70% probability the trial will be statistically successful at the final analysis. This is the natural framing for investors who think about expected value and risk-adjusted returns. Even large pharmaceutical companies use internal PPoS calculations as portfolio-management tools for deciding which Phase III programs to continue and which to terminate.
A common communication failure is demanding that PPoS equal power. “We need 90% predictive probability” as a funding criterion means the funder needs to see, at halftime, that the team is 90% likely to win by the required margin. That is an extraordinarily high bar mid-trial, far higher than is typically achievable without an enormous interim effect size. The practical solution is to show funders example data presentations (Kaplan-Meier curves, hazard ratios, mean differences) and work backward to the PPoS associated with each one, building intuition for what a “fundable” interim result looks like.


Assurance and Portfolio Optimization
Assurance (sometimes called Bayesian predictive probability of success) extends the PPoS concept from trial execution to program planning (O’Hagan, Stevens, and Campbell 2005). Where PPoS conditions on the accumulated data at a specific interim time point, assurance is computed before the trial starts: power assumes a specific true effect size and computes the probability of observing a significant result under that assumption, while assurance integrates over a distribution of plausible true effects and computes the average probability of a successful outcome across that distribution.
For portfolio management, assurance is the more relevant quantity. A Phase III program powered at 85% for an assumed hazard ratio of 0.80 sounds high, but if the sponsor’s internal evidence places substantial uncertainty on whether the effect is 0.70 or 0.90, the assurance (averaged over that uncertainty) might be 55-60%. Portfolio managers who optimize based on power alone are systematically overestimating the probability of success for their programs; assurance provides a more realistic forecast.
Assurance calculations also make uncertainty transparent. A program team that disagrees about the likely effect size can run assurance under both assumptions and see how dramatically the probability of success changes, which is more productive than arguing about which single effect size to assume for power.

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.8 Platform Trial Economics
The economic case for platform trials (described in detail at Section 13.6) is a reduction in cost per scientific question answered. When sponsors each build separate Phase III programs for drugs targeting the same disease, approximately half of the enrolled patients receive placebo across all programs simultaneously, generating information only about the control-arm trajectory rather than about any experimental treatment. A platform with a shared control arm redirects those patients to experimental arms, substantially reducing the total number of patients required to answer each question while maintaining statistical power (Saville and Berry 2016).
Patient count is only part of it. Platform infrastructure (site contracts, databases, regulatory submissions, DSMBs, monitoring infrastructure) represents a substantial fixed cost that does not scale with the number of programs run in parallel. Amortizing this fixed cost across multiple arms makes the per-arm cost of subsequent arms a fraction of the cost of a standalone trial. REMAP-CAP investigated many therapies across its multiple treatment domains over its lifespan; each of those questions would have required years of infrastructure development if approached as a standalone trial.
The first-arm problem is the primary economic barrier to platforms. The sponsor of the platform’s first arm bears the full fixed cost of building the arena before any amortization benefit materializes. This means platforms in academic or disease-advocacy settings (Healey ALS, I-SPY 2, SNAP) typically require philanthropic or government funding for the first arms; once the platform is proven, commercial sponsors engage at much lower marginal cost. This structural challenge explains why perpetual platforms have succeeded most readily in conditions with strong advocacy communities or NIH investment, while diseases without those resources remain served primarily by standalone trials.

title: 6  Economics of a Trial
text:
6.9 Strategic Implications
The largest economic levers in a trial are rarely the per-procedure line items. They are the decisions about which programs to fund, when to stop them, and how to share fixed infrastructure across scientific questions.
For sponsors and their funders, this argues for judging programs on assurance instead of power: a program powered at 85% can carry a true probability of success closer to 55-60% once uncertainty in the effect size is taken into account, and stopping such a program early (or structuring a seamless design with an administrative funding checkpoint) protects far more capital than any procedure-level negotiation. For CROs, differentiated value is moving from manual throughput toward execution excellence and the quality systems that can demonstrate control as routine work becomes software-mediated. For sites, financial viability depends on budgeting that captures the indirect and administrative costs (Table 6.4) that per-visit fees routinely miss, so that negotiated compensation actually covers personnel and infrastructure. And for the patients at the center of the enterprise, designs that move cost off the participant are both an ethical obligation and, increasingly, an advantage in recruitment and retention.

title: 7  Phase I: Human Pharmacology
text:
7.1 Starting Dose Selection and Risk Mitigation
Until the first human dose, everything known about a compound comes from test tubes, cell cultures, and animal models. Phase I is where someone has to convert all of that into a number of milligrams, hand it to a person, and then find out how quickly the drug reaches the bloodstream, how long it stays there, what biological effects it produces, and at what dose the adverse ones become unacceptable.
First-in-human strictly names only the initial study in a development program; Phase I as a category covers every study designed principally to assess safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics in humans (International Council for Harmonisation 2021). That work is increasingly the domain of small companies. Emerging Biopharma (EBP) sponsors accounted for 65% of all Phase I trial starts in 2024, more than twice the share of large pharmaceutical companies (24%) (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025).
The subjects are usually healthy volunteers, since exposing sick people to a drug whose behavior in humans is completely unknown would be inappropriate. Oncology is the standing exception, along with certain other therapeutic areas where the expected toxicity is too significant to put in front of a healthy person.
The starting dose is calculated from preclinical data and set far below anything expected to cause toxicity; Section 7.1 works through that calculation and the alternative framework for high-risk biologics. Escalation follows prespecified rules: each cohort is dosed and observed for signs of toxicity before the next may go higher, and the sequence continues until the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) is reached or the desired pharmacological effect is achieved.
Two frameworks convert animal data into a first human dose, and for TGN1412 the gap between them was orders of magnitude. Which one governs depends on the compound class and on the plausible mechanisms of adverse effects.
NOAEL-based approach. The No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) in the most appropriate animal species (by default, the most sensitive) is converted to a human equivalent dose using a body-surface-area correction (\(\text{HED} = \text{NOAEL} \times (\text{animal weight}/\text{human weight})^{0.33}\), with FDA’s standard 60 kg human) and then divided by a safety factor (10 by default, raised or lowered with a stated rationale) to arrive at the Maximum Recommended Starting Dose (MRSD) (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2005). If the human equivalent of the pharmacologically active dose falls below the MRSD, the starting dose may be lowered further. For small molecules with conventional pharmacology and a well-characterized safety profile in animals, this calculation is generally sufficient.
MABEL approach. The Minimal Anticipated Biological Effect Level (MABEL) was developed for compounds whose pharmacological activity in humans begins at doses far below any observable toxicity in animals. It integrates receptor occupancy modeling, in vitro pharmacological activity data, ex vivo assays on human cells, and animal PK/PD to identify the lowest dose expected to produce any measurable biological effect. EMA’s 2017 guideline on FIH trials (European Medicines Agency 2017) calls for MABEL to be estimated alongside the pharmacologically active dose (PAD), and recommends that the starting dose be anchored to the MABEL, the PAD, or the NOAEL according to how much uncertainty remains about the human relevance of the non-clinical findings and about the intended target. In practice the MABEL anchor is the one chosen when a compound is highly potent, acts through a cytokine-mediated mechanism, or engages a target expressed on circulating immune cells. TGN1412 failed precisely because the NOAEL-based MRSD did not capture the potent receptor-mediated cytokine cascade; a MABEL-based approach would have produced a starting dose orders of magnitude lower.
In practice, sponsors calculate both estimates and select the more conservative. A large gap between the MABEL and the NOAEL-derived MRSD is itself a risk signal that calls for protocol-level mitigation.
Sentinel dosing. To limit how many subjects are exposed to a new dose at once, FIH protocols routinely dose sentinels first: within each cohort, one subject receives the investigational drug and one receives placebo, ahead of the rest by an interval set from the compound’s half-life and the plausible onset of an adverse reaction (commonly 24 to 48 hours). After that interval, the DSMB or Safety Review Committee reviews the sentinel data before the remaining members are dosed per the cohort’s pre-specified active:placebo allocation, which is majority active. EMA’s first-in-human guideline endorses staggered dosing within cohorts (European Medicines Agency 2017), and it is now both regulatory expectation and routine practice for biologics and immunologically active compounds.
Stopping rules. FIH protocols typically prespecify stopping criteria at three levels; the criteria below are common examples, and each rule should state whether the stop is a temporary halt or a final end to dosing (European Medicines Agency 2017). Subject-level rules discontinue one person’s dosing immediately for any Grade 3 or higher adverse event, a cytokine elevation above a pre-specified threshold, or a defined change in cardiac rhythm or ECG morphology. Cohort-level criteria suspend enrollment pending a safety review when a sentinel subject has a DLT, when two subjects in the cohort have severe adverse reactions (in the same organ system or not), or when any laboratory finding meets a pre-specified threshold of clinical concern. Study-level criteria stop dosing across the trial: a potentially drug-related death, a Grade 4 cytokine release syndrome, or, in a healthy-volunteer trial, a single serious adverse reaction in any subject, expected or not.
For immunologically active compounds, cytokine panels (IL-6, IFN-γ, TNF-α) belong in the protocol as early biomarkers of immune dysregulation, checked at pre-specified timepoints before clinical symptoms develop.
Every foreseeable safety event should have a pre-written response in the protocol before the first subject is dosed, because the alternative is deciding in real time under clinical pressure.

title: 7  Phase I: Human Pharmacology
section: 7.2 Single and Multiple Ascending Dose Studies
text:
7.2 Single and Multiple Ascending Dose Studies
Most Phase I programs run both a single ascending dose (SAD) study and a multiple ascending dose (MAD) study. In the SAD, small cohorts (typically 6 to 8 subjects) receive a single dose each, with placebo typically included in each cohort to help distinguish drug effects from background noise; safety and pharmacokinetics are reviewed and found acceptable before the next cohort receives a higher dose.
The MAD then gives the drug repeatedly over days or weeks, and asks what a single dose cannot: whether the drug accumulates, how long it takes to reach steady state, and whether repeated exposure is still tolerated. It bridges from the artificial world of single doses to the clinical reality of chronic treatment.

title: 7  Phase I: Human Pharmacology
text:
7.3 Characterizing Pharmacokinetics
A primary goal of Phase I is to determine how the drug moves through the body: its pharmacokinetics (PK) (International Council for Harmonisation 2021). The raw material is a series of concentrations measured in blood (and sometimes other fluids) at multiple time points after dosing; Table 7.1 lists what pharmacokineticists compute from that curve.



Table 7.1: Key Pharmacokinetic Parameters












PK Parameter
Symbol
Definition
Formula
Clinical Implication




Maximum Concentration
Cmax
Peak drug concentration achieved
Observed directly from PK curve
Indicates peak exposure; related to tolerability


Time to Maximum
Tmax
Time to reach peak concentration
Observed directly from PK curve
Related to absorption rate; affects onset of action


Area Under Curve
AUC
Total exposure over time
\(\int_0^{\infty} C(t) \, dt\)
Proportional to amount absorbed; key PK/PD metric


Half-life
t1/2
Time for concentration to decrease by 50%
\(t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693 \times V_d}{CL}\) (one-compartment)
Sets time to steady state (about 4-5 half-lives); guides dosing interval


Clearance
CL
Volume of plasma cleared per unit time
\(CL = \frac{Dose}{AUC}\) after an IV dose (\(CL/F\) after an oral dose)
Efficiency of drug elimination; guides dosing


Volume of Distribution
Vd
Apparent volume drug distributes into
\(V_d = \frac{Dose}{C_0}\) (IV bolus, one-compartment)
Suggests tissue distribution; affects loading doses


Bioavailability
F
Fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation
\(F = \frac{AUC_{oral}/Dose_{oral}}{AUC_{IV}/Dose_{IV}}\)
Determines oral vs. IV dose equivalence






Half-life is the main guide to the dosing interval: a 4-hour half-life typically requires three or four doses daily, while a 24-hour half-life allows once-daily dosing. Caffeine’s is about 5 hours, which is why morning coffee wears off by afternoon; some antidepressants exceed 100 hours, which is why missing a dose matters less and why side effects persist after discontinuation. Formulation and pharmacodynamics can override half-life: extended-release products stretch the interval, and a drug that binds its target irreversibly can act long after it has left the plasma.
Volume of distribution reveals where the drug goes. A Vd close to plasma volume (about 3 liters) suggests the drug stays in the bloodstream, useful for treating blood infections but unable to reach intracellular targets. A Vd of hundreds of liters, far exceeding actual body volume, indicates extensive tissue binding: the drug accumulates in fat, muscle, or specific organs. Chloroquine’s Vd exceeds 200 liters per kilogram because it concentrates in tissues, which is why it needs loading doses and why it persists for weeks after the last dose.
Clearance sets the dose needed to hold therapeutic levels: high clearance means rapid elimination and so higher or more frequent doses, low clearance means accumulation and careful titration to avoid toxicity. Impaired kidney or liver function can reduce clearance, which is why these populations may need dose adjustments; whether they do depends on how much exposure changes and how wide the drug’s therapeutic range is.
Bioavailability explains why oral and intravenous doses differ. At 50%, an oral dose must be twice the IV dose to reach the same exposure. Some drugs fall below 10%, making oral administration impractical; others are destroyed by stomach acid or extensively metabolized by the liver before reaching circulation (the “first-pass effect”).
Pharmacokinetics tells us what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics (PD) tells us what the drug does to the body. Phase I studies often include pharmacodynamic endpoints: biomarkers or biological effects that indicate the drug is producing its intended action. If such a biomarker correlates with drug exposure, and if it is a reasonable predictor of clinical effect, PK/PD modeling can link the two and guide the choice of dose and regimen for Phase II.

7.4 Special Studies
Beyond first-in-human and dose escalation, Phase I typically carries a set of specialized studies (Table 7.2) (International Council for Harmonisation 2021; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a):

Study Type
Purpose
Design
Regulatory Expectation




Bioavailability
Determine what fraction of dose reaches circulation
Compare oral vs. IV administration (absolute) or different formulations (relative)
Required for oral formulations


Bioequivalence
Show new formulation performs like reference product
Crossover design comparing test vs. reference; assess if 90% CI of AUC/Cmax ratio within 80-125%
Required for generics and major formulation changes; a BCS-based biowaiver can replace the in vivo study for some immediate-release oral products


Food Effect
Assess how meals affect absorption
Crossover comparing fed vs. fasted states
Required; informs label dosing instructions


Drug-Drug Interaction (DDI)

Test investigational drug with probe substrates/inhibitors/inducers of CYP450 enzymes
Required for commonly co-administered drugs


Hepatic Impairment
PK in patients with liver dysfunction
Compare normal vs. mild/moderate/severe hepatic impairment
Required if drug significantly metabolized


Renal Impairment
PK in patients with kidney dysfunction
Compare normal vs. mild/moderate/severe renal impairment
Expected if the drug is likely to be used in patients with impaired renal function, even if not renally eliminated (a reduced design may then suffice) (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024c)


Elderly Subjects
PK in aged population ($$65 years)
Compare young vs. elderly PK parameters
Geriatric PK expected for drugs used in the elderly; population PK can replace a dedicated study if enough older patients are enrolled


Thorough QT
Assess cardiac repolarization risk
High therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses; measure QTc prolongation
Required unless waived by alternative data






Together they let a sponsor recommend a dose for everyone who might need the drug, accounting for physiological differences and potential interactions. Some of that evidence no longer requires a trial: FDA and EMA now accept physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling and model-informed drug development (MIDD) to supplement or waive some dedicated drug-drug interaction and organ-impairment studies, extrapolating exposure to untested populations from validated mechanistic models.

title: 7  Phase I: Human Pharmacology
section: 7.5 Phase I in Oncology: Dose Escalation Design
text:
7.5 Phase I in Oncology: Dose Escalation Design
Oncology is the exception to the healthy-volunteer rule. Anticancer drugs often cause significant toxicity, and the people who need them face serious illness with limited treatment options, so Phase I oncology studies are conducted in patients.
The objective has traditionally been the MTD: the highest dose that causes unacceptable toxicity in no more than a defined fraction of patients. Dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) are the pre-specified adverse events (typically Grade 3 or 4 by the CTCAE system) that draw the toxicity boundary, observed over a fixed observation window (commonly 21 or 28 days, matching the first treatment cycle) after each dose.

The 3+3 Design and Its Limitations
The 3+3 design has been the workhorse of oncology Phase I trials for decades. Three patients receive the starting dose; if none experiences a DLT the dose is escalated; if one does, three more are enrolled at that dose, and escalation continues only if none of them has a DLT; if two or more patients at a dose experience DLTs, the dose is declared too high and the next lower dose, usually confirmed in six patients, is the MTD. The design is simple and transparent, requiring no statistical software.
Simulation studies show that the 3+3 often fails to select the correct MTD, and that it tends to err low rather than high (Le Tourneau, Lee, and Siu 2009). The consequences are patients treated below the true MTD and an uncharacterized upper part of the dose-response curve. The cause is structural: the design makes each decision using only the cohort at the current dose, ignoring what the trial has already learned at every other dose, which makes it statistically inefficient (O’Quigley, Pepe, and Fisher 1990).


Modern Dose-Escalation Designs
Two families of escalation designs are the main alternatives to the 3+3 in sponsored oncology trials. Both require specifying a target toxicity rate (typically 20-25% in modern practice, lower than the old “highest tolerated dose” convention), and interval designs also use an acceptable toxicity interval around it (e.g., 15-35%).
Rule-based “interval” designs (BOIN, mTPI, i3+3). These methods compare the observed DLT rate at the current dose to a target interval and make a simple escalate/stay/de-escalate decision without fitting a dose-toxicity curve across all doses. The Bayesian Optimal INterval (BOIN) design, which FDA designated fit-for-purpose for dose finding in December 2021 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025), is a prominent example: it derives optimal decision boundaries from the target toxicity rate and the acceptable interval through a closed-form calculation, minimizing the probability of incorrect escalation decisions (Liu and Yuan 2015). BOIN and related methods (mTPI-2, i3+3) can be pre-computed into a decision table before the trial, which makes them operationally tractable. Their limitation is that each escalation decision uses only the data at the current dose; BOIN pools information across doses only at the end, when isotonic regression selects the MTD (Yuan et al. 2016).
Model-based designs (CRM, BLRM). The Continual Reassessment Method (CRM) fits a simple dose-toxicity model (a one-parameter curve in O’Quigley’s original formulation) after each patient with complete DLT information, updating the model and assigning the next cohort to the dose estimated to be nearest the target toxicity (O’Quigley, Pepe, and Fisher 1990). The Bayesian Logistic Regression Model (BLRM) is a two-parameter extension that provides more realistic uncertainty quantification (Neuenschwander, Branson, and Gsponer 2008). By borrowing information across all tested doses simultaneously, model-based designs use the accumulating data more efficiently than the 3+3, and their advantage over interval designs is greatest when many dose levels are studied or the true MTD lies at an extreme of the tested range. In published head-to-head simulations, BOIN’s average MTD-selection accuracy is comparable to the CRM’s (Liu and Yuan 2015). The tradeoff is operational complexity: decisions require real-time statistical computation as each patient’s DLT outcome becomes available, and the prior distribution for the dose-toxicity curve requires careful elicitation from clinical and historical data.
Escalation with Overdose Control (EWOC) is an additional constraint applied with model-based designs: a dose is allocated only if the posterior probability that its DLT rate exceeds the upper bound (e.g., 35%) is below a threshold (e.g., 25%). Unlike the absolute exclusion rules in interval designs, EWOC exclusion is temporary: as the model accumulates data and revises its estimate of a dose’s toxicity, a previously excluded dose can be reconsidered (Babb, Rogatko, and Zacks 1998).






NoteChoosing a dose-escalation design



There is no universally superior design. Table 7.3 summarizes the practical trade-offs.

Beyond the operational question the table settles, two things push toward a model-based design. The first is the number of doses: with many dose levels, model-based designs gain a larger relative advantage because they can skip doses on the way up and borrow more efficiently. The second is a low target toxicity rate, since at low targets interval methods may be too conservative and model-based designs with EWOC handle the situation more gracefully. Whichever design is chosen, simulate it across a range of plausible dose-toxicity scenarios before the trial begins, assessing MTD-selection accuracy, probability of overdosing, and expected sample size.




From MTD to Optimal Dose: Project Optimus
For decades the regulatory pathway rewarded finding the highest dose patients could tolerate, on the assumption that more was better. Then post-hoc analyses of several approved oncology drugs showed that doses below the MTD would have produced equivalent efficacy with substantially less toxicity. FDA’s Project Optimus, launched in 2021 for oncology, exists to generate that evidence prospectively (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021, 2024b): the right dose is the one that optimizes the balance of efficacy and tolerability, which is not always the maximum patients can survive.
The FDA guidance on dosage optimization for oncology biologics and drugs, issued as a draft in January 2023 and finalized in August 2024, sets out FDA’s recommendations for optimizing dosage during development, much of which falls to early-phase programs (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b):
Evidence across multiple candidate doses. Escalating to the MTD and declaring it the recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) is no longer enough. Sponsors are expected to characterize at least two candidate RP2Ds through expansion cohorts, seamless Phase I/II designs, or randomized dose-comparison substudies, with the criteria for selecting among those candidates written into the protocol before enrollment begins.
Pharmacodynamic and patient-reported evidence. Dose characterization now includes efficacy biomarkers (receptor occupancy, PD markers mechanistically linked to the drug’s activity) and patient-reported outcomes measuring symptom burden and quality of life, alongside the traditional clinical safety assessments. A dose that is more tolerable by PRO metrics is meaningful, even when adverse event grades are equivalent.
Randomized dose comparison. That guidance says explicitly that sponsors should randomize where feasible, in place of uncontrolled parallel-cohort expansion. The randomization need not be powered for formal hypothesis testing: cohorts of, say, 20 to 40 patients per dose can suffice, with pre-specified endpoints covering activity and tolerability and a defined decision rule for RP2D selection. What matters is that the rule exists before the data do.
Biologically active dose. For drugs with clear PD markers, the biologically active dose (BAD) has gained regulatory traction: if PK/PD modeling demonstrates that a dose below the MTD achieves full target coverage (e.g., sustained receptor occupancy above 80%), escalating further is unlikely to improve efficacy and may add toxicity; only activity and tolerability data compared across dosages can settle the question. Project Optimus gives sponsors a path to justify selecting the BAD rather than the MTD as the RP2D, provided the exposure-response relationship for the PD marker is reproducible across the tested dose range.
Project Optimus was launched for oncology, but its logic is spreading. Immunology, gene therapy, and other areas where the relationship between dose and effect is non-linear and toxicity can be severe and irreversible are now having the same dose-finding discussions.






NoteCombination escalation: added dimensions



Oncology increasingly relies on drug combinations, typically pairing a checkpoint inhibitor with a targeted or cytotoxic agent. Combination escalation then has to solve three problems that single-agent escalation never faces.
Two-dimensional dose space. With two drugs each tested at multiple levels, the toxicity surface spans a grid, and exhaustive testing of every combination is infeasible. Escalation designs must prespecify the rules for moving through the grid, although adaptive designs pick each next combination from the accumulating data rather than following a fixed path. A BLRM with an interaction term models how the two drugs’ toxicities combine, while model-free designs such as the BOIN combination design and the Product of Independent Beta Probabilities Escalation (PIPE) design estimate each combination’s DLT rate directly, without a parametric dose-toxicity model (Lin and Yin 2017; Mander and Sweeting 2015). Assuming that the two toxicities arise independently is not the same as assuming they add: two independent 20% risks give a 36% chance of at least one DLT, not 40%.
Scheduling. The sequence and timing of combination dosing often drives tolerability independently of dose: the same total doses may be tolerated when the two drugs are given sequentially but not when they are given simultaneously. Combination protocols must specify schedule as well as dose, and treat a schedule change as a form of dose modification requiring safety review under the protocol.
Attribution. When a toxicity occurs, determining whether it belongs to Drug A, Drug B, or the combination is frequently impossible. DLT definitions and cohort decision rules must prespecify how attribution uncertainty is handled, with the rationale stated in the protocol rather than settled at a case review meeting after the event.

title: 7  Phase I: Human Pharmacology
text:
7.6 The Phase I-Phase II Transition
Phase I trials are small by design, and everything after them is sized from what they produce: a safety database characterizing adverse events across a range of doses, pharmacokinetic parameters to guide dosing decisions, pharmacodynamic data linking exposure to biological effects, and, most critically, a recommended Phase II dose that balances safety against expected efficacy and initial proof of mechanism. By identifying that dose, Phase I researchers move the drug from laboratory hypotheses into human biology.
The handoff is also one of several go/no-go decisions that punctuate drug development. Unexpected toxicity, poor pharmacokinetics, or an absent pharmacodynamic effect can end the program here. Such early terminations, while disappointing, are far preferable to late-stage failures.
The geographic footprint of this work is shifting, with China-headquartered companies accounting for 30% of global trial starts in 2024 (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2025). AI-assisted approaches to trial design and simulation, including enrollment and feasibility modeling and prognostic digital twins for covariate adjustment, are covered in Chapter 26.






NoteDiscussion Questions




A T-cell engager for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma has potent cytokine-release activity in ex vivo human blood assays at concentrations well below those toxic in non-human primates. The NOAEL-based MRSD is 10-fold higher than the MABEL-derived starting dose. Which starting dose framework would you recommend to the sponsor, and what protocol-level safeguards would you require to accompany that choice?
The 3+3 design selects the correct MTD less reliably in simulation than interval and model-based designs, yet it remains in use. What institutional, regulatory, and operational factors sustain its use, and under what specific circumstances, if any, does its use remain defensible?
FDA’s dosage-optimization guidance recommends comparing multiple candidate dosages. For a drug whose primary PD marker (target receptor occupancy) is technically feasible but not validated as a predictor of clinical response, how should the sponsor operationalize the dose-selection criteria in the protocol before data are seen?
A combination Phase I program pairs a checkpoint inhibitor (approved as monotherapy, with two dose levels under consideration for the combination) with a novel SMAC mimetic (dose-escalating). The development team proposes a simple row-by-row escalation through a dose grid, assuming additive toxicity. What are the statistical and clinical limitations of that assumption, and what design alternatives would you propose?
A sentinel stopping rule specifies that dosing of the full cohort is suspended if a DLT occurs in a sentinel subject. A sentinel subject at dose level 3 develops Grade 3 transaminase elevation at hour 36 that resolves completely by hour 72. The medical monitor argues this is manageable and not clinically meaningful. Walk through the considerations for deciding whether to invoke the stopping rule or proceed with cohort dosing.

title: 8  Phase II: Exploratory
text:
8.1 The Dose-Response Relationship
Approximately 70% of drugs that enter Phase II never advance to Phase III (Biotechnology Innovation Organization, QLS Advisors, and Informa Pharma Intelligence 2021). Phase I established that the drug can be given to humans with acceptable safety; Phase II must establish that giving it to humans accomplishes something worthwhile. That is the first controlled exploration of whether an investigational drug produces the therapeutic effects that preclinical research suggested it might, and the question shifts from “is this drug safe?” to the more consequential “does this drug actually work?”
The exploration occurs in two stages (see Table 8.1). Early Phase II studies (sometimes called Phase IIa) seek proof of concept: evidence that the drug produces some measurable therapeutic effect in patients with the target condition. Later Phase II studies (Phase IIb) take that signal and turn it into a dose (International Council for Harmonisation 2021):
Understanding how response changes with dose is one of the most critical (and challenging) objectives of Phase II (International Council for Harmonisation 2021). The relationship is rarely simple.
At very low doses, there may be no detectable effect; the drug is present but at concentrations too low to produce meaningful target engagement. As doses increase, response emerges and grows. Eventually, a plateau is reached where higher doses produce little additional benefit. At still higher doses, toxicity may begin to outweigh efficacy.
Dose-finding studies have to characterize that curve well enough to select the optimal dose for Phase III: high enough to produce meaningful efficacy and low enough to minimize toxicity, and sitting where small dose differences do not produce large response differences. Common dose-finding approaches are summarized in Table 8.2.
Whatever the approach, a few principles hold (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 1994). The doses studied should bracket the expected optimal dose, above the target as well as below. Placebo should be included wherever it is ethical, both to quantify the drug’s effect over background and to account for the often-substantial placebo response in many indications; without a placebo group, a positive dose-response slope still shows that the drug has an effect, but not how large that effect is. And because exposure-response relationships are often more interpretable than simple dose-response relationships, the analysis should incorporate pharmacokinetic data.

The Emax Model
The most widely used mathematical description of dose-response is the Emax model, borrowed directly from pharmacology (MacDougall 2006):
\[E(d) = E_0 + \frac{E_{\max} \cdot d^{\gamma}}{ED_{50}^{\gamma} + d^{\gamma}}\]
where \(E_0\) is the baseline (placebo-level) response, \(E_{\max}\) is the maximum drug effect above baseline, \(ED_{50}\) is the dose producing half the maximum effect, and \(\gamma\) (the Hill coefficient) controls the steepness of the curve. When \(\gamma = 1\) the model reduces to the simple three-parameter Emax model (\(E_0\), \(E_{\max}\), \(ED_{50}\)); letting \(\gamma\) be a free fourth parameter gives the sigmoid (S-shaped) Emax, or Hill, model, with \(\gamma > 1\) producing progressively steeper curves.
For practitioners, the model’s value is that it compresses that whole shape into a few interpretable parameters and names the region where Phase III dosing belongs: the plateau, high enough for reliable efficacy but not so high that the incremental toxicity of further dose increases outweighs any additional benefit.
When preclinical or Phase IIa data suggest a plausible range for \(ED_{50}\) and \(E_{\max}\), those values can serve as Bayesian priors in Phase IIb dose-finding, so the dose-response estimate updates as the trial accumulates data.


MCP-Mod: Combining Significance Testing with Dose-Response Modeling
A purely comparative analysis of dose-response data (testing each dose against placebo with separate t-tests) is statistically inefficient: it cannot interpolate between doses to find the optimal one, and applying multiple comparisons corrections loses power. MCP-Mod (Multiple Comparison Procedures combined with Modeling) was developed as a principled solution (Bretz, Pinheiro, and Branson 2005), and it runs in two sequential steps:

Multiple comparison step. The analyst pre-specifies a family of candidate dose-response models (e.g., Emax, linear, quadratic, logistic, exponential) and, for each one, an optimally weighted contrast test comparing the dose groups against placebo, with the weights chosen to maximize power if that model is correct. The largest of these contrast statistics is compared with a multiplicity-adjusted critical value, so the proof-of-concept test controls Type I error across all candidate models.
Modeling step. If the test is significant, each candidate model is fitted to the data and the best-fitting model is selected (by the largest contrast test statistic, by an information criterion such as AIC, or by averaging across the candidate models). That model then estimates the dose-response curve and identifies the target dose: the dose estimated to produce a pre-specified target effect (e.g., 80% of \(E_{\max}\), or a clinically meaningful threshold).

For sponsors and CROs, the payoff is a dose recommendation backed by a fitted dose-response curve and a statistically defensible selection procedure, so the Phase III team carries forward a model-based rationale instead of “dose 3 looked best numerically.” Both FDA and EMA have recognized MCP-Mod as an acceptable dose-response analysis method: EMA issued a formal qualification opinion in 2014 (EMA Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2014) and FDA designated it fit-for-purpose for dose finding in May 2016 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025a).

title: 8  Phase II: Exploratory
text:
8.2 Endpoint Selection
The ideal endpoint would be the clinical outcome we ultimately care about: survival, resolution of disease, or clinically meaningful symptom improvement. But these outcomes often require large samples or long follow-up to observe.
Phase II studies therefore often use surrogate endpoints: measurements that are expected to predict clinical outcome but can be observed more quickly and in smaller populations (see examples in Table 8.3) (International Council for Harmonisation 1998). The ICH E9(R1) estimands framework gives a structured way to define precisely what treatment effect is being estimated (International Council for Harmonisation 2019), including how intercurrent events such as treatment discontinuation, use of rescue medication, or switching to alternative therapy will be handled in the analysis. For example, a Phase II diabetes study using HbA1c as a surrogate must define whether the estimand reflects treatment effect while patients remain on therapy (a “while on treatment” strategy) or the effect regardless of treatment adherence (a “treatment policy” strategy).
FDA’s Patient-Focused Drug Development guidance series presses sponsors to build patient perspectives into endpoint selection, particularly through clinical outcome assessments (COAs) that capture treatment benefit as the patient experiences it (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023). The biomarker most convenient to measure is not always the outcome that matters to the patient.

Surrogates buy speed at a price. Not every change in a surrogate translates to clinical benefit: Drug A might lower blood pressure more than Drug B yet produce no better cardiovascular outcomes. Using surrogates in Phase II is generally accepted, since the goal there is to detect signals and select doses, but the relationship between surrogate and clinical benefit must be established if the surrogate is to support full regulatory approval; a surrogate only reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit can support accelerated approval for a serious condition, with confirmation deferred to post-marketing trials.

title: 8  Phase II: Exploratory
text:
8.3 Adaptive Designs
Beyond the traditional approach to Phase II (design a study, run it to completion, analyze the results), adaptive designs modify the trial as data accumulate. Sample size can be re-estimated to maintain statistical power in the face of unexpected variability, ineffective doses dropped and new ones added to better characterize the dose-response relationship, and randomization shifted toward the better-performing arms (see Section 12.8). At the far end, a seamless Phase II/III design transitions directly into the confirmatory stage on interim evidence (see Section 12.4).






NoteFDA Support for Adaptive Designs



The FDA has issued guidance supporting the use of adaptive designs when appropriately planned (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019): pre-specify the adaptation rules, control Type I error across the adaptation, and maintain the integrity of the trial despite the modifications. For Phase II, advanced Bayesian frameworks are increasingly used to handle these adaptations (including stopping for futility, dropping arms, or response-adaptive randomization), supported by rigorous simulation workflows to maintain statistical integrity (Granholm et al. 2025).

title: 8  Phase II: Exploratory
section: 8.4 Stopping for Futility: Predictive Probability of Success
text:
8.4 Stopping for Futility: Predictive Probability of Success
Whether to stop early when interim data are discouraging is one of the hardest calls in a running Phase II trial. Continuing a trial that is unlikely to succeed wastes resources and delays alternative programs; stopping prematurely risks abandoning a drug that would have succeeded with more time.
The classical approach to futility is conditional power: given the observed interim data and an assumed true treatment effect (often the interim estimate, sometimes the effect assumed at the design stage), what is the probability of achieving a significant result at the final analysis? A conditional power below 20% is a common (though arbitrary) threshold for stopping.
A more principled alternative is the predictive probability of success (PPoS), described in detail at Section 12.7.1. PPoS integrates over the entire posterior distribution of the treatment effect instead of conditioning on a point estimate: it asks “given everything we’ve seen, what is the probability that this trial will succeed if we complete it?” That accounts for the statistical uncertainty in the interim estimate, which is often substantial in Phase II when sample sizes are small. A trial that has seen a modest positive trend with wide uncertainty has a meaningfully different PPoS than one where the interim estimate is close to zero with tight confidence.






TipFutility stopping in practice



A sponsor or DSMB using PPoS for futility monitoring should pre-specify both the stopping threshold (for example, PPoS \(< 0.05\) to \(0.20\), depending on the indication and the sponsor’s willingness to continue for potential upside) and the interim time points at which the analysis is run. Triggering a futility stop mid-trial without pre-specification creates regulatory and operational risk. Simulations across a range of plausible treatment effects should also verify the rule’s operating characteristics: that it does not stop trials with genuine efficacy too frequently.


The transition from Phase II to Phase III is the Phase II decision (see Figure 8.1). By this point, a sponsor has typically invested tens to hundreds of millions of dollars and several years of development time (DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016). Proceeding to Phase III will require several hundred million dollars more. And the probability of success in Phase III, even with positive Phase II data, is far from certain.

That decision weighs the strength of the efficacy evidence, the acceptability of the safety profile relative to the disease burden, whether an optimal dose for Phase III has been identified, and the drug’s commercial viability and competitive position.
Attrition is not uniform. In some therapeutic areas, central nervous system disorders for example, the failure rate runs above the 70% overall rate. Yet the failures serve a clear purpose. A rigorous Phase II program that kills an ineffective drug prevents a far costlier failure in Phase III by learning that the drug does not work before hundreds of millions of additional dollars are spent.

title: 8  Phase II: Exploratory
text:
8.5 Biomarkers
Throughout Phase II, biomarkers provide mechanistic insight that complements clinical endpoints. The most direct question is target engagement: is the drug hitting its intended target? Others track pathway modulation, whether the biological pathway is being affected as expected, and early disease response, the first signs that a therapeutic effect is appearing.
Biomarkers earn their place when clinical endpoints take time to manifest. Cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease occurs slowly; biomarkers of amyloid plaque or tau pathology may provide earlier signals that a drug is having biological effect, even if clinical improvement is not yet evident.
Biomarker changes do not always translate to clinical benefit. A drug might successfully engage its target without producing meaningful therapeutic improvement. The ultimate test remains clinical outcomes, but biomarkers help illuminate the path.

title: 9  Phase III: Confirmatory
text:
9.1 Characteristics of Phase III Trials
The transition from Phase II to Phase III often commits a sponsor to hundreds of millions of dollars on top of 5-7 years of prior work, all of it staked on a therapeutic benefit that Phase II could only suggest. Phase II asks whether a drug might work. Phase III has to demonstrate that it does, with the statistical rigor and methodological quality that regulatory agencies require for approval.
These large, well-controlled pivotal trials, classified as confirmatory under ICH E8(R1), generate the primary evidence regulators require for marketing approval and establish the safety profile with sufficient precision to support labeling (International Council for Harmonisation 2021).
Table 9.1 sets the two phases side by side (International Council for Harmonisation 2021).
Size is the first difference. Enrolling hundreds to thousands of patients, depending on the indication and endpoints, provides the statistical power to detect clinically meaningful treatment effects with high confidence. Rigor is the second: randomized, controlled designs minimize bias and confounding, and placebo controls (when ethically appropriate) or active comparators allow observed effects to be attributed to the investigational drug and not to other factors.
Phase III also moves closer to routine care. Early studies occur in specialized Phase I units; Phase III takes place in hospitals, clinics, and medical offices where patients receive routine care, under conditions intended to approximate the drug’s eventual clinical use. Trials typically run at multiple sites, often across multiple countries, and this multicenter approach helps ensure that the study population is representative of the intended patient population and that results are generalizable across different healthcare settings and geographical regions.
