title: 16  Randomization and Blinding
text:
16.1 Types of Randomization
For decades, hormone replacement therapy was thought to prevent heart disease, on the strength of observational studies showing that women who took hormones had lower rates of heart attacks. When randomized trials were finally conducted, they showed the opposite: combined hormone therapy increased the risk of coronary heart disease by roughly 29% and stroke by roughly 41% (Rossouw et al. 2002). The observational studies had been confounded. Women who chose to take hormones were healthier to begin with.
The same confounding arises at the bedside. A physician enthusiastic about a new treatment prescribes it to patients who seem likely to benefit and withholds it from those who seem too sick to respond. The treated patients do better. Nothing in the data can say whether that is the treatment or the selection.
The methodological history of medicine is full of treatments that looked effective in uncontrolled studies and proved worthless, or even harmful, when properly tested. Randomization and blinding are what stand between a trial and that history. Chapter 13 treated both as design-level choices; what follows is the mechanics.
Randomization eliminates the confounding (Cox 2009). A coin flip (or its statistical equivalent) decides who receives treatment and who receives control, so the groups are comparable at baseline and differences that emerge afterwards can be attributed to the treatment itself. Cox identifies three broad purposes for randomization: to avoid selection and other biases in a publicly convincing way, to provide a unified approach to estimating error in standard designs, and to provide a basis for exact tests of significance. Of these, bias avoidance is the most compelling in clinical trials, since failure to randomize appropriately may fatally compromise an investigation, and it is also what convinces those not directly involved in the trial that the comparison is fair.
The methods in Table 16.1 differ in how tightly they control group sizes and in how easily the next assignment can be guessed, and tighter control usually costs some unpredictability.
Simple randomization is a coin flip for each participant. In a large trial that works well enough; in a trial randomizing 20 patients, chance can produce 13 in one group and 7 in the other. Bradley Efron addressed the problem in 1971 with the biased coin design, which increases the probability of assigning to the underrepresented group when imbalance develops (Efron 1971).

With blocks of 4, a block might run ABAB, ABBA, BABA, or any of the six arrangements with two A’s and two B’s. After every complete block, the groups are guaranteed to be equal in size.
Stratified randomization goes further, running a separate randomization sequence inside each subgroup defined by an important prognostic factor. If disease severity predicts outcome, patients might be stratified as mild, moderate, or severe and randomized independently within each stratum, so the groups stay balanced on severity even when overall enrollment skews toward one level.
Minimization (or dynamic allocation) gives up randomizing each patient independently (Taves 1974; Pocock and Simon 1975). The algorithm reads the current imbalance among enrolled patients and assigns each new one to reduce it: if the treatment group has more older patients, the next older patient may be somewhat more likely to go to control. Balance can hold on several factors at once, and simulation studies show that minimization gives better-balanced groups than restricted or unrestricted randomization (Scott et al. 2002). A 2023 tutorial found minimization particularly beneficial when numerous major prognostic factors are known, when many centers of varying sizes recruit patients, or when the sample size is moderate (Coart et al. 2023).

title: 16  Randomization and Blinding
text:
16.2 Maintaining Randomization Integrity
Investigators have held sealed envelopes up to the light to read the assignment inside (Schulz 1995). That gesture is the whole problem: if the next allocation can be predicted or influenced, randomization has already stopped protecting against bias.
Allocation concealment is the mechanism that prevents it, and numbered envelopes were its old, sometimes inadequate form. Modern trials use Interactive Response Technology (IRT): computer or telephone systems that release the assignment only after the investigator has committed to enrolling a specific patient.
Once randomization occurs, the assignment should be followed. Treatment crossover, where patients switch from their assigned group to another, can blur the distinction between groups and complicate analysis. Sometimes it is unavoidable, as when patients on placebo deteriorate and ethical obligations require access to active treatment, and the analysis then has to account for it.
The 2025 revision of ICH’s Good Clinical Practice guideline, E6(R3), frames randomization and blinding as factors critical to trial quality and builds them into its quality-by-design expectations (International Council for Harmonisation 2025). A dedicated provision, Safeguard Blinding in Data Governance, directs sponsors to control access to unblinded data and to document any unblinding, planned or unplanned. They must also guard against inadvertent unblinding by the vendors and service providers who handle trial data.
crumbs: Part III: Phase III Deep Dive
16  Randomization and Blinding

title: 16  Randomization and Blinding
text:
16.3 The Power of Blinding
If randomization protects against bias in allocation, blinding protects against bias in everything that follows.
Suppose the investigators know which patients are receiving the experimental drug. Consciously or not, they might monitor those patients more closely, interpret a symptom more charitably, or encourage them to continue despite side effects. Patients who know they are receiving active treatment might report more improvement due to expectations. Where the outcome is subjective (pain, mood, quality of life), these biases can be substantial. Even a supposedly objective outcome is exposed: a radiologist who knows a patient is on active treatment might interpret a borderline scan as showing improvement. Blinding addresses these concerns by keeping treatment assignment unknown to those who might be influenced by it.
crumbs: Part III: Phase III Deep Dive

title: 16  Randomization and Blinding
text:
16.4 Levels of Blinding
Open-label trials make no attempt at blinding. They are common when the interventions are too different to disguise, surgery versus medication for instance, and they are susceptible to observer bias. Single-blind trials conceal the assignment from patients, which reduces participant expectations. Double-blind trials, the industry standard, conceal it from investigators as well. Triple-blind designs, the most rigorous, withhold it from those performing the statistical analysis too, until the study is formally concluded.

title: 16  Randomization and Blinding
text:
16.5 Technical Aspects of Blinding
Treatment and placebo must be indistinguishable in appearance (color, size, shape), taste, smell, and texture. A capsule and a tablet may both need over-encapsulation to match.
Unblinding procedures must be in place for emergencies. When a participant has a medical crisis and the treating physician needs the treatment assignment, the blind has to break for that one individual and hold for everyone else.
Side effects can compromise blinding on their own. A distinctive adverse effect (dry mouth, dizziness, skin discoloration) can let participants and investigators guess the assignment, which is why trials sometimes include perception of assignment assessments to evaluate whether blinding was maintained. When true blinding is not possible at all, blinded assessment salvages part of it: an assessor whose only contact with patients is the evaluation itself may remain blind when other study staff cannot, and imaging can be read by radiologists with no knowledge of assignment.

title: 16  Randomization and Blinding
section: 16.6 The Challenge of Device and Behavioral Trials
text:
16.6 The Challenge of Device and Behavioral Trials
How do you blind a patient to whether they received surgery? How do you blind a therapist to whether they are delivering cognitive behavioral therapy or a control intervention? Devices, surgical procedures, and behavioral interventions are where blinding is hardest.
Sham procedures are one answer. Control patients in a surgical trial may receive anesthesia and incisions but not the actual procedure. This is ethically controversial, since exposing patients to surgical risk without potential for direct benefit strikes some as unacceptable, and it may still be the only way to separate the effects of the procedure from placebo effects and expectation.
Active comparator designs sidestep the question. Both groups receive an intervention, and the trial asks which one is better.
Decisions about randomization and blinding shape the rest of the trial architecture. Each additional treatment arm complicates stratification and balance. The planned duration of blinding has to cover cross-over periods and long-term follow-up. Sponsors must also decide how to handle treatment discontinuations: a patient who stops the study medication still needs follow-up and data collection, or the randomized comparison loses its integrity.

title: 16  Randomization and Blinding
text:
16.7 Advanced Topics
Two randomization approaches extend beyond the fixed-probability designs above: response-adaptive randomization, which updates allocation probabilities as outcome data accumulate, and covariate-adaptive randomization, which conditions allocation on patient characteristics measured at enrollment.

Response-Adaptive Randomization
Response-adaptive randomization (RAR) shifts allocation probabilities during the trial in response to accruing outcome data, sending more patients to whichever arm is performing better. The ethical motivation is direct: if one treatment is proving superior, fewer patients should be assigned to the inferior arm during the trial itself.
The randomized play-the-winner rule of Wei and Durham (Wei and Durham 1978) is among the most transparent RAR designs. A success on one arm adds a ball of that treatment’s color to an urn; a failure adds a ball of the other treatment’s color. Each new patient draws from the urn, so the accumulating success rates steer allocation toward the better arm. Later Bayesian formulations implement the same intuition via Thompson sampling: at each allocation, compute the posterior probability that each arm is best and assign the next patient with that probability (see Section 12.8 for the statistical mechanics).
The most influential and contested application of play-the-winner ended with one patient in the control arm. Bartlett and colleagues were evaluating extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for newborns with severe respiratory failure, a condition with near-certain mortality untreated (Bartlett et al. 1985). In the 1985 trial that one infant died, and the eleven assigned to ECMO all survived. The ethical appeal was obvious: very few infants were exposed to the inferior arm. The evidentiary problem was equally clear. A trial with one control patient cannot estimate the control-arm survival rate with any precision, and the result was vigorously contested. A subsequent UK collaborative ECMO trial using conventional equal randomization confirmed the benefit (UK Collaborative ECMO Trial Group 1996).
ECMO remains the reference case for the central tension in RAR. Full treatment of the statistical debate, including temporal-trend bias, the Proschan objection, and the conditions under which RAR is and is not appropriate, is at Section 12.8.






NoteWhen RAR is useful and when it is not



RAR is most defensible in multi-arm settings (three or more arms) where the goal is to efficiently identify the best arm, particularly in early-phase or platform trials. In two-arm Phase III confirmatory trials, the power loss and potential for bias under RAR are rarely worth the patient-protection benefit, and conventional equal randomization is generally preferred (Korn and Freidlin 2011; Proschan and Evans 2020). Where RAR is used, two mitigations are practical: a burn-in period (equal allocation for the first N patients before adaptation begins) and a protect-control safeguard (never reducing the control arm below a minimum proportion).




Covariate-Adaptive Randomization
Covariate-adaptive randomization extends minimization, folding patient characteristics into allocation in more sophisticated ways (Atkinson 2002; Lin, Zhu, and Su 2015). Randomizing one patient at a time creates its own exposure: whoever knows the previous allocations may be able to predict the next assignment, which could enable selection bias. Atkinson carefully compared procedures that trade covariate balance against unpredictability (Cox 2009). FDA’s 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment recommends that sponsors specify the covariate-adjusted analysis prospectively, before unblinding, and include any stratification factors in that analysis model; complex covariate-adaptive randomization designs should be discussed with the review division in advance (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023).
For the mathematical foundations of randomization theory and practice, see Rosenberger and Lachin (Rosenberger and Lachin 2016); for response-adaptive methods specifically, Hu and Rosenberger (Hu and Rosenberger 2006).






NoteDiscussion Questions




Minimization is sometimes described as “not truly random” because the allocation of each patient is at least partly deterministic given the current enrollment counts. Some regulatory agencies have expressed concern about this. What is the substantive statistical concern (selection bias, inference validity, or both), how serious is it in practice, and what design modifications (e.g., a probabilistic minimization rule with a biased coin) address the concern?
A Phase III sponsor using response-adaptive randomization in a two-arm cardiovascular outcomes trial argues the design is justified because the trial will run for four years and it would be unethical to continue assigning patients to a placebo if the drug is clearly superior at year two. A statistician objects that temporal confounding could bias the estimate in a multi-year trial. Construct the statistician’s argument precisely, and propose the minimum safeguards that would make RAR defensible in this specific setting.
A trial investigator states: “We have allocation concealment, so blinding is not necessary for our open-label surgical trial.” Explain why allocation concealment and blinding protect against different sources of bias, using a concrete example from a surgical or device trial context to illustrate each.
A sponsor planning a 120-patient Phase II trial proposes to stratify by six prognostic factors (each binary), generating 64 possible strata. Most strata will have 0-2 patients. What specific statistical and operational problems arise from over-stratification at this sample size, and what would you recommend instead?
A placebo-controlled antipsychotic trial achieves double-blind status for capsule appearance and taste, but 68% of patients correctly guess their treatment assignment at the end-of-study perception survey, predominantly due to sedation and weight gain in the active arm. The primary endpoint is a subjective symptom rating scale. What are the implications for interpreting the primary efficacy result, what additional analyses could help bound the bias, and how should this be reported in the publication?

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.1 The Endpoint Hierarchy
In 1987, the FDA approved zidovudine (AZT) for HIV based on a trial stopped early for improved survival after 8 to 24 weeks of follow-up (Fischl et al. 1987). In 2011, the FDA revoked accelerated approval for bevacizumab in breast cancer after confirmatory trials found a much smaller effect on progression-free survival, the endpoint behind the approval, and no significant gain in overall survival to offset serious toxicity. In 2021, the approval of aducanumab for Alzheimer’s disease sparked controversy because the drug reduced amyloid plaques (the surrogate) but did not clearly improve cognition (the clinical outcome).
All three turn on one question: what should a trial measure to show that a drug works? The answer drives the design, the sample size, and the regulatory strategy, and in the end decides whether patients gain access at all.
An endpoint is the defined outcome a trial is designed to measure, the variable that answers the central question: did the treatment work? Some are assessed at a fixed time, such as the end of treatment or follow-up; others, such as the time to a first event, are captured as they occur.
Endpoints must be specified before the trial begins. The primary endpoint is the one the trial will be judged on: a Phase III trial with survival as its primary endpoint succeeds if the treatment group lives significantly longer than the control group, and fails if it does not. Secondary endpoints add information but do not determine the trial’s overall success.
Choosing the right endpoint means balancing what matters clinically (does the patient feel better? live longer?) against what is practical (can we measure it reliably, in a reasonable timeframe, with an affordable sample size?). That tension runs through everything that follows.
At the apex of the hierarchy (Table 17.1) sits what we ultimately care about: whether patients live longer, feel better, or function more effectively. These clinical endpoints (sometimes called hard endpoints) measure patient outcomes directly. Survival is the paradigm: either the patient is alive or they are not. There is no ambiguity, no measurement error, no room for interpretation.
Below them sit surrogate endpoints: measurements that are not themselves clinical outcomes but are reasonably expected to predict them. Blood pressure stands in for stroke and heart attack, viral load for AIDS progression, tumor shrinkage for cancer survival.
Further down are biomarkers: measurable characteristics that indicate biological processes, disease states, or responses to intervention. A biomarker can be a surrogate, but one that reliably reflects drug activity may still fail to predict clinical benefit.

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.2 Clinical Endpoints
In oncology, overall survival (OS) is the gold standard: the most reliable way to determine whether a cancer treatment extends life. In heart failure, the composite of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization captures both mortality and major morbidity.
Progression-free survival (PFS), the time from randomization to objective tumor progression or death, is often used as a primary oncology endpoint when waiting for OS would make a trial impractically long. FDA accepts PFS as a basis for approval in many settings, but treats it as a judgment call, not an automatic substitute for clinical benefit: the magnitude of the delay, whether tumor-related symptoms improve, and the drug’s toxicity all matter, because a longer time to progression does not by itself establish that patients live longer or feel better (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018).
That reliability comes at a price in trial size and duration. Events can be relatively rare and outcomes slow to develop, so a survival endpoint in a slowly progressing cancer can mean thousands of patients followed for years, with everything that implies for cost, time to approval, and patient access to therapy.
Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) ask the patient directly. How do you feel? What is your quality of life? Can you perform daily activities? Standardized questionnaires capture a perspective that may differ from what objective measurements suggest.
Regulators and payers increasingly want that perspective on record: a drug that moves a biomarker without making patients feel better is worth less than one that relieves symptoms. But responses can be influenced by expectations, mood, and cultural factors, so the instrument itself has to be shown to work.
Unlike a blood test, a questionnaire cannot be calibrated against a physical standard, so PROs are validated psychometrically instead, to prove they measure what they claim to. Content validity, usually established through qualitative interviews with patients, shows that the instrument covers the relevant symptoms; reliability makes the measure stable and reproducible; construct validity checks the score against other known measures of the disease; and sensitivity to change confirms the instrument can detect meaningful improvements. Regulators require this evidence before approving a labeling claim based on a PRO (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023b).
Smartphones and wearables have produced a newer category: endpoints derived from Digital Health Technologies (DHTs), which promise to replace the snapshot of a brief clinical assessment with continuous real-world monitoring. Digital biomarkers such as subtle changes in gait or voice may predict disease progression.
Validation is the hurdle. Regulators must be convinced that the device measures the concept accurately, that the measurement correlates with clinical status, and that the data is secure and attributable (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a). The FDA’s Digital Health Center of Excellence exists to guide these tools into regulatory decision-making.

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.3 Surrogate Endpoints
A surrogate can be measured sooner and in fewer patients, which can accelerate development and cut cost. The reasoning is clean: if intervention A lowers blood pressure more than intervention B, and lower blood pressure reduces cardiovascular events, then A should reduce cardiovascular events more than B.
But the logic can fail. The relationship between surrogate and outcome may not hold under all circumstances: an intervention might move the surrogate through a pathway that does not influence clinical outcomes, or affect clinical outcomes through pathways the surrogate never captures.
The CAST trial of the late 1980s tested antiarrhythmic drugs in post-heart attack patients. The drugs effectively suppressed the abnormal heart rhythms they were designed to treat, and the surrogate looked excellent. The trial was stopped early because treated patients were more likely to die than those on placebo. The trial report called the mechanism of the excess deaths unknown (Echt et al. 1991): the rhythm abnormalities may have been a marker of underlying heart damage rather than a cause of death, and the drugs that suppressed them may have added cardiac risks of their own.
Hormone replacement therapy improved lipid profiles and was widely prescribed for cardiovascular prevention on the strength of surrogate reasoning and observational data. Then the Women’s Health Initiative randomized trial showed that, despite the favorable lipid effects, hormone therapy increased cardiovascular events (Rossouw et al. 2002). The surrogate had predicted the wrong outcome.
The FDA distinguishes between validated surrogates (where the relationship to clinical outcome is well established) and reasonably likely surrogates (where the relationship is plausible but not fully established). The latter can support accelerated approval for serious conditions, but sponsors must then confirm the clinical benefit in post-marketing studies.
Molecular surrogates are moving through exactly this pathway now. In blood cancers, minimal residual disease (MRD), the small population of cancer cells that highly sensitive assays can detect after treatment, has emerged as a candidate surrogate for long-term survival. In April 2024, the FDA’s Oncologic Drugs Advisory Committee voted unanimously (12-0) that MRD is an appropriate endpoint to support accelerated approval in multiple myeloma, where confirming a progression-free or overall survival benefit can take many years (Landgren and Devlin 2025). In solid tumors, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) clearance is being studied as an analogous early signal in adjuvant trials. These molecular markers promise dramatically smaller and faster trials, but they carry the same obligation as every surrogate before them: the effect on the marker must ultimately be confirmed to predict the effect on how patients live and feel.

The primary endpoint is the outcome the trial is designed and powered to assess, the basis for the primary analysis and usually the endpoint regulatory decisions rest upon. Secondary endpoints fill in around it: other aspects of efficacy, safety, or tolerability, outcomes in subpopulations, the durability of effects over time. Table 17.2 sets out how each category is analyzed and interpreted.
What a secondary endpoint is worth depends on the primary. If the primary is negative (no statistically significant difference between treatment groups), positive secondaries are difficult to interpret: they may represent chance findings from multiple comparisons. If the primary is positive, they confirm and characterize the result.
The problem behind those chance findings is multiplicity. With a conventional significance threshold of 0.05, one in twenty tests will be “positive” by chance alone, so the more endpoints a trial tests, the higher its overall probability of a false positive finding. Multiplicity adjustment (such as hierarchical testing, gatekeeping procedures, or graphical approaches) controls the inflation.

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.5 Composite Endpoints
A composite endpoint combines multiple outcomes into a single measure. A participant might be counted as having an event if they experience any one of: death, heart attack, stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina. In the standard time-to-first-event analysis, each participant contributes only their first component event, and all components carry equal weight regardless of clinical severity (a hospitalization counts the same as a death). Because death precludes any later event, it acts as a competing risk for the non-fatal components.
Composites offer statistical efficiency: events are more common, since many participants will have at least one component, so smaller sample sizes may suffice. They also give a fuller picture of disease burden, capturing multiple manifestations of benefit or harm.
The cost is interpretive. If the composite is positive overall, which components drove it? Is a treatment that reduces hospitalizations but has no effect on death meaningfully beneficial, and should a drug that moves only the minor events be approved?
Components should be clinically related and of roughly similar importance; death and mild headache are not.
crumbs: Part III: Phase III Deep Dive
17  Endpoints and Outcomes

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.6 Time-to-Event Endpoints
A time-to-event endpoint records how long until a participant experiences the outcome, which, given long enough follow-up, lets the analysis separate a treatment that reduces eventual event rates from one that only delays them.
Survival analysis methods (Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank tests, Cox proportional hazards models) are designed for this kind of data. They accommodate participants who have not yet experienced an event (censored at the time of analysis) and those who drop out before one occurs.
Many of these analyses assume proportional hazards: the hazard ratio is constant over time. If a treatment lowers the hazard (the event rate among patients still event-free) by 30% at month 6, it should also lower it by 30% at month 12; the relative reduction in cumulative risk is smaller than 30% and shrinks as events accumulate. When this assumption is violated (as when a treatment takes time to work, or when its effects wane over time) alternative methods may be needed.
crumbs: Part III: Phase III Deep Dive

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.7 Ordinal Endpoints
Many outcomes that appear binary are actually ordered. A patient with heart failure may die, be hospitalized, remain symptomatic but outpatient, or be nearly asymptomatic; collapsing that spectrum into “event” or “no event” discards clinically meaningful information.
Ordinal endpoints keep the ordering, treating the outcome as a ranked scale. The modified Rankin Scale (mRS) in stroke trials is the canonical example: it runs from 0 (no symptoms) through 6 (death), with each step representing a clinically distinct level of functional disability (Saver 2007). The WHO Clinical Progression Scale used in COVID-19 trials similarly ranked patients from “uninfected” (score 0) to “dead” (score 10), with intermediate steps for degrees of oxygen support and hospitalization (WHO Working Group on the Clinical Characterisation and Management of COVID-19 infection 2020).
The standard analysis for ordinal outcomes is the proportional-odds (PO) model, a generalization of logistic regression (Agresti 2010). It assumes the treatment odds ratio is the same at every cut-point of the ordinal scale (on treatment, the odds of being in a better category than the reference are \(OR\) times higher, regardless of where the cut-point is placed). When that assumption holds, the model uses all the information in the ordinal scale instead of dichotomizing at an arbitrary threshold. The PO assumption can be checked with a score test and, if it is violated, the model replaced by a proportional-hazards model on discrete time or by non-parametric rank tests.
For sponsors the benefit is power: at a given sample size, an ordinal analysis is typically more powerful than a binary analysis of the same data, because the ordinal outcome carries more information. For regulators the benefit is interpretability, since an effect that shifts the entire distribution toward better categories says more about clinical benefit than a count of patients crossing one threshold.

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.8 The Win Ratio and DOOR
A composite of “death or hospitalization” counts a 2-day readmission the same as death, which misrepresents clinical priority. Two related methods restore the ranking a composite flattens.
The win ratio adjudicates every possible pair of patients (one from the treatment arm, one from the control) against a hierarchy of outcomes: check the most severe outcome first, death, and if one patient wins on it, that patient’s arm wins the pair; if the pair is tied on death, check the next outcome, hospitalization, and so on (Pocock et al. 2012). The statistic is the number of pairs the treatment patient wins divided by the number the control patient wins, with tied pairs excluded. Investigators set the hierarchy before the trial, which makes the clinical value judgment explicit. Win ratio analyses have been used in heart failure, oncology, and COVID-19 trials.
Desirability of Outcome Ranking (DOOR) extends the same idea to continuous outcomes and patient-reported data (Evans et al. 2015). Every patient receives a score (their DOOR) from a pre-specified combination of clinical outcomes, adverse events, and, optionally, patient preferences. Patients are ranked from worst to best, and the summary statistic is the probability that a randomly selected treatment patient has a better DOOR than a randomly selected control patient, with ties counted as half (\(P[T > C] + 0.5\,P[T = C]\)); no difference between arms gives 0.5, and a value above 0.5 means a treated patient is more likely to do better than worse, across the entire outcome spectrum (Evans and Follmann 2016). DOOR is most valuable when benefit and harm have to be summarized together, as in antibiotic trials where one measure should capture cure, adverse events, and resistance emergence.

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
section: 17.9 Estimands and Death as an Intercurrent Event
text:
17.9 Estimands and Death as an Intercurrent Event
The ICH E9(R1) estimands framework (International Council for Harmonisation 2019) formalized a question that had long been implicit in trial design: what treatment effect, precisely, is the trial trying to estimate? An estimand is the complete specification of the treatment comparison: the population, the treatment and control, the endpoint variable, how intercurrent events are handled, and the population-level summary measure.
Intercurrent events are events that occur after treatment initiation and affect either the interpretation or the observability of the endpoint. Treatment discontinuation, rescue medication use, and crossover to the other arm are common examples. Death is the hardest case.
When the primary endpoint is a non-fatal outcome (symptom score, functional status, quality of life), death is an intercurrent event that makes the outcome unobservable: a dead patient has no quality-of-life score. ICH E9(R1) defines five strategies for handling intercurrent events, and the choice among them for death fundamentally changes the estimand:

Composite (variable) strategy: treat death as a component of the endpoint itself, typically by assigning it the worst possible score. This estimates the effect on the composite of survival and the non-fatal outcome.
Hypothetical strategy: estimate what the outcome would have been if the patient had survived. This is a counterfactual that requires modeling assumptions.
Principal stratum strategy: restrict the estimate to the subpopulation of patients who would survive under either treatment assignment (the survivor average causal effect).
While on treatment strategy: use the outcome only up to the intercurrent event; for death, E9(R1) calls this while alive, and the estimand concerns symptoms or function while the patient is alive. Treatment discontinuation, a different intercurrent event, needs its own strategy.
Treatment policy strategy: use the endpoint value regardless of whether the patient discontinued treatment or took rescue medication. Unlike the strategies above, it offers no way to handle death, because a non-fatal outcome such as quality of life simply does not exist once the patient has died.

The practical consequence for trial teams is that an endpoint cannot be chosen without specifying its estimand at the same time: a quality-of-life endpoint and a symptom-improvement endpoint can be the same measurement and still be different estimands, depending on how death is handled. Pre-specifying it prevents post-hoc ambiguity about what the trial demonstrated and keeps the analysis aligned with the clinical question that motivated the trial.

title: 17  Endpoints and Outcomes
text:
17.10 Endpoint Selection in Practice
Regulators generally favor well-validated clinical outcomes, but sponsors must also confirm that the endpoint captures benefit patients and payers will recognize. Operationally, the endpoint has to be measurable with enough precision to maintain statistical power, and timed to avoid unnecessary delay while still providing a reliable prediction of long-term benefit. For patient-reported outcomes, established and validated instruments are the most direct route to findings that are reproducible and credible to external stakeholders. AI-based endpoint assessment, including automated image scoring, wearable-derived digital biomarkers, and NLP extraction of outcomes from clinical notes, is covered in Chapter 26.

title: 18  Site Selection and Feasibility
text:
18.1 Site Identification
A clinical trial exists only on paper until it enrolls patients, and patients are enrolled at clinical sites: hospitals, academic medical centers, private practices, or specialty clinics where investigators conduct the research. Industry surveys consistently show that patient recruitment is among the most common reasons for trial delays, and the wrong sites are where slow enrollment and poor data quality can begin. Historically, a Tufts CSDD benchmark of more than 150 trials run between 2008 and 2010 found that roughly 11% of investigative sites fail to enroll a single patient, with an additional 37% under-enrolling relative to their targets (Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development 2013; Getz 2012). For a significant portion of activated sites, the substantial investment in startup and training yields little to no scientific data. More recent Tufts CSDD benchmarking is somewhat more encouraging: comparing site-activation and enrollment metrics across 2012, 2019, and 2023, Lamberti and colleagues found that actual enrollment exceeded planned enrollment for a majority of studies and that timelines were often shorter than expected, though achievement varied by region and site type (Lamberti et al. 2024).
For a Phase III trial requiring 1,000 patients, a sponsor might need 100 or more sites across multiple countries, each capable of identifying eligible patients, conducting the study procedures competently, maintaining regulatory compliance, and producing high-quality data. Finding sites that meet all these criteria, and that are genuinely committed to the trial, is harder than it might appear.
The search for sites begins with investigators who have access to the target patient population. A rheumatoid arthritis trial needs rheumatologists. An advanced lung cancer trial needs oncologists at centers that see late-stage disease. A rare disease trial may need the handful of specialists worldwide who see enough patients to contribute meaningfully.
Access to patients matters most: a distinguished investigator who rarely sees the target population will not enroll patients. Geographic distribution matters for global trials, where regulatory authorities may require data from relevant populations and where sponsors want to understand drug effects across regions, and prior experience with the sponsor, the therapeutic area, or clinical research generally can indicate capability.
Databases of investigators, clinical trial registries, publication records, and prior trial performance all inform site identification, as do sponsor relationships with key opinion leaders and clinical networks. What those sources turn up ranges from large academic medical centers (AMCs) and integrated health systems to small, independent physician practices and site networks (see Figure 18.1).
Figure 18.1: Distribution of Clinical Research Site Types (2024). Data from WCG Clinical (2024).
The pool of available investigators is shrinking. A 2004 survey found that about 13% of physicians actively served as clinical investigators (Harris Interactive 2004); the 2024 WCG Clinical Research Site Challenges Report documents the number of unique U.S. investigators falling roughly 78%, from a pandemic-inflated peak of over 28,000 in 2020 to approximately 6,200 in 2024, alongside a 57% decrease in U.S. trial starts over the same period (WCG Clinical 2024). That headline overstates the structural trend: measured from the pre-pandemic level of about 23,000 investigators, the decline is closer to 73%, still a steep erosion of the base. The 2024 investigator and trial-start counts are also preliminary, drawn from a partial-year ClinSphere snapshot that exaggerates the single-year drop from 2023; WCG’s more recent site-challenges reporting has continued to show the same downward direction of travel.
The two trends in Figure 18.2 are distinct. The investigator pool surged with the pandemic in 2020 and then crashed, while new trial starts held relatively stable, peaking near 2,000 in 2021, before falling to fewer than 800 in 2024. Several forces drive that decline. COVID-19-related clinical activity, which peaked in 2021, has dropped substantially. Biopharma funding slowed sharply in 2022 and only partially rebounded in 2023, remaining well below its 2020-21 pandemic peak and constraining emerging-biopharma companies (IQVIA Institute for Human Data Science 2024). With the cost of bringing a single novel asset to launch, failures included, now estimated at $2.6-2.7 billion (Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2026; DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016), sponsors have grown risk-averse, concentrating capital on existing late-stage pipelines instead of new early-phase starts. Mounting regulatory hurdles and administrative burdens, meanwhile, have pushed study start-up past 60 days at most sites, discouraging new starts during periods of economic uncertainty (WCG Clinical 2024).
Other pressures are structural. Increasing clinical demands leave physicians with limited bandwidth for research, while research team staffing shortages further strain site capacity. This has exacerbated the “one and done” phenomenon, where approximately 66% of physicians who participate in a clinical trial do so only once before exiting the research ecosystem (WCG Clinical 2024). The consequences of this investigator attrition for recruitment and retention are discussed further in Chapter 19.
Figure 18.2: U.S. Investigators Participating in Clinical Trials Compared to New Trial Starts (2018-2024). Data from WCG Clinical (2024).
In that same 2004 survey, among physicians not involved in clinical trials, 38% cited lack of opportunity as the main reason for not serving as a Principal or Sub-Investigator, while 32% indicated that the time commitment is prohibitive (Harris Interactive 2004). Those constraints, compounded by the current exit of experienced investigators, make site identification a search for a rare combination: expertise, patient access, and operational bandwidth.
Historically, clinical trials have often failed to represent the diverse populations that will ultimately use the investigated therapies, which compromises the external validity of the results and can obscure important differences in safety or efficacy across demographic groups. The Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022 (FDORA) requires sponsors to submit Diversity Action Plans for Phase III trials (and certain other pivotal studies) to the FDA, but only for studies that begin enrolling more than 180 days after FDA publishes final guidance on the plans (U.S. Congress 2022). That statutory requirement stands, but its implementing guidance has been in flux: FDA’s June 2024 draft Diversity Action Plans guidance was withdrawn following a January 2025 executive order on diversity, equity, and inclusion, then restored under court order weeks later, and its final version was not issued by the statutory deadline (Grossi 2025). A separate December 2025 final guidance, Enhancing Participation in Clinical Trials, kept the emphasis on representative enrollment while dropping the “diversity” framing (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025). Until that final guidance appears the submission requirement has not taken effect, so sponsors should confirm the current posture rather than treat the mandate as settled.
Site selection is the primary operational lever for achieving diversity goals, which means engaging sites embedded in underrepresented communities: community hospitals, federally qualified health centers (FQHCs), or practices in geographic areas with high demographic density of the target populations. Those sites may lack the dedicated research infrastructure (study coordinators, -80°C freezers, secure storage) found in major academic centers, so the assessment must weigh a site’s potential capability with appropriate support alongside its current capability. The goal is a site network that geographically and demographically mirrors the epidemiology of the disease.

18.2 Feasibility Assessment
Once potential sites are identified, a feasibility assessment evaluates whether each site can realistically conduct the study. It typically involves questionnaires completed by site staff and may be supplemented by in-person or virtual visits. Table 18.1 summarizes the questions it asks and the answers that count as red flags.



Table 18.1: Site Feasibility Evaluation Criteria










Category
Key Questions
Red Flags




Patient Access

Investigator
Prior trial experience? Enrollment track record?

Infrastructure
Dedicated research staff? Equipment? Data systems?

Regulatory

Commitment

Each row calls for judgment. A site’s count of eligible patients has to be checked against the trials it is already running; investigator review covers licensure as well as enrollment track record; infrastructure means space for study procedures and laboratory capabilities along with dedicated research staff; and regulatory readiness turns on the efficiency of the local IRB and on any institutional requirements that could delay startup. Commitment is gauged from PI availability and coordinator turnover history, since a part-time PI or high turnover can undermine execution even at an otherwise well-resourced site.

title: 18  Site Selection and Feasibility
text:
18.3 The Enrollment Prediction Problem
Sites are notoriously over-optimistic about how many patients they will enroll. An investigator who claims to see 50 eligible patients per month and predicts enrolling 30 may ultimately enroll 3.
The gap has several sources. Investigators may not accurately know how many of their patients meet eligibility criteria: the criteria are often more restrictive than general clinical practice. Patients who appear eligible on paper may decline participation or prove ineligible upon screening, competing trials may draw away others, and staff turnover or other operational issues may limit enrollment capacity.
Experienced sponsors treat site predictions with skepticism and routinely discount them, often steeply (Getz 2008). Historical performance in prior trials is a more reliable guide than investigator optimism.

title: 18  Site Selection and Feasibility
text:
18.4 Financial and Contractual Negotiations
Between a qualified site and an activated one lies the negotiation of the Clinical Trial Agreement (CTA) and the site budget, and it is a consistent bottleneck: industry benchmarks show that the cycle time from site selection to site initiation is driven more often by contract execution than by regulatory approval (WCG Clinical 2024).
The CTA is a legally binding contract governing the relationship between sponsor and institution, addressing liability, indemnification, intellectual property rights, data ownership, and publication policy. Negotiations can be protracted, particularly with large academic medical centers that adhere to rigid institutional policies regarding indemnification and subject injury. For global trials, these agreements must also align with local laws regarding data privacy and anti-bribery regulations.
The site budget requires a granular accounting of both per-patient costs and overhead fees. A well-constructed one covers per-subject costs for clinical procedures, investigator time, and pharmacy services; startup fees for the administrative effort of regulatory submission and staff training; pass-through costs for variable expenses such as IRB fees and participant travel; and an institutional overhead surcharge applied to direct costs.
A related exercise, especially for U.S. sites, is the coverage analysis. Before a trial opens, the site reviews each protocol-required procedure to determine which costs may be billed to a participant’s insurance as routine clinical care and which must be paid by the sponsor as research costs. In the United States this determination rests on the Medicare Clinical Trial Policy (National Coverage Determination 310.1, “Routine Costs in Clinical Trials”) and, for commercial plans, the Affordable Care Act’s requirement that the routine patient costs of qualifying clinical trials be covered. Getting it wrong exposes the institution to double-billing and false-claims liability, so it demands specialized revenue-cycle expertise. Coverage analysis is one component of the study start-up work (alongside budgets and contracts) that sites most often identify as their leading source of start-up delay (WCG Clinical 2024).

Operational Bottlenecks by Site Type
The administrative burden of study start-up falls unevenly across the research ecosystem. According to the 2024 WCG Clinical Research Site Challenges Report, “Study Start-up” remains the single largest operational obstacle for larger institutions (academic medical centers, health systems, and community hospitals), with 43% of these sites identifying it as a primary challenge (WCG Clinical 2024). In contrast, smaller independent sites, physician practices, and site networks report start-up as a top challenge only 24% of the time, focusing instead on recruitment and retention as their primary burden (39%).
The timelines diverge accordingly. Approximately 60% of independent sites and physician practices report being able to initiate studies in under 60 days; 77% of academic medical centers, health systems, and community hospitals report start-up timelines exceeding 60 days, often because of the complexity of managing multiple internal stakeholders, the lack of centralized research administration, and bureaucratic regulatory layers (WCG Clinical 2024). Across all site types in the United States, “Budgets and Contracts” remain the single largest bottleneck, cited by 77% of sites as the primary contributor to start-up delays (see Figure 18.3).








Figure 18.3: Largest Contributors to Study Start-Up Timelines in the U.S. (2024). Data from WCG Clinical (2024).





Sponsors design their selection and activation strategy around these profiles, often favoring independent networks for rapid enrollment and academic centers for complex therapeutic areas or highly specialized patient populations.
Budget negotiation requires balancing fiscal discipline with the reality that sites must cover their costs to remain viable. Underfunding a site invariably shows up later as slow data entry and as deprioritization against better-funded trials.

The Site Initiation Visit (SIV) formalizes training. During the SIV, study personnel review the protocol in detail, walk through study procedures, demonstrate equipment, set up data systems, and ensure that essential supplies are in place. The investigator and key site staff must participate; their engagement (or lack thereof) often signals future performance.
Following the SIV, the site is authorized to begin screening and enrolling patients. The time from site selection to the point at which a site is cleared to enroll (the site activation time), and from there to the first patient enrolled, can range from weeks to months depending on regulatory complexity, contract negotiations, and site responsiveness.
A global network needs training delivered consistently across languages and time zones, usually through a combination of e-learning platforms and regional investigator meetings. Communication has to strike a balance: enough information to keep sites aligned, without overwhelming staff with unnecessary updates. Performance management systems track real-time metrics (enrollment rates, data quality, query resolution times) to identify the sites that need additional support or, in extreme cases, closure. Sponsors treat high-performing sites as long-term partners, and investment in those relationships through transparent communication and professional support improves enrollment, data quality, and site retention across the drug development program.
Global trials add complications of their own. Regulatory requirements differ by country, and language barriers affect training and documentation. Cultural factors influence patient willingness to participate in research, expectations about investigator relationships, and approaches to adverse event reporting. Standard of care may differ across regions, affecting choice of comparator and interpretation of results, while patient populations may differ in disease characteristics, comorbidities, and concomitant medications. Some regions may have limited research infrastructure requiring more intensive support, while others may have mature research environments but intense competition for investigators and patients. All of it feeds back into trial design and analysis.

title: 19  Patient Recruitment and Retention
text:
19.1 Strategies for Recruitment
A trial cannot succeed without patients. Getting enough of them, quickly enough, is one of the most persistent problems in clinical research. Enrollment periods projected to take months stretch into years. Sites expected to contribute dozens of patients contribute single digits. Some trials are abandoned altogether when enrollment proves impossible.
The Forum on Drug Discovery, Development, and Translation identifies participant recruitment as one of the most “onerous” and high-risk steps in the entire development process, characterized by significant cost, time, and likelihood of failure (Wagner et al. 2018). Industry surveys have historically identified recruitment and staffing as the primary bottlenecks, but by 2024 the “Complexity of Clinical Trials” (38%) had overtaken recruitment and retention (36%), study start-up (35%), and site staffing (31%) as the top challenge facing research sites (Figure 19.2) (WCG Clinical 2024). Nearly half (47%) of all sites (and 50% of U.S. sites) reported that these operational challenges forced them to reduce the number of studies they agreed to participate in during the preceding year (WCG Clinical 2024).
Sites respond by adding capacity and by shedding work. Hiring additional staff (42%) and prioritizing training (36%) are the common answers, but many sites also elect to participate in fewer studies (27%) or to select trials with less complex designs (21%) to stay operationally viable Figure 19.1.
The pressure has been building for a long time. Trials have grown larger, target populations more specialized, and competition for the same subjects more intense; decades of Tufts CSDD benchmarking document steadily rising protocol complexity and enrollment targets, with more procedures and stricter eligibility criteria per study (Getz, Smith, and Kravet 2023; Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development 2021). Yet only a small fraction of eligible patients ultimately enroll, even though public-perception surveys consistently find that most people say they would be willing to consider a trial if asked. That gap between stated willingness and actual enrollment is what recruitment strategy exists to close.
Slow recruitment has cascading consequences. Patients wait longer for therapies that might help them, sites stay open and under oversight while the budget runs, and every month of delay shortens the effective patent life of a drug that works. A prolonged enrollment period may also compromise scientific validity by introducing population heterogeneity.
Start with the calculus each prospective participant faces, weighing perceived risks against potential benefits. Patients with serious illness may see a trial as their most promising treatment option; patients whose condition is already well managed weigh uncertain medical risks against the practical burden of frequent visits and travel. Altruism enters the calculation, and so does the patient’s trust in the healthcare system, a trust that a community’s historical experience with clinical research can shape.
Recruitment is an attrition problem. Figure 19.3 shows the shape: between the target population and the patients who actually enroll, a different barrier removes people at every stage. Reaching enough of them means working several channels at once (Table 19.1).

Provider referral depends on a physician or other clinician spotting an eligible patient and raising the option. Because most patients are not actively seeking trials, provider engagement is a primary driver of enrollment; because busy clinicians may not think to mention a trial to an appropriate patient, education and reminders are part of the work. Direct-to-patient advertising goes around the clinic, using television and radio advertisements, online banner ads, social media campaigns, and search engine marketing, all of it subject to regulations governing what claims such advertising can make. Decentralized trial elements work on burden instead of awareness, bringing the trial to patients who cannot easily travel to a traditional research site.

title: 19  Patient Recruitment and Retention
text:
19.2 AI/ML-Enabled Recruitment and Patient Engagement
AI and machine learning can help recruitment along two routes: making eligibility and outreach computable, so that organizations can find potentially eligible participants in real-world data with less manual effort, and supporting scalable, consistent communication that reduces friction and helps sustain retention. Both are socio-technical systems whose value depends on data quality, workflow design, and human oversight, and both can introduce new risks if deployed without governance.

Making eligibility computable: feasibility and EHR-based identification
Before outreach begins, sponsors and sites have to decide whether the protocol is operationally plausible at all: how many patients are likely to qualify at a site or network, and which criteria will drive the screen failures. Data-driven feasibility answers those questions from historical EHR and claims data, estimating cohort size and anticipating operational constraints such as visit cadence, laboratory requirements, and competing studies. That shifts planning from informal judgment toward testable assumptions, though the validity of any estimate depends on how well eligibility criteria can be represented in data and how representative those data are of the intended trial population (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b; Hripcsak and Albers 2013).
Automated identification from EHRs is a pipeline: translate protocol criteria into a computable phenotype, execute it against clinical data, then put the candidate list in front of a clinician or coordinator before anyone is contacted or screened. Many criteria map cleanly to structured elements (diagnosis codes, medications, laboratory values, procedures, and timestamps); others reside in unstructured notes (symptom narratives, imaging interpretations, nuanced exclusions), which is why natural language processing complements rules and statistical models when candidate lists are assembled (Hripcsak and Albers 2013).
Standardization through common data models and cohort tooling, exemplified by OHDSI and the OMOP Common Data Model, lets a cohort definition execute consistently across sites in a federated manner (Hripcsak et al. 2015; Overhage et al. 2012). Standards-based interoperability supports the same workflows through APIs: SMART on FHIR supports substitutable applications that retrieve patient-level data, and the FHIR Bulk Data Access specification supports population-level exports for governed research workflows (Mandel et al. 2016; Health Level Seven International 2024). Because EHR data were not originally collected for research, the practical constraints are often provenance, missingness, and fitness-for-purpose, not model choice alone; sponsors should align their use of EHR data with regulatory expectations for documentation, traceability, and data integrity in clinical investigations (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018).


Engagement, retention, and equity in AI-mediated workflows
Communication technologies can answer common questions, deliver consistent study education, collect structured pre-screening information, send scheduling reminders, and route complex concerns to a human. The design challenge is to reduce coordinator load and participant burden without creating misleading medical advice or undue influence, which puts human-AI interaction design and clear escalation paths at the center (Amershi et al. 2019). The evidence base for conversational agents in health remains mixed and context-dependent, with systematic reviews noting that many evaluations are early-stage and heterogeneous, and often lack robust safety assessment even when user satisfaction is high (Laranjo et al. 2018). In trials, electronic informed consent and remote communication can reduce friction, but they must preserve comprehension, voluntariness, and proper documentation (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016).
A model that prioritizes outreach or determines who is contacted first is deciding who gets access to research, which amplifies privacy, bias, and accountability risks; reliance on proxies such as cost or utilization can encode structural inequities even when overall accuracy appears high (Obermeyer et al. 2019). A defensible approach therefore includes explicit inclusion goals, audit trails for cohort logic and model versions, subgroup performance checks, and clear procedures for human review and overrides (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023; World Health Organization 2021; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a, 2025). Recruitment-facing tools should be documented with enough transparency for review and replication, and AI-enabled protocols and reports can be structured using emerging extensions such as SPIRIT-AI, CONSORT-AI, and TRIPOD+AI, depending on whether the system is a trial intervention, a reporting artifact, or an operational prediction model (Rivera et al. 2020; Liu et al. 2020; Collins et al. 2024).

title: 19  Patient Recruitment and Retention
text:
19.3 Barriers to Recruitment
Lack of awareness remains a primary obstacle: many eligible patients never learn that a trial for their condition exists, or how to reach one. Those who do learn are often excluded by restrictive eligibility criteria, disqualified by a common comorbidity or a routine medication. Those who qualify may still find the logistics impossible, since intensive testing schedules and dietary constraints can be incompatible with daily work and family life. An informed consent process misaligned with a patient’s culture or language can also feel intimidating or exclusionary.

Geographic Access and Rural Populations
Between 2008 and 2022, only 42.4% of U.S. counties hosted at least one Phase 1-3 cancer clinical trial, and rural counties were significantly less likely to have a trial site (Gu et al. 2024). In 2022, 86% of nonmetropolitan counties had no active cancer treatment trials, compared to 44% of metropolitan counties (Unger, McAneny, and Osarogiagbon 2025). Research sites concentrate in urban academic medical centers, systematically excluding rural populations.
Nearly 17% of the U.S. population over age 35 lives more than 100 miles from an NCI-funded trial site, and that burden falls disproportionately on low-income individuals (Shriver et al. 2025). Travel distance, time away from work, and unreliable transportation reinforce one another, and for many rural patients the combination rules out participation entirely.
Rural populations experience higher cancer mortality rates and different disease patterns, yet remain systematically underrepresented in the trials that generate treatment evidence. Outcomes data suggest that the treatment disparity may be largely attributable to access rather than biology: an analysis of 36,995 patients in 44 SWOG trials found that rural and urban patients achieved similar survival outcomes when given uniform access to care through clinical trial participation (Unger et al. 2018).
Community-based trial networks can narrow that gap. The NCI Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP) is one, and in the SWOG network-group trials described above, which enrolled patients from 1986 to 2012, 19.4% of participants came from rural areas, the same as the rural share of the U.S. population with cancer (Unger et al. 2018; Unger, McAneny, and Osarogiagbon 2025).
Decentralized elements attack the travel itself. Telemedicine, remote monitoring, home visits by nurses, remote consent, virtual study visits, and direct-to-patient drug shipment reduce travel burden and can maintain data quality while expanding access; a small pilot comparing decentralized and conventional site models reported that 89% of patients in the decentralized arm completed the study versus 60% in the conventional arm (Sommer et al. 2018), though such comparisons may reflect selection effects, since the sites and patients willing to adopt decentralized elements may differ systematically. Mobile clinics go one step further, taking trial and screening activities directly into rural communities while maintaining protocol compliance: the Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center coordinates a mobile mammography program that brings breast cancer screening to women in rural areas of Appalachia (Unger, McAneny, and Osarogiagbon 2025).
Operationally, geographic barriers are a site-selection problem: they call for the same deliberate reach beyond high-volume academic centers, and the same investment in building site capability where it is thin, that Chapter 18 describes.

title: 19  Patient Recruitment and Retention
text:
19.4 The Importance of Retention
Enrollment is the first half of the problem. High dropout rates can severely reduce a trial’s statistical power and introduce bias, particularly if the attrition is related to treatment response or side effects. Retention is won in the details of participant experience: flexible scheduling, timely compensation, and clear, empathetic communication from study staff. Central to all of it is the relationship between the investigator and the participant, since patients who feel personally connected to the research team are more likely to continue through to the study’s conclusion.

Physician Participation and the “One and Done” Phenomenon
The same attrition runs on the investigator side, and it deepens the recruitment crisis. The base of active U.S. investigators has shrunk sharply, and most physicians who serve on a trial never do so again, the “one and done” phenomenon documented in Chapter 18. Among the reasons they leave are the complexity of modern protocols, the mounting technology burden, and financial structures that fail to account for the heavy time investment required relative to routine clinical care. Each departure costs the industry expertise it must then replace by onboarding new, less-experienced sites, which slows development further.
The attrition extends to the research staff as well. High turnover among clinical research coordinators (CRCs) and nurses disrupts continuity and increases the risk of documentation errors, and while turnover rates have stabilized somewhat in 2024, a significant portion of the industry still faces high churn, complicating the long-term viability of sites (see Figure 19.4).








Figure 19.4: Yearly staff turnover rates at clinical research sites (2024). Data from WCG Clinical (2024).







Strategic Enrollment and Generalizability
An accrual target can be met with the wrong patients. Enrollment has to reflect the populations that will ultimately use the treatment, and the reason is scientific before it is regulatory: drug metabolism, disease expression, and treatment response vary systematically across age, sex, genetic factors, and comorbidities.
Pharmacokinetics differ substantially by age, driven by changes in renal and hepatic function, body composition, and drug-drug interactions from polypharmacy. Sex affects drug distribution through body fat percentage, metabolism through CYP enzyme activity, and disease pathways through hormonal influence. Genetic polymorphisms in drug-metabolizing enzymes such as CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 vary in frequency across populations and can alter therapeutic response and toxicity profiles. The disease phenotype itself may differ: hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease show distinct clinical presentations and progression patterns across demographic groups.
If trial enrollment systematically excludes the elderly, women, or specific genetic backgrounds, the resulting efficacy and safety data may not generalize to real-world use: a treatment optimized for a narrow trial population may be suboptimal, or even unsafe, when prescribed more broadly. Pediatric dosing cannot be reliably extrapolated from adult trials, and elderly patients with multiple comorbidities may experience different benefit-risk profiles than younger, healthier trial participants.
Representative enrollment requires intentional design: site selection that reaches diverse geographies and care settings, eligibility criteria that do not unnecessarily exclude common comorbidities, and recruitment strategies that address logistical barriers (transportation, language, visit burden). Regulatory guidance increasingly expects sponsors to justify enrollment targets based on the intended-use population and to monitor accrual across relevant subgroups during the trial (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a). That guidance and its recent turbulence, including the withdrawn-then-restored 2024 Diversity Action Plans draft and the December 2025 final Enhancing Participation in Clinical Trials guidance that dropped the explicit “diversity” framing, are detailed in Chapter 18. The statutory basis for representative enrollment and its scientific rationale are unchanged.


Digital retention toolkit: engagement beyond enrollment
Traditional retention frameworks addressed dropout and loss to follow-up through clinic visits, phone calls, and mailed reminders (Meinert 2013). In the DCT era, retention increasingly depends on digital engagement: app-based reminders, SMS check-ins, telehealth visits, and patient portals that reduce the friction of continued participation (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024c).
Digital engagement requires infrastructure and continuing attention. Executed poorly, it can feel intrusive or impersonal and may increase dropout rather than reduce it.






TipChecklist: Digital Retention Toolkit




Platform selection: validated ePRO/eCOA and patient communication platforms with accessibility features (screen reader compatibility, multilingual support, offline functionality where relevant).
Message cadence and content: prespecified reminder schedules; personalized content where feasible; clear escalation paths for non-response.
Telehealth integration: defined workflows for remote visits (scheduling, consent for recording if applicable, documentation, safety escalation).
Help desk support: accessible support for technical issues, with defined response times and escalation to site coordinators for clinical questions.
Retention monitoring: dashboards tracking visit completion, ePRO compliance, and engagement metrics; predefined thresholds for coordinator outreach.
Participant feedback loop: mechanism for participants to report burden concerns or technical issues, with documented response and protocol amendment pathways if patterns emerge.

title: 20  Logistics and Project Management
text:
20.1 Organizational Framework and Roles
A large Phase III trial might involve 200 clinical sites across 25 countries, 3,000 patients, half a dozen specialized vendors, and a timeline of 4 years. Each patient visit generates data that must be captured, cleaned, and locked. Each site requires contracts, regulatory approvals, training, monitoring, and closeout, and each country applies its own regulatory requirements, language considerations, and import procedures for investigational drugs. Temperature-sensitive biologics must be shipped in validated cold chains that hold -70°C across continents, and randomization systems must be available 24/7 to assign treatments the moment a patient qualifies. All of it has to happen without compromising the scientific integrity that makes the trial’s results meaningful.
This is the domain of clinical trial logistics: the practical coordination of people, documents, supplies, and processes that converts a protocol on paper into executed research. A brilliant study design means nothing if the drug never reaches the patient, if the data are lost in transmission, or if the site closes before enrollment completes.
A clinical trial runs on delegated work. Accountability does not travel with it. Sponsors hand work to CROs and specialized vendors, principal investigators hand tasks to coordinators and sub-investigators, and each transfer moves the work without moving the ultimate responsibility for it.
crumbs: Part III: Phase III Deep Dive
20  Logistics and Project Management

title: 20  Logistics and Project Management
text:
The Key Players
The sponsor initiates, manages, and finances the trial. Pharmaceutical companies, biotech firms, academic institutions, and government agencies all serve as sponsors. The sponsor owns the trial and bears ultimate responsibility for its conduct, including investigator selection, monitoring, and regulatory compliance (21 CFR 312.50).
The investigator, usually a physician designated as the Principal Investigator (PI), takes responsibility for the trial at a specific site. The PI supervises the research team, ensures patient safety, obtains informed consent, and guarantees that the protocol is followed faithfully. Though the PI may delegate tasks to coordinators and sub-investigators, regulatory accountability cannot be delegated: the PI who signs FDA Form 1572 is held responsible for all trial conduct at that site.
Contract Research Organizations (CROs) are specialized service providers that sponsors hire to conduct trial activities. CROs may provide anything from a single service (such as monitoring or data management) to full end-to-end trial management. Grand View Research estimated the global healthcare CRO market at $59.6 billion in 2025 (Grand View Research 2026).
The study coordinator, also called the Clinical Research Coordinator (CRC), works at the site under the PI’s supervision. Coordinators are the workhorses of clinical research, managing patient visits, collecting data, maintaining regulatory documents, and serving as the primary point of contact between the site and the sponsor or CRO.
Vendors provide specialized services: central laboratories analyze specimens, electronic data capture companies provide software platforms, imaging core labs review scans, and interactive response technology vendors manage randomization and drug supply.


Delegation, Accountability, and Partner Selection
Delegation follows specific rules. Sponsors may transfer obligations to CROs through written agreements (21 CFR 312.52); once transferred, the CRO assumes regulatory responsibility for those tasks, while the sponsor must still oversee the CRO’s performance, review monitoring reports, and verify that delegated tasks are executed properly. As industry observers note, the sponsor remains captain of the ship even when the CRO handles navigation: the sponsor is still responsible for reaching the destination safely. At the site, a delegation log documents which coordinators, sub-investigators, and nurses perform which tasks, and the PI remains accountable for all of it.
Selecting the right partner is therefore a critical project management task, and it typically follows a path defined by internal SOPs. Before contacting vendors, the sponsor must define exactly what is being outsourced, ranging from a specific functional service (such as data management alone) to a full-service model where the CRO handles everything from site selection to the final clinical study report. The sponsor then issues a Request for Proposal (RFP) outlining study specifications (protocol synopsis, number of patients, number of sites, timeline) and asking vendors to provide detailed budgets and proposals. Vague requirements produce vague, incomparable bids.
Top candidates are then invited to a bid defense meeting. Price is on the table, but so is chemistry: the sponsor meets the team who will run the project, not the salespeople, and assesses their experience in the therapeutic area, their available staffing, and whether their systems (EDC, CTMS) are compatible with the sponsor’s infrastructure.
The contract that follows formalizes a scope of work, and managing that scope is a primary duty of the project manager: work outside it triggers a change order to adjust budget and timeline, and uncontrolled scope creep is a common cause of budget overruns.

title: 20  Logistics and Project Management
text:
20.2 Biospecimen Logistics
In many modern trials, particularly in oncology and rare diseases, the collection, processing, and transport of biospecimens (blood, tissue, urine, or other biological materials) is a primary logistical thread. Clinical data can be captured electronically; biospecimens are physical assets that require sophisticated chain-of-custody and stability controls.
The chain has several links, and each of them can fail. Sites collect under strict protocol-defined procedures that fix the timing relative to dosing and the collection tubes or kits to be used. Many specimens then require immediate processing at the site (centrifugation, aliquoting) before freezing. Storage means calibrated -20°C or -80°C freezers with alarm systems, since an unnoticed temperature excursion loses the sample. Specialized couriers move the material in dry ice or liquid nitrogen to central laboratories or biorepositories. Throughout, a “Biospecimen Log” or specialized software tracks each sample from the patient to the final analysis, maintaining the link between the participant and their biological data while preserving confidentiality.
A missed collection window or a temperature excursion during transit can lose critical exploratory or primary endpoint data, which makes biospecimen management a high-risk component of the trial’s operational design.
