title: 22  Clinical Monitoring
text:
22.7 Trial Governance Committees
Clinical trials, and large Phase III studies especially, also run under specialized governance committees supplying independent expertise and accountability.

Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB)
The Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB; see Section 9.6 for alternate names) provides independent oversight of accumulating safety and efficacy data. It sees unblinded comparative results that are normally withheld from the sponsor and the investigators, which is what allows it to recommend stopping a trial early for safety, futility, or overwhelming efficacy.
Composition typically runs to 3-7 members: clinical experts in the disease area, a biostatistician experienced in interim analyses, and sometimes an ethicist or patient representative. Members must be independent, free from conflicts of interest with the sponsor and uninvolved in the trial’s conduct.
The DSMB operates under a charter that settles in advance what it will examine and what it may do: scope of review (safety only, or safety and efficacy), meeting frequency and the triggers for ad hoc meetings, statistical stopping rules and decision thresholds, the process for communicating recommendations to the sponsor, and confidentiality requirements.
DSMB meetings typically include an open session (where the sponsor presents trial status without unblinding) and a closed session (where the unblinded statistician presents interim analyses to DSMB members only). The DSMB may recommend: continue as planned, modify the protocol, stop enrollment, stop treatment, or stop the trial entirely. Recommendations go to the sponsor, who retains authority for final decisions but must document the rationale if departing from DSMB advice.






NoteNote: Committee Documentation as an Inspection Artifact



Committee governance is a documentation problem: committees matter operationally only insofar as their processes are specified, followed, and evidenced. Meinert’s emphasis on formal committee structures and procedures remains relevant even as meeting modalities shift (e.g., secure virtual or hybrid meetings) (Meinert 2013). From a GCP and inspection standpoint, the relevant artifacts include charters, membership independence and conflict management, meeting minutes, recommendation letters, and controlled distribution of any unblinded information (International Council for Harmonisation 2025).




DSMBs for Platform and Adaptive Trials
A platform DSMB may be overseeing six, eight, or ten treatment arms at once, each at a different stage of enrollment and maturity. The SNAP platform (S. aureus bacteremia) had a single DSMB reviewing multiple treatment domains at once. A DSMB member handed a standard two-column comparison table can form a judgment quickly. The platform equivalent requires holding in mind which arms are still enrolling, which have closed, and which interim result from one domain might change conduct in another.
The board has to be constituted for that complexity. Not every member can be an expert in every arm’s therapy, so domain-specific consultants are sometimes added for particular reviews. Conflicts of interest are harder to manage too: where several companies’ drugs are under evaluation at once, members with no relationship to any sponsor are difficult to find, and disclosure and recusal procedures must be detailed in the charter.
When a single arm fails, the recommendation is arm closure, not trial termination, and the DSMB has to say so precisely: “close domain B for futility in the MSSA population; continue all other domains as specified.” A partial stop of that kind requires a charter that explicitly anticipates arm-level action and specifies how the remaining platform continues without the closed arm. Spillover needs anticipating as well. If domain A’s success changes the standard of care and with it the control event rate for domain B, that has to be surfaced.
Complex Bayesian adaptive platforms also require real-time statistical computation for interim analyses that a DSMB’s own biostatistician may not be equipped to run independently. The standard solution is a separate unblinded statistical team (sometimes called the independent statistical center) that prepares the interim analysis package for the DSMB. This team is firewalled from the sponsor’s statisticians and has full access to unblinded data. The charter must specify exactly what it prepares, what forms of results reach the DSMB (for example, which summaries the sponsor may see in the open session, and in what aggregated form), and how results are archived to support audit.
Adjusting for temporal trends, to account for changes in background treatment or disease severity over the trial’s lifespan, creates a presentation problem of its own: should the DSMB see raw observed data or model-adjusted comparisons? Raw safety data from different time periods may not be directly comparable without the adjustment, and DSMB members without statistical modeling backgrounds may struggle to evaluate model-adjusted estimates. For safety reviews in particular, where model-adjusted data may require machinery that is not readily available, a DSMB may see raw event counts alongside model-adjusted efficacy summaries. The unblinded statistician should be prepared to explain what the model is doing and what a DSMB member would see in the raw data, so the board can calibrate its judgment.
The COVID anticoagulation multi-platform RCT, pooling REMAP-CAP, ATTACC, and ACTIV-4a, used a novel governance structure: each platform kept its own DSMB, but all three reviewed the same combined analyses, produced under a common statistical analysis plan, and coordinated their recommendations. Each platform could then satisfy its own regulatory obligations (each had its own sponsor, protocol, and regulatory and ethics approvals) while the adaptive stopping decisions were made on the full combined evidence. The coordination required detailed pre-specification of how stopping decisions would be communicated across platforms.


Endpoint Adjudication Committees
Where endpoints are subject to interpretation (cardiovascular events, disease progression, cause of death), a Clinical Events Committee (CEC) or Endpoint Adjudication Committee provides independent, blinded review. Adjudication is what keeps endpoint determinations consistent across sites and investigators: a myocardial infarction diagnosed at one hospital should meet the same criteria as one diagnosed at another. The CEC reviews source documents (ECGs, troponin values, imaging) and applies protocol-defined criteria to classify events.
Operationally, adjudication adds timeline pressure. Cases must be prepared, reviewed, and adjudicated before database lock, and large trials with thousands of potential events may require dedicated adjudication infrastructure and close coordination with data management.


Steering Committees
A Steering Committee (SC) provides scientific oversight and guidance on protocol interpretation, drawing its membership from the principal investigators, sponsor representatives, and sometimes independent experts. Its authority is whatever the sponsor delegates to it, from advice alone to primary responsibility for the study’s design and the quality of its conduct (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2006). It may recommend protocol amendments, interpret eligibility questions, and guide publication strategy. It should remain blind to outcomes by treatment arm, and the distinction between scientific guidance (SC) and safety oversight (DSMB) must be maintained to preserve the DSMB’s independence.
AI tools for remote monitoring, risk-signal prioritization, and automated source data review within risk-based quality management frameworks are covered in Chapter 26.

title: 23  Safety Monitoring and Reporting
text:
23.1 Investigator Responsibilities
A patient in a trial has a heart attack. From the moment the investigator learns of it a clock runs: the report must reach the sponsor immediately (most protocols write that as within 24 hours), and if it turns out to be a life-threatening reaction nobody expected, the sponsor then has 7 calendar days to reach regulators in every country where the study is running. However thoroughly a drug has been studied in laboratories and animal models, the first patients to receive it are pioneers, and pioneers face risks. Safety reporting is how the rest of the trial finds out in time to act.
Each category below carries its own reporting obligation (Table 23.1).
An adverse event (AE) is any untoward medical occurrence in a trial participant, caused by the investigational drug or not. A patient who develops a cold during a trial has experienced an adverse event. So has a patient hospitalized for a condition entirely unrelated to the study drug. The net is cast this wide to keep a potential safety signal from being missed, though rare or delayed ones may surface only after the drug reaches a larger, more diverse population (Chapter 10).
A serious adverse event (SAE) meets one of six criteria: it results in death, is life-threatening, requires hospitalization (or prolongs existing hospitalization), causes persistent or significant disability, is a congenital anomaly, or is otherwise medically important. Seriousness says nothing about causality (an SAE may have nothing to do with the study drug), but it triggers expedited reporting and heightened scrutiny.
Seriousness is a regulatory classification driven by an event’s outcome (the six criteria above). Severity describes intensity, most often graded on the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) scale that runs from Grade 1 (mild) through Grade 2 (moderate), Grade 3 (severe), and Grade 4 (life-threatening) to Grade 5 (death). The two move independently. A high-grade but asymptomatic laboratory abnormality that meets no seriousness criterion is severe without being serious; a mild event that lands the patient in hospital is serious whatever its grade.
Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are adverse events thought to be caused by the investigational product, and deciding which events qualify is one of the most consequential clinical judgments in a trial. The evidence is circumstantial: timing, biological plausibility, and whether anything else explains the event. Investigators and sponsors both grade their certainty, though many scales are in use and none is an international standard (International Council for Harmonisation 1994). On one common five-level scale, “Definite” requires a clear temporal link, a positive response when the drug is withdrawn or reintroduced, and no alternative explanation. As the evidence weakens, events fall to “Probable” or “Possible,” depending on the strength of the temporal link and the plausibility of other causes. “Unlikely” and “Unrelated” sit at the far end, where the timing is improbable or an extraneous cause (a pre-existing condition, a traumatic accident) supplies a clear alternative.
Suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions (SUSARs) are serious adverse reactions whose nature or severity is not consistent with the drug’s reference safety information, the list of expected reactions in the Investigator’s Brochure or an alternative document such as an approved drug’s label (International Council for Harmonisation 1994, 2010, 2025). They trigger the most expedited reporting, because they are new safety information that may change how the drug is viewed. A reaction the brochure mentions only as a class effect, or a listed one in a more specific or more severe form (hepatic necrosis where only hepatitis is listed), still counts as unexpected (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024).
Cutting across this hierarchy is the adverse event of special interest (AESI): an event, serious or non-serious, that the protocol or safety plan singles out for heightened, often accelerated monitoring because of a specific concern about the drug or its class. An AESI is tracked and reported on a protocol-specified timeline regardless of where it otherwise falls among the categories above. Drug-induced liver injury, suicidal ideation, and, for immunomodulatory therapies, cytokine release syndrome are common examples.
Immediate SAE reporting, and everything upstream of it, is a site obligation: investigators bear primary responsibility for protecting the participants in front of them. The duty begins with recognizing an adverse event as one. From there it must be documented thoroughly and reported on the timelines the protocol and the regulations set (serious events that are themselves study endpoints, such as deaths in a mortality trial, may follow the protocol’s schedule unless there is evidence suggesting the drug caused them); the SAE window is tight so that the sponsor can assess a potential signal promptly and act if warranted.
The participant still has to be treated. A drug may need to be interrupted, a dose adjusted, a concomitant medication prescribed. Clinical judgment guides those decisions, though protocols typically provide guidance on dose modification and stopping rules.

text:
23.2 Sponsor Responsibilities
A sponsor sees what no single site can: safety information from every site and every participant lands in one place. Figure 23.1 traces the path from an event at the site to a report at the regulator.

The sponsor must decide whether an incoming SAE report triggers expedited reporting. Fatal or life-threatening SUSARs must be reported within 7 calendar days, with as complete a report as possible following within a further 8 days (15 days in total); other SUSARs must be reported within 15 calendar days (International Council for Harmonisation 1994). They go to regulatory authorities in every country where the study is being conducted.
Information also has to travel back down. A newly identified risk, a pattern of adverse events, or a change in the benefit-risk assessment prompts a safety report that goes to every investigator on the study.
Once a year the aggregate picture is compiled into a Development Safety Update Report (DSUR) and submitted to regulatory authorities (International Council for Harmonisation 2010), covering the drug’s safety profile across all ongoing studies.

title: 23  Safety Monitoring and Reporting
text:
23.3 Safety Data Management and Analysis
Every SAE lives in two places: the clinical database, which holds all trial data, and the safety database, which holds distinct pharmacovigilance records for SAEs. Reconciling the two is a critical quality control step, and Figure 23.2 shows how it runs.






flowchart LR
    Plan[Recon Plan] --> GenSafety[Safety DB<br/>SAE Report]
    Plan --> GenClinical[Clinical DB<br/>AE Listing]
    
    GenSafety --> Compare{Compare}
    GenClinical --> Compare
    
    Compare -->|Discrepancies| Query[Query]
    Compare -->|Reconciled| Done["Reconciled;<br/>document & close"]
    Query --> Site[Site<br/>Resolution]

    Site --> UpdateSafety[Update<br/>Safety]
    Site --> UpdateClinical[Update<br/>Clinical]

    UpdateSafety --> Compare
    UpdateClinical --> Compare

    classDef process fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#7b1fa2,stroke-width:1px
    classDef decision fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#f57c00,stroke-width:2px

    class Plan,GenSafety,GenClinical,Query,Site,UpdateSafety,UpdateClinical,Done process
    class Compare decision




Figure 23.2: Reconciliation Process between Clinical and Safety Databases






Analyzing Laboratory Safety Data
A laboratory adverse event is often just a number moving, with no symptom to announce it. The analysis has to go looking. Treatment-Emergent Abnormal Values (TEAVs) pick out patients who moved from a normal baseline to an abnormal post-treatment state. Shift tables (typically 3x3 matrices of patient status, e.g., Low, Normal, High, before versus after treatment) show where a population moved as a whole. Clinically significant changes flag values past a defined threshold, such as >3x Upper Limit of Normal for liver enzymes, where the concern is organ toxicity.

23  Safety Monitoring and Reporting

title: 23  Safety Monitoring and Reporting
text:
23.4 Signal Detection
A safety signal is a potential drug-safety risk that warrants further investigation. The simplest way to find one is to count: if headache occurs in 30% of patients on drug and 10% on placebo, this suggests a drug effect. But many adverse events are tracked at once, so some of those gaps open by chance: frequency-based methods treat an unadjusted difference as a flag for closer review rather than proof of harm, and while adjusting for multiple comparisons limits false alarms, the greater concern in safety analysis is usually missing a real signal (International Council for Harmonisation 1998).
Counting alone misses a good deal. Pattern recognition looks past raw frequencies at the shape of the data: a cluster of similar events, events concentrated at a particular dose, or events emerging only after prolonged treatment may suggest a drug effect when no individual rate is statistically significant. Disproportionality analysis, run on databases of spontaneous reports, asks whether an event makes up a larger share of one drug’s reports than of the reports for all other drugs: if liver injury is reported disproportionately often for a drug, that warrants attention, though a reporting ratio is not an incidence rate (European Medicines Agency 2017). A single case can also carry the argument: a rare event occurring shortly after drug administration in an otherwise healthy patient may be drug-related on its own, which is what individual case assessment is for.
Modern pharmacovigilance increasingly applies data mining and machine learning to large databases, though human judgment remains essential for assessing clinical significance.
For trials involving serious conditions, significant risks, or large participant populations, an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) reviews unblinded accumulating data at predetermined intervals and may recommend stopping a trial early for safety, futility, or overwhelming efficacy. Its composition, charter, and operating procedure are covered in Section 9.6 and Chapter 22.
crumbs: Part III: Phase III Deep Dive
23  Safety Monitoring and Reporting

title: 23  Safety Monitoring and Reporting
text:
23.5 Regulatory Reporting Requirements
The obligations are largely harmonized across major markets, but each jurisdiction has its own legal instrument and reporting channel. In the United States, expedited IND safety reports are governed by 21 CFR 312.32 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024): sponsors must send an IND safety report to the FDA and all participating investigators as soon as possible and no later than 15 calendar days after determining that the information qualifies, which covers SUSARs but also findings from other studies or from animal or in vitro testing that suggest a significant risk, and any clinically important increase in the rate of a serious suspected adverse reaction. An unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction must also reach the FDA within 7 calendar days of the sponsor’s initial receipt of the information, and relevant follow-up information is submitted as soon as it is available. The European Union imposes parallel obligations through the Clinical Trials Regulation and its associated guidelines (European Medicines Agency 2022), with the EudraVigilance database centralizing safety reporting across member states. Beneath both regimes sit the ICH E2A and E2B guidelines (International Council for Harmonisation 1994, 2013), which supply the harmonized safety definitions and the electronic transmission standards that let a single report move between systems.
Inadequate or late safety reporting can trigger clinical holds and warning letters, and, for egregious violations, criminal penalties.

title: 23  Safety Monitoring and Reporting
text:
23.6 The Benefit-Risk Calculation
A drug for a minor condition that causes serious adverse events may be unacceptable. The same drug for a life-threatening condition with no alternatives may be essential. The benefit-risk calculation interprets safety data in the context of the disease being treated and the benefits on offer, a considered judgment made by regulators but also by individual patients and their physicians.
Under its PDUFA V commitments the FDA adopted a structured Benefit-Risk Framework, now used to organize the review of every new drug and biologic across four dimensions: Analysis of Condition, Current Treatment Options, Benefit, and Risk and Risk Management (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023). The framework does not reduce the decision to a score; it disciplines the reasoning, making explicit what is known, what is uncertain, and how identified risks will be managed. The European Medicines Agency pursues the same end through its PrOACT-URL approach and an effects table that lays favorable and unfavorable effects side by side.
The calculation is never final. As more patients receive a drug and follow-up lengthens, a risk that seemed acceptable early in development may prove unacceptable once the magnitude or nature of the harm is better understood. AI approaches to pharmacovigilance signal detection, aggregate case review, and benefit-risk visualization are covered in Chapter 26.

title: 24  Essential Documents and the Trial Master File
text:
24.1 Critical Essential Documents
When an FDA inspector arrives at a clinical trial site, they do not re-run the study. They interview patients, who have long since completed their participation, generally only when they suspect serious problems (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2020). They cannot observe the blood draws, the physical exams, or the conversations between investigators and participants. What they can do is examine the paper trail: the carefully maintained documentation that reconstructs how the trial was conducted.
This is why documentation matters: in clinical research, the record is the trial. A consent form signed and dated before procedures began documents that informed consent was obtained. A delegation log with training records shows that the person drawing blood was qualified, and a temperature log that the investigational product was stored correctly. Without these documents, there is no evidence that the trial was conducted properly. Without that evidence, the data cannot be trusted.
ICH E6(R2) Section 8.1 defines essential documents as those that “individually and collectively permit evaluation of the conduct of a trial and the quality of the data produced” (International Council for Harmonisation 2016). They serve operational purposes during the trial and evidentiary purposes afterward, spanning a lifecycle that runs from pre-trial preparations through active data recording and safety monitoring to final reconciliation and archiving.
In 2025, ICH E6(R3) restructured this material as essential records in Appendix C. Where E6(R2) Section 8 prescribed a minimum list, which could be supplemented or, where justified before the trial began, reduced (International Council for Harmonisation 2016), E6(R3) defines essential records more broadly, as the documents and data, in any format, that permit evaluation of the trial’s conduct and the reliability of its results, and asks sponsors and investigators to judge on risk-proportionate grounds which records are essential for a given trial. The individual files keep their names and purposes; what changes is the emphasis, as E6(R3) ties the essential record set more explicitly to the trial’s design and risks (International Council for Harmonisation 2025).
The sponsor manages the Trial Master File (TMF), the repository of the sponsor’s study-wide and site-specific essential documents, now increasingly electronic for real-time tracking and secure global access. Each clinical site keeps its own Investigator Site File (ISF) covering its conduct of the trial. Sponsors increasingly offer electronic site files (eISF) to streamline this, but the investigator remains personally responsible for the ISF’s completeness and accuracy, whether digital or physical.
Table 24.1 lists documents that draw particular scrutiny during inspections, where each is held, and what inspectors look for.
Under 21 CFR Part 54 (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b), sponsors must collect and, in the marketing application, disclose (or certify the absence of) the relevant financial interests of each clinical investigator in a covered clinical study, including those of a spouse or dependent child: compensation tied to the study outcome, a proprietary interest in the tested product, significant equity (more than $50,000 in a publicly traded sponsor, or any equity in a privately held one), and other significant payments exceeding $25,000 beyond the costs of conducting the study, tracked during the trial and for one year after it ends. The requirement does not forbid such interests; it makes them visible, so that reviewers can judge whether a conflict might have biased the trial’s conduct or interpretation.

title: 24  Essential Documents and the Trial Master File
text:
24.2 The Quality Standard: ALCOA++
A blood pressure reading without a signature and date is useless; an adverse event narrative without an author cannot be verified. ALCOA is the shorthand for the properties that make a clinical trial record trustworthy. Chapter 21 tabulates the base ALCOA principles in Table 21.1 and describes the ALCOA+ and ALCOA++ extensions.
Each record must be attributable: it must be clear who created it, when, and under what circumstances. Records must be legible, readable and intelligible years later to anyone who needs to review them. They must be contemporaneous, created at the time the activity occurred rather than reconstructed from memory days or weeks afterward, and original, the first capture of the data, or a certified copy that preserves its content and context, rather than a transcription that might introduce errors (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024c). And they must be accurate, truthfully reflecting what actually happened.
ALCOA+ and then ALCOA++ added requirements aimed at electronic systems and long-term data integrity. Records must be complete, with no missing fields, unexplained gaps, or deleted entries; consistent, following the same format and logic across the trial; and available, retrievable for review or inspection when needed. They must also be enduring, readable throughout the required retention period, which is a challenge when file formats and storage media become obsolete. The second plus adds traceable: every value can be followed through its full lifecycle, with audit trails documenting any change.

title: 24  Essential Documents and the Trial Master File
text:
24.3 TMF Management and Oversight
A trial generates documents continuously (protocols are amended, investigators added, IRB approvals renewed, monitoring visits conducted, safety events reported), and each must reach the right file within a reasonable timeframe. Targets vary by document type and organization; a sponsor SOP might call for filing within 5-10 business days of receipt or creation, a target that is easily missed when trial teams are stretched thin.
An inspector asks to see “the informed consent form for patient 101-005 at the time of their third visit” and expects an answer within minutes. A well-organized ISF can produce the signed form, and the TMF the version the ethics committee had approved by then. The TMF Reference Model provides a standardized taxonomy for organizing TMF documents, defining zones (such as Trial Management, Regulatory, and Site Management), sections within each zone, and specific artifact types within each section. Originally convened under the Drug Information Association, the model has been stewarded by CDISC since 2022 (TMF Reference Model Initiative 2024).
TMF health metrics track whether the file is complete and current: typically filing lag (average time from document creation to filing), completeness rate (percentage of expected documents actually present), and quality score (percentage of documents passing quality review without issues). Sponsors set targets, perhaps 95% completeness and 90% quality. Sites that fall behind receive additional attention, and persistent deficiencies may trigger for-cause audits.
During site visits, monitors verify that the Investigator Site File holds every required document in its current version, signed and dated where required. They also reconcile the site file against the sponsor’s central TMF. Deficiencies noted in a monitoring report become action items that must be resolved before the next visit.
Missing essential documents can hold up database lock when the gaps bear on participant safety or the reliability of the data, a problem that can delay regulatory submissions by months when discovered late. Inspectors who find disorganized or incomplete TMFs may question the overall quality of trial conduct, and in extreme cases regulators can refuse to rely on a trial’s data when the TMF cannot demonstrate that it was conducted according to GCP.

title: 24  Essential Documents and the Trial Master File
text:
24.4 Archiving and Retention
The commitment to documentation does not end when the last patient leaves or the final report is signed, and retention periods are set by regional regulation rather than by any single global rule. In the United States, FDA 21 CFR 312.57(c) requires sponsors to keep records for two years after a marketing application for the drug is approved or, if none is approved, for two years after investigational shipment and delivery stop and FDA is notified, while 312.62(c) runs an investigator’s two years from approval for the indication under investigation or, failing that, from discontinuation of the investigation with FDA notified; the EU Clinical Trials Regulation (536/2014, Article 58) requires the trial master file to be archived for at least 25 years after the trial ends; and ICH E6(R3) defers to the applicable regional requirement, adding that investigators should keep their records until the sponsor says they are no longer needed, if that is later. Because a global trial must satisfy the strictest jurisdiction, sponsors commonly adopt a single retention policy sized to the longest applicable period, which for a trial with EU sites means at least 25 years (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a; European Medicines Agency 2022; International Council for Harmonisation 2025).
The investigator is responsible for site record retention, the sponsor for the overall TMF. Investigators have faced regulatory action years after their trials concluded, when inspectors discovered that site files had been improperly destroyed or were incomplete.
A large Phase III trial generates tens of thousands of pages across dozens of sites. Monitors spend substantial portions of their visits reviewing regulatory binders, and study coordinators give hours each week to filing, organizing, and reconciling documents. Electronic systems have improved efficiency without eliminating the burden: documents still must be created, reviewed, signed, filed, and retained.
The principle underneath is simple: in clinical research, the documentation is the proof. If a procedure was performed but not documented, regulators will question whether it occurred. If consent was obtained but the form is unsigned, the enrollment is problematic. Contemporaneous, complete, and accurate documentation is the foundation on which the credibility of clinical evidence rests.

title: 25  Clinical Trial IT Infrastructure
text:
25.1 The Modern Clinical Trial Ecosystem
A decade ago, sponsors managed clinical data through a patchwork of vendor systems that rarely communicated: EDC databases that could not talk to randomization systems, trial master files stored in SharePoint folders with manual indexing, and clinical trial management systems that required spreadsheet reconciliation to produce accurate enrollment counts. Data flowed through exports, imports, and emails, and every handoff added latency, transcription errors, and audit risk.
What replaced it is the subject of this chapter: the four systems that now form the transactional backbone of a trial, Electronic Data Capture (EDC), Clinical Trial Management Systems (CTMS), electronic Trial Master Files (eTMF), and Randomization and Trial Supply Management (RTSM), plus the platform market shaping them and the regulatory framework (21 CFR Part 11, EMA’s guideline on computerized systems in clinical trials, GMP Annex 11, and ICH E6) that governs computerized systems in clinical research.
These platforms determine what data a trial can capture and integrate, and whether their records hang together decides whether it is inspection-ready. They are also the substrate for the AI and automation tools discussed in Chapter 26: without validated, well-integrated core systems, advanced analytics and agentic automation have nothing reliable to operate on. Technology can reduce friction and surface risks earlier. What makes it defensible in an inspection is validation, governance, and oversight.
Today’s leading platforms aspire to unified architectures where patient data, operational metrics, essential documents, and supply chain signals flow through shared data models. In the best-integrated environments, particularly single-vendor platforms like Veeva Vault, a single site action can cascade through the whole stack: randomize a patient and enrollment counts update in CTMS dashboards, treatment-specific CRF pages unlock in the EDC, drug shipment requests trigger in the supply management system, and expected document checklists populate in the eTMF. Many sponsors do not work in that environment. They still run heterogeneous stacks with systems from multiple vendors, connected through middleware and custom integrations that require configuration, maintenance, and periodic reconciliation. How far the integration goes varies widely from one organization to the next, but the direction of travel is the same: fewer manual handoffs, and the shared data infrastructure on which analytics and automation depend.

Figure 25.1: The Modern Clinical Trial Technology Stack





Electronic Data Capture (EDC) replaces paper case report forms with validated electronic forms that capture patient data at the point of care. When a coordinator records a blood pressure reading, administers a questionnaire, or documents an adverse event, that data flows into the EDC. Built-in edit checks flag impossible values (a heart rate of 500?) or logical inconsistencies (an adverse event dated before the patient enrolled) in real-time, catching errors before they propagate. Every efficacy and safety analysis in the submission traces back to data captured here (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023).
Clinical Trial Management System (CTMS) is the operational command center. Where EDC holds patient data, CTMS holds the state of the trial: which sites are open, how many patients each has enrolled, when the next milestone or monitoring visit falls due, what the budget burn rate looks like. It manages contracts and payments, and it generates the operational metrics sponsors use to assess trial health (Grand View Research 2025). It is what keeps a 50-site, 14-country trial from descending into chaos.
Electronic Trial Master File (eTMF) is the regulatory archive. A single trial generates thousands of documents: the protocol and its amendments, informed consent forms, IRB approvals, investigator CVs, monitoring reports, safety letters, correspondence. Regulators require sponsors to maintain a complete Trial Master File as evidence that the trial was conducted properly, and eTMF systems organize it according to the TMF Reference Model (originally convened under DIA, now stewarded by CDISC), tracking document completeness and inspection readiness (TMF Reference Model Initiative 2024). When an FDA inspector arrives, the eTMF is the first artifact they examine.
Randomization and Trial Supply Management (RTSM), sometimes called Interactive Response Technology (IRT), handles treatment assignment and drug supply. When a patient is eligible for randomization, the RTSM system assigns them to a treatment arm according to the randomization scheme, maintaining the blind while ensuring balanced allocation. At the same time it tracks investigational product inventory at each site and triggers resupply shipments. For trials with temperature-sensitive biologics or personalized therapies, RTSM is mission-critical (Clinical Leader 2024).
The four exchange data continuously. Complete a monitoring visit and the report is filed in eTMF while the visit status updates in CTMS. That constant traffic is why unified platforms like Veeva Vault, which house all four systems in a single architecture, have gained so much traction (Veeva Systems 2024b).

title: 25  Clinical Trial IT Infrastructure
text:
25.3 Regulatory Framework for Computerized Systems
Every computerized system in a trial, from a validated EDC platform to an AI-enabled document classifier, operates inside a regulatory framework that dictates how it must be validated, documented, and overseen. What an inspector expects to see as evidence depends on which tier of that framework a requirement sits in.

Enforceable Standards vs. Recommendations
Failure to comply with an enforceable requirement can result in warning letters, clinical holds, or rejection of a submission. Guidance documents represent FDA or EMA “current thinking” and are generally recommendations, not mandates, though departing from them without justification invites scrutiny. An exception is FDA guidance issued under section 745A(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, such as the standardized study data guidance, which binds sponsors to the electronic submission formats it specifies (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021). Validation and Documentation Requirements
AI systems and computerized systems used in clinical trials must meet the same validation requirements as any other regulated software. Which standards apply depends on the regulatory jurisdiction and the system’s role: 21 CFR Part 11 in the United States; in the EU, EMA’s 2023 guideline on computerized systems and electronic data in clinical trials, with GMP Annex 11 governing systems used in manufacturing (see Table 25.5). Both jurisdictions require that computerized systems generating, modifying, or storing electronic records that FDA or EU regulations require sponsors to maintain or submit meet validation and control standards (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023, 2024; European Medicines Agency 2023; European Commission 2011). In practice that means documented evidence that the software performs as intended, AI model verification included; computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails recording every system action that creates, modifies, or deletes an electronic record; unique user identification, authentication, and role-based permissions; controls that keep data attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, and accurate (ALCOA); and documented procedures for system use, maintenance, and change control.
ICH E6(R3), adopted in January 2025, adds computerized systems requirements that bear directly on AI (International Council for Harmonisation 2025). A system must be validated as fit for the specific use it is put to in the trial, and the validation effort is expected to be proportional to the system’s impact on patient safety and data reliability. A dedicated data governance section requires documented data and records management, and the guideline recognizes data from wearables, sensors, and automated systems as primary source data.

title: 26  AI Agents in Clinical Development
text:
26.1 Agentic AI in Clinical Workflows
Agents can draft text. Whether one runs inside a trial turns on something else: can it operate within a regulated environment at all, preserving data integrity, producing audit-ready traces, and remaining under accountable human oversight? The 2024 EMA reflection paper on AI and risk-based approaches for AI use in drug development formalizes that expectation (Unlearn.AI 2025; European Medicines Agency 2024; National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023; Amershi et al. 2019).
Clinical trials run on a layered digital infrastructure: the core transactional systems the previous chapter described (EDC, CTMS, eTMF, RTSM), integration middleware, and the analytics and automation services that continuously convert operational events into risk signals and decisions. Cloud adoption and regulatory acceptance of technology-enabled trial conduct, including decentralized elements and digital health technologies for remote data acquisition, have accelerated the shift toward that model (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024, 2023c). This chapter takes up that top layer, along with the methodological approaches changing how trials are designed and how evidence is generated.
The transition is conceptual as much as technological: from automation as a feature (dashboards, rules engines, isolated machine-learning models) to automation as an operating model, in which software agents can plan, execute, and verify multi-step workflows across the clinical operations stack. This shifts the trial from a linear “pipeline” towards a dynamic, electronic map of activities, where information infrastructure identifies bottlenecks and navigates the “diverse web of failure-prone iterative learning loops” that characterize modern drug development (Wagner et al. 2018). “Agentic AI” here is a design pattern: “compound” systems that combine models with retrieval, tools, and control logic, grounded in computer science work on “generative agents” that simulate human-like behavior and goal-directed action (Park et al. 2023; Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research 2024). Preliminary findings from 2024-2025 benchmarks suggest agentic systems can improve clinical task performance by up to 60 percentage points over base language models in specific tasks such as evidence retrieval and task planning, though most improvements are more modest and results vary considerably by task and study design (Abou Ali, Dornaika, and Charafeddine 2026). The same shift converges with Digital Twin “Moonshots”, which aim to integrate personalized digital twins directly into medical records to optimize both clinical care and trial participation (Duke Center for Virtual Imaging Trials 2024).
The money has moved accordingly. The clinical trial software market was estimated at about USD 11 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of about 11% through 2033 (Grand View Research 2025), with AI applications growing rapidly within it (Fortune Business Insights 2024). None of that is evidence of clinical benefit on its own, but it explains why sponsors, CROs, and platform vendors are reorganizing workflows around automation and AI-mediated operations.
Pull the right protocol amendment from an eTMF. Verify whether a site has an updated IRB approval. Check that a safety narrative is consistent with the underlying case data. Each of these is a retrieval and verification problem under audit constraints, not a “creative writing” task, and none of them is settled by calling a model once.

title: 26  AI Agents in Clinical Development
text:
Building Blocks and System Architecture
The recent resurgence of “agents” is a systems shift. Agentic systems orchestrate multiple calls, state, and tools to complete a task, decomposing goals, retrieving context, taking actions, and iterating on feedback (Cheng et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024). On the Berkeley AI Research account of “compound AI systems,” reliability gains often come from engineered compositions (retrievers, checkers, constrained tool calls, repeated sampling) rather than from a single monolithic model invocation (Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research 2024).
Three technical ideas recur. Structured intermediate reasoning, such as chain-of-thought prompting, can improve performance on complex tasks, though it does not guarantee correctness in the presence of missing or stale information (Wei et al. 2022). Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) externalizes “memory” into a maintained knowledge base and, when paired with citations to retrieved sources, can supply provenance (Lewis et al. 2020; Douze et al. 2024). Coupling reasoning with tool use, where a model decides when to query, calculate, or fetch, also yields more controllable trajectories than purely generative text (Yao et al. 2023).
Agents also need consistent interfaces to external systems, and tool calling standards such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) aim to standardize how AI applications connect to data sources and actions, turning “integration” into a first-class design surface (Anthropic 2025). In regulated contexts the payoff is not novelty; it is enforceable access controls, a log of every tool invocation, and agent actions a reviewer can follow.
Clinical workflows are naturally multi-role (data management, monitoring, safety, regulatory, sites), and multi-agent frameworks formalize that by allocating roles and coordinating conversations among specialized agents (Wu et al. 2023). Empirical analyses, however, show that such systems fail in predictable ways: specification gaps, coordination failures, and weak verification loops (Cemri et al. 2025). “Agent quality” therefore has to be measured on cost, robustness, and reproducibility alongside task accuracy (Kapoor et al. 2024), which is where evaluation is heading: benchmarks now emphasize realistic multi-step work with tool use and resource constraints, and propose clearer reporting of cost and reproducibility (Chan et al. 2024; Cappello et al. 2025). Human-in-the-loop debugging and steering tools are emerging so that multi-step traces can be inspected and edited (Epperson et al. 2025).
Run agents concurrently across several workflows and the operational concerns become first-order: context windows turn into a managed resource, tools must be scheduled and access-controlled, and traces must be stored in an auditable way. Emerging “agent runtime” proposals make this explicit by separating agent applications from shared services such as scheduling, context management, and access control (Mei et al. 2024). Pipeline frameworks that treat agent workflows as composable graphs add systematic optimization and regression testing across versions, which matters in any environment where changes must be validated rather than “shipped and hoped” (Khattab et al. 2023).
One risk remains whatever the architecture. Agentic systems can create an illusion of competence, in which fluent outputs are mistaken for validated decisions: a known socio-technical risk in scientific work, where productivity gains may coexist with a decline in genuine understanding and critical scrutiny (Messeri and Crockett 2024). Human-AI interaction guidelines answer it by making uncertainty visible, supporting oversight and correction, and ensuring users understand system limitations, principles that map directly to quality management and inspection readiness (Amershi et al. 2019).

section: 26.2 Regulatory Framework for AI in Clinical Trials
text:
26.2 Regulatory Framework for AI in Clinical Trials
Most of what FDA and EMA have said about AI in drug development is guidance: influential, expected of sponsors, and not legally binding. One AI-specific instrument in this section is law, and it is not a medicines regulation at all. The validation and documentation requirements for computerized systems (21 CFR Part 11, EMA’s computerized-systems guideline, Annex 11, ICH E6) are covered in Chapter 25.

The 10 Guiding Principles for Good AI Practice
In January 2026, FDA (CDER and CBER) and EMA jointly published Guiding Principles of Good AI Practice in Drug Development, the first joint regulatory statement establishing foundational expectations for AI across the drug product lifecycle (U.S. Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency 2026). The ten principles represent international consensus on what “good practice” means here.






NoteJoint FDA-EMA Guiding Principles (January 2026)



The following is quoted verbatim from the joint FDA-EMA document:

Human-centric by design The development and use of AI technologies align with ethical and human-centric values.
Risk-based approach The development and use of AI technologies follow a risk-based approach with proportionate validation, risk mitigation, and oversight based on the context of use and determined model risk.
Adherence to standards AI technologies adhere to relevant legal, ethical, technical, scientific, cybersecurity, and regulatory standards, including Good Practices (GxP).
Clear context of use AI technologies have a well-defined context of use (role and scope for why it is being used).
Multidisciplinary expertise Multidisciplinary expertise covering both the AI technology and its context of use are integrated throughout the technology’s life cycle.
Data governance and documentation Data source provenance, processing steps, and analytical decisions are documented in a detailed, traceable, and verifiable manner, in line with GxP requirements. Appropriate governance, including privacy and protection for sensitive data, is maintained throughout the technology’s life cycle.
Model design and development practices The development of AI technologies follows best practices in model and system design and software engineering and leverages data that is fit-for-use, considering interpretability, explainability, and predictive performance. Good model and system development promotes transparency, reliability, generalizability, and robustness for AI technologies contributing to patient safety.
Risk-based performance assessment Risk-based performance assessments evaluate the complete system including human-AI interactions, using fit-for-use data and metrics appropriate for the intended context of use, supported by validation of predictive performance through appropriately designed testing and evaluation methods.
Life cycle management Risk-based quality management systems are implemented throughout the AI technologies’ life cycles, including to support capturing, assessing, and addressing issues. The AI technologies undergo scheduled monitoring and periodic re-evaluation to ensure adequate performance (e.g., to address data drift).
Clear, essential information Plain language is used to present clear, accessible, and contextually relevant information to the intended audience, including users and patients, regarding the AI technology’s context of use, performance, limitations, underlying data, updates, and interpretability or explainability.



All ten operationalize one expectation: AI in drug development must be validated, documented, and maintained with the same rigor as any other regulated activity, plus extra attention to what makes AI different, its data-dependency, its potential opacity, and its tendency to drift over time.


The FDA Risk-Based Credibility Framework
FDA’s January 2025 draft guidance “Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence to Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products” (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025) sets out a seven-step risk-based framework and, though still a draft, represents FDA’s expected approach for evaluating AI-generated evidence.






ImportantScope of FDA AI Guidance



The FDA guidance applies when AI is used to produce information or data intended to support regulatory decision-making regarding safety, effectiveness, or quality. It does not apply to AI used in drug discovery (the in-scope drug product life cycle begins at nonclinical development, so not all pre-IND work is excluded), nor to AI used purely for operational efficiencies such as internal workflows and resource allocation that do not impact patient safety, drug quality, or study reliability.


The Seven-Step Credibility Assessment Process:

Define the Question of Interest: What specific question, decision, or concern is the AI model addressing?
Define the Context of Use (COU): What is the specific role and scope of the AI model? Will other evidence be used alongside it?
Assess Model Risk: Combine model influence (contribution of AI evidence relative to other evidence) with decision consequence (significance of adverse outcomes from incorrect decisions). See Figure 26.1 for how common AI applications map onto this two-dimensional risk space.
Develop a Credibility Assessment Plan: Document model architecture, training data, evaluation methods, and performance metrics, with rigor proportional to model risk.
Execute the Plan: Implement the credibility assessment activities.
Document Results: Prepare a credibility assessment report with any deviations from the plan.
Determine Adequacy: Evaluate whether model credibility is sufficient for the COU.

WarningCritical Principle: Human Accountability Cannot Be Delegated to AI



Under ICH E6 GCP and FDA regulations, the investigator is responsible for medical decisions affecting trial participants, and the sponsor is responsible for trial conduct and data integrity. AI can support these decisions but cannot replace the accountable human. An investigator cannot defend a protocol deviation by stating “the AI said it was acceptable.”




AI Model Lifecycle Maintenance
Unlike static software, AI models may degrade or drift over time as input data distributions change. Both FDA and EMA guidance therefore expect lifecycle maintenance for models deployed over extended periods: in manufacturing (quality control, process optimization), in pharmacovigilance (case classification, signal detection), and in any AI system whose performance may change as new data arrives. Five activities make it up.

Performance monitoring: Define metrics and thresholds; monitor on risk-based frequency.
Drift detection: Identify when input data diverges from training data distribution.
Revalidation triggers: Pre-define conditions requiring model retesting or retraining.
Change management: Evaluate model changes through the applicable change-control process (for manufacturing models, the pharmaceutical quality system).
Regulatory notification: Report changes impacting model performance per applicable requirements (e.g., 21 CFR 314.70 for manufacturing changes under an approved NDA).







TipEMA on Incremental Learning



For pharmacovigilance applications, EMA permits a “more flexible approach” where incremental learning can continuously enhance models. However, the MAH retains responsibility to validate, monitor, and document model performance as part of the pharmacovigilance system.




When to Engage Regulators

EMA-Specific Considerations
The EMA reflection paper (September 2024) introduces terminology that differs somewhat from FDA’s. It sorts applications by high patient risk, meaning AI uses affecting patient safety such as dosing or treatment assignment, and by high regulatory impact, meaning AI uses substantially affecting regulatory decisions such as primary endpoint analysis. The rigor of the credibility assessment should be proportional to both. Five positions follow from that framing.

Transparent models preferred: “The use of transparent models is preferred” to strengthen accountability. Black box models may be acceptable if transparent models show unsatisfactory performance, with additional documentation and monitoring requirements.
Frozen models for pivotal trials: “Prior to the database lock and subsequent unblinding…the data pre-processing pipeline and all models should be frozen and documented in a traceable manner in the statistical analysis plan.”
Prospective validation for high-impact uses: “Prior to model deployment in high regulatory impact settings, such as in relation to the primary endpoint, performance should be tested with prospectively generated data (future calendar time) that is acquired in a setting or population representative of the intended context of use.”
No incremental learning in pivotal trials: “Incremental learning approaches are not accepted, and any modification of the model during the trial requires a regulatory interaction.”
Human-in-the-loop for precision medicine: AI-driven indication or posology recommendations are “high patient risk as well as high regulatory impact” and require “fall-back treatment strategies in cases of technical failure.”



The EU AI Act
This is the instrument that is law. The European Union’s AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024) is the first comprehensive, binding AI statute, and it applies horizontally across sectors rather than being specific to medicines. Having entered into force in August 2024, it applies in phases: prohibitions on a narrow set of unacceptable-risk practices from February 2025, obligations for general-purpose AI models from August 2025, and the core obligations for high-risk systems originally due from August 2026, with a further tranche tied to regulated products (via the Medical Device Regulation and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation) from August 2027. The Digital Omnibus on AI, provisionally agreed in May 2026 and in force from 27 July 2026, deferred both high-risk tranches: standalone (Annex III) systems now apply from 2 December 2027 and product-embedded (Annex I) systems from 2 August 2028. The Article 50 transparency obligations kept their 2 August 2026 start, except that providers of generative AI systems already on the market before that date have until 2 December 2026 to mark their outputs, in machine-readable form, as artificially generated (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2026).
Most AI used in trial operations (document filing, query triage, feasibility scoring) is not “high-risk” under the Act’s definitions, so its obligations are light: providers and deployers must take measures to support their staff’s AI literacy, and Article 50’s transparency duties apply only to particular functions, such as systems that interact directly with people or generate synthetic content (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024, 2026). AI that functions as, or is a safety component of, a regulated medical device can fall into the high-risk tier, inheriting obligations layered on top of the device regulations. The Act sits alongside, not in place of, the EMA reflection paper and the Clinical Trials Regulation, so sponsors running EU trials should assess where each AI application falls under its classification: a system treated as “decision support” under GCP may still trigger binding obligations under the Act.


Practical Implications: A Decision Framework

Summary: The Regulatory Bottom Line
Five things hold throughout. Human accountability for medical decisions and regulatory compliance cannot be delegated to AI; investigators, sponsors, and MAHs retain responsibility. Rigor of validation, documentation, and oversight should scale with model risk, which combines decision consequence and model influence. In pivotal trials, EMA expects the data pipeline and every model used for confirmatory analysis to be frozen and documented in the statistical analysis plan before database lock and unblinding; non-prespecified changes made after the data are opened make the results post hoc, unsuitable as confirmatory evidence (European Medicines Agency 2024). Models that keep operating over time, in manufacturing and pharmacovigilance, need performance monitoring, drift detection, and change management. For high-risk applications, early consultation with FDA or EMA aligns expectations before a late-stage objection becomes expensive.

Faro Health exemplifies the approach. Instead of writing a static Word document, study teams design the trial in a structured cloud platform. The AI scores the complexity of the schedule of assessments against real-world data to predict operational burden, shows the team which visits pile too many procedures onto one patient, and then generates the protocol document and Schedule of Activities from the structured design (Faro Health 2024).
Phesi takes simulation further, drawing on data from over 100 million patients to model trial outcomes before the protocol is finalized. Their Digital Patient Profile reduces the likelihood of the “zero-enrollment site” problem mentioned in Chapter 18.

Finding the right patients remains the perennial bottleneck. Benchmarking studies suggest that recruitment and retention often take substantially longer and cost more than planned, and that each day of delay can be economically material for sponsors in some therapeutic areas (Lamberti et al. 2024; Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2025). Once data starts flowing, it must be cleaned, and wearables generate 1,000+ data points per patient per day. At that volume manual query resolution stops being sustainable. The emerging approach layers several AI techniques across the data pipeline, each suited to a different kind of quality problem; Table 26.5 profiles the leading tools.
Rule-based checks remain the foundation: programmed validations that flag impossible values (negative ages, dates in the future) or logical inconsistencies (randomization before consent). They are deterministic, fast, auditable, and well-understood.
Machine learning anomaly detection adds statistical pattern recognition. Models trained on historical trial data can identify unusual distributions, digit preferences suggestive of fabrication, or sites whose data patterns diverge from comparators, which means they surface problems nobody anticipated during study design.
Large language models (LLMs) parse the free-text fields, adverse event narratives, medical history, concomitant medication entries, for inconsistencies invisible to structured checks: a narrative describing “chest pain radiating to left arm” against a coded adverse event of “headache.”
Cross-domain validation checks EDC entries against central lab results, device uploads against visit schedules, and ePRO responses against clinical observations; discrepancies across domains often indicate transcription errors or protocol deviations.
The output is a set of automated actions: auto-generated queries with draft text for site response, risk flags that prioritize monitoring attention, trend alerts that surface site-level quality patterns, and quality reports for oversight review (Figure 26.5). title: 26  AI Agents in Clinical Development
text:
26.4 Emerging Methodologies and Operational Solutions
Innovation in clinical trials is not limited to software; it includes new methodological frameworks that use real-world data, federated learning, and digital simulations to rethink the evidence-generation process.

Solving Logistical Challenges with IT
Modern trials face significant logistical friction (see Section 20.6.1). The challenges are structural: supply chains that must deliver temperature-sensitive products to thousands of endpoints, sites overwhelmed by redundant data entry across disconnected systems, protocols too complex for manual compliance tracking, and global operations fragmented across time zones and organizations. These are coordination problems, and coordination problems respond to better information infrastructure, as Table 26.6 illustrates.
Supply chain complexity has intensified with decentralized trials and direct-to-patient distribution. Traditional approaches relied on spreadsheets and email to track inventory and shipments; delays were discovered after the fact. Modern systems integrate IoT sensors that monitor temperature, location, and chain of custody in real time. AI-based demand forecasting uses enrollment trajectories and visit schedules to predict resupply needs before stockouts occur. The result is reduced waste (fewer expired products) and fewer patient visits disrupted by supply failures.
Site burden accumulates when coordinators must enter the same data into multiple systems: pulling information from the electronic health record, transcribing it to the EDC, and reconciling discrepancies later. EHR-to-EDC integration automates the flow of structured data (lab values, vital signs, demographics) from the source system to the trial database, reducing transcription errors and freeing coordinator time for patient-facing work. This integration requires careful validation and mapping, but when implemented well, it addresses one of the most persistent complaints from clinical sites.
Protocol deviations often result from complexity: too many visits, too many procedures, too many eligibility criteria for staff to track manually. Real-time nudge systems monitor visit windows and upcoming assessments, alerting coordinators before a deviation occurs rather than flagging it retrospectively. Detection systems analyze patterns across sites to identify systematic compliance failures that may indicate training gaps or protocol design problems.
Global operations compound all of these challenges. When a trial spans 25 countries, 80 sites, and multiple CRO partners, fragmented regional teams operating from different data sources create reconciliation overhead and conflicting reports. Unified command centers aggregate operational data into a single platform, providing consistent metrics, standardized escalation pathways, and a shared view of trial status across all stakeholders.

Novel Methodological Approaches
This section covers a set of approaches that challenge traditional assumptions about how evidence is generated and compared: using observational data to support decisions (RWE), using historical or synthetic comparators to reduce concurrent control enrollment, and using models to predict counterfactual outcomes. All remain subjects of active regulatory and scientific debate.
Clinical research data are fragmented across institutions, each with privacy regulations, competitive interests, and technical barriers to sharing. Federated learning addresses this by training models collaboratively without centralizing data: algorithms travel to data sources, train locally, and share only model updates (gradients or weights) rather than patient records. Owkin has applied federated learning to construct external control arms from real-world data distributed across hospital networks. Their 2025 publication in Nature Communications described the method, FedECA, and deployed it across cancer centers in France, Spain, and the United States without pooling patient data; the authors note that the shared updates could in theory still be exploited to recover patient information, and they tested differential privacy as a safeguard (Ogier du Terrail et al. 2025). The practical value is clearest in rare diseases and oncology, where recruiting concurrent controls may be infeasible or ethically questionable. However, the approach requires sophisticated infrastructure, standardized data formats across institutions, and careful attention to the comparability of patient populations.
Digital twin is borrowed from engineering, where virtual models of physical systems enable simulation and optimization (Laubenbacher, Sluka, and Glazier 2021). In clinical research the term means a computational model that predicts an individual patient’s disease trajectory under control conditions, based on baseline characteristics and historical data from similar patients (Sel et al. 2025; Ross et al. 2024).
Unlearn.AI’s PROCOVA methodology is the worked example. Models trained on historical patient data generate, for each enrolled patient, a prognostic score forecasting that patient’s likely outcome on the control arm; the score then enters the primary analysis as a baseline covariate, reducing residual variance and allowing smaller control groups while preserving unbiased treatment effect estimates and Type I error control (European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2022; Ross et al. 2024). The European Medicines Agency issued a favorable qualification opinion in September 2022 (European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2022), and FDA has acknowledged the methodology’s acceptability through regulatory interactions.
What EMA qualified was not “twin replaces a randomized patient.” It qualified PROCOVA as a covariate adjustment method, analogous to using baseline HbA1c or age as a covariate in an ANCOVA, except that the covariate is itself the forecast of a deep neural network trained on historical data. The randomized control arm is still required; what the method saves is sample size, not concurrent randomized controls.
A team evaluating PROCOVA therefore has one question to answer. Standard covariate adjustment using well-chosen baseline predictors (baseline disease score, amyloid level, MMSE) can achieve much of the same variance reduction without a machine learning model, so the value of PROCOVA turns on whether the deep neural network predicts the 18-month outcome better than those covariates do. Indication by indication, that is not settled.






ImportantAI in regulated trials: proprietary models require transparency



If the prognostic score driving the analysis comes from a proprietary black-box model, FDA and EMA cannot independently verify the model’s behavior, and sponsors cannot audit whether the prediction is stable across the training data and population. Any AI or machine learning model used as part of a primary statistical analysis in a regulated trial should be written down in enough detail that a third party can reprogram it from the specification and improve it as new data emerge. A score delivered without the model behind it is a governance risk even when regulators have accepted the method class, because acceptance of a method class is not acceptance of any specific model implementation.




Real-World Evidence and Regulatory Considerations
The randomized controlled trial remains the gold standard for establishing causal treatment effects, but real-world evidence (RWE) is playing an expanding role in drug development and regulatory decision-making. Real-world data (RWD) is data on patient health and health care delivery collected routinely rather than for a traditional trial: electronic health records, claims databases, disease registries, wearable devices, and patient-generated data. Analyzed appropriately, in observational studies or within randomized designs such as pragmatic trials, it yields evidence about drug safety, effectiveness, and utilization patterns, and the distinction matters: RWD is the raw data, RWE the clinical evidence derived from it through rigorous analysis (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018).
For safety, RWE has long been used in post-marketing surveillance, detecting rare adverse events that trials were not powered to identify. For effectiveness, FDA acceptance is more cautious but expanding: the 21st Century Cures Act directed the agency to evaluate RWE for approving new indications for existing drugs and for satisfying post-marketing study requirements, and FDA’s 2023 final guidance on RWE for regulatory decisions emphasized that data relevance, reliability, and analytic rigor determine acceptability, not the mere existence of a large dataset (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023b).
Single-arm trials with external controls compare treated patients against matched historical or concurrent observational cohorts; they are most defensible in diseases with well-characterized natural history and no effective standard of care. Hybrid designs randomize a reduced control arm and borrow information from external data to increase statistical precision. Post-marketing effectiveness studies use RWD to ask whether efficacy demonstrated under controlled conditions survives contact with real-world populations carrying the comorbidities and concomitant medications that pivotal trials excluded.
The core challenge is confounding: in observational data, treatment selection is not random. Patients who receive a therapy may differ systematically from those who do not, and these differences, rather than the treatment itself, may explain observed outcomes. Propensity score methods, instrumental variables, and target trial emulation frameworks attempt to address confounding, but none can fully substitute for randomization. Unmeasured confounders remain a fundamental limitation.
Nonrandomized RWE is most credible when the outcome is objective and reliably captured in routine care, the comparison is against natural history rather than an active comparator, the patient population in the RWD source is demonstrably similar to the trial population, and sensitivity analyses show robustness to plausible unmeasured confounding. Even then, regulators typically treat such evidence as supportive rather than dispositive for efficacy claims: it strengthens a submission that already contains randomized evidence.
FDA’s 2023 draft guidance on externally controlled trials sets out how to build an external control arm from patient-level data from other clinical trials or from real-world data, addressing data quality, comparability, and bias mitigation (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a). It emphasizes that external controls are most appropriate when concurrent randomization is infeasible or unethical, and when the disease has a well-characterized natural history with reliable outcome measurement in routine care.
In 2020, FDA accepted a hybrid synthetic control arm (SCA) design for Medicenna Therapeutics’ planned Phase III trial in recurrent glioblastoma, a precedent-setting acceptance of a hybrid external control in a registrational trial for an indication that had previously relied on conventional randomized controls. In that design, matched external controls make up two-thirds of the pooled control arm, cutting prospective control enrollment by approximately two-thirds relative to conventional 1:1 randomization (Medicenna Therapeutics Corp. 2020; Medidata Solutions 2020).
An SCA constructs the external comparator from patient-level data in historical trials rather than recruiting new control patients. Medidata’s platform draws on a database spanning over 38,000 trials and 12 million patients to statistically match historical controls to current trial populations. The approach is most applicable in rare or life-threatening diseases with inadequate standard-of-care, where historical control data are plentiful and disease progression is well-characterized; hybrid designs, which add historical controls to a smaller concurrent control arm, are one way to extend it to later-stage trials.
Legitimate skepticism attaches to all of this, and it is specific. Verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ) remain incompletely standardized. A 2025 review in npj Digital Medicine called VVUQ frameworks essential for bringing digital twins into clinical practice, argued that VVUQ processes should be standardized as far as possible for quality assurance and risk management, and noted that continually updated digital twins pose a regulatory challenge that FDA’s existing medical-device framework does not fully address (Sel et al. 2025). Uncertainty is the piece most often underemphasized: the same review observes that uncertainty quantification is often lacking in modeling work, even though it is what attaches confidence bounds to a model’s predictions (Sel et al. 2025). A single predicted outcome per patient is therefore inadequate; a digital twin used as a counterfactual should report a distribution of plausible outcomes, not a point estimate.
Model opacity carries a cost that is easy to overlook. PROCOVA is a special case of classical ANCOVA: the adjustment covariate is a prognostic score from a model trained on independent historical data, in Unlearn’s implementation a proprietary machine-learning model (Ross et al. 2024; European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2022). EMA qualified the adjustment procedure but not any procedure for building that model, which leaves each sponsor to develop and validate the prognostic model for its own trial, and it expects sponsors to justify the advantage PROCOVA can attain over ANCOVA adjusting for individual covariates (European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2022). When model details are withheld, sponsors and regulators cannot interrogate, replicate, or improve the methodology, and EMA’s reflection paper on artificial intelligence in the medicinal product lifecycle expects models that influence regulatory decision-making to be fully documented, traceable, and open to independent assessment (European Medicines Agency 2024).
Data quality and completeness constrain all approaches. In oncology, the data needed to model tumor dynamics are often noisy, incomplete, and subject to collection burden (Venkatesh, Raza, and Kvedar 2022), and statistical models layer their own uncertainty on top, particularly when predictions must generalize across populations and disease subtypes.
Comparability assumptions underpin every external control approach. If the historical population differs systematically from the current trial population (because standard of care, patient selection, or measurement practices have changed), treatment effect estimates may be biased regardless of the sophistication of the matching algorithm.
In a JAMA Special Communication published online in October 2024 (January 2025 issue), then-FDA Commissioner Robert Califf and senior FDA officials listed digital twins that generate simulated clinical records to predict placebo-group response among the current and potential uses of AI in clinical research, alongside matching individuals to trials and harmonizing data cleaning, and called for flexible, risk-based regulatory schemes (Warraich, Tazbaz, and Califf 2025). FDA’s January 2025 draft guidance on AI in drug development makes that risk basis concrete: the oversight and credibility evidence expected for a model scale with its influence on a regulatory decision and the consequence of an incorrect decision, and operational uses that do not affect patient safety, drug quality, or the reliability of study results fall outside its scope (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025).
Opaque, proprietary methods may therefore face higher evidentiary bars than interpretable, well-documented ones, with sponsors expected to show statistical validity, model transparency, reproducibility, and appropriate characterization of uncertainty. 26.5 Future Impact and Economics
The technologies in this chapter bear on the cost drivers of clinical development: shorter cycle times, smaller samples, and less coordination labor, set against new operational complexity.

AI Impact on Trial Operations
Recall the economics from Chapter 6: $2.7 billion to bring a drug to market (Deloitte’s 2025 cohort), $40,000 per day to operate a Phase II/III trial, and, on average, roughly $800,000 per day in opportunity cost from delays, rising to $1.3-1.4 million per day in the most affected therapeutic areas (Z. P. Smith, DiMasi, and Getz 2024; Z. Smith, DiMasi, and Getz 2024; Deloitte Centre for Health Solutions 2026). AI-enabled tools are being applied to each of these cost drivers (see Table 26.8), though the realized impact depends on implementation quality, governance, and the specific operational context.
